en: Preface to the *Yishe* (Personal Reflections) on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra of the Great Buddha-Usnīsa*.

What is meant by "personal reflection"? I am ashamed of my superficial learning and lack of breadth in见闻 (jìnwén—what has been seen and heard). Desiring to engage with the Mahāyāna, I have extended these narrow views;
this is truly a discourse from my own breast and mind, and is certainly not a comprehensive or universal treatise. In private, I consider the intent of the Dharma...
Its depth is profound; how could those of small wisdom possibly fathom it? The Buddha-mind is unfathomable, and even those of the Three Vehicles can only perceive it vaguely.

Nevertheless, it does not hinder them from manifesting its essential form according to their respective knowledge, nor from each explaining the causes of the body through speech adapted to the inclinations of various directions.
It is because of the ocean of the *tathāgatagarbha* that its magnitude appears relative to one's perspective; yet for those who drink from it, the seawater does not become deep or shallow.
When the sun-wheel of wisdom is seen from either the east or the west, how could there be "self" or "other" in the reflection of the sun?

Thus, while those of the three vehicles equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths, each realizes the holy vehicle according to their respective capacity. While the ten realms together receive the single sound [of the Dharma],...
The attainment of benefit for both the noble and the ordinary truly depends upon the mind; how could it concern written words? Failure likewise rests with oneself;
it does not necessarily stem from others. If one can follow the finger to see the moon, once the moon is seen, one realizes that the moon does not reside in the finger.

If one awakens to the Way through hearing sounds, once the Way is awakened to, one understands that the Way is fundamentally not sound itself. To be deluded by oneself and pursue external objects is to turn every word one utters into error.
Transforming external objects into one’s own realization, whatever is taken up is entirely so. While reading the scriptures, I have had silent insights;
yet, as my understanding of their meaning remains insufficient, I venture to offer a few words of analysis. Where characters are ambiguous or erroneous, I briefly express my own views.

As I interpret and record these thoughts, I have compiled them into a volume and kept it in my private chambers, not yet daring to present it to others. Recently, while observing the summer retreat at Dongta, I have held discussions that further benefited my contemplation.

The various masters happened to see my private manuscript and resolved to carve it into woodblocks; though I tried to stop them, they would not desist. They have taken the initiative to propagate it themselves.
If it happens to accord with the truth, I shall use this to repay the Buddha’s kindness. For those who fabricate errors out of a lack of comprehensive wisdom, I offer my repentance.
At this time,
the Mid-Autumn Festival of the year Bingchen, the forty-fourth year of the Great Ming Wanli era,
the junior disciple of the thirty-second generation successor of the orthodox Cao-Dong lineage, the śramaṇa from Guyue Yunmen Xiansheng Temple.
*Annotated Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:
Personal Reflections by the Later Scholar, the Śramaṇa Zhànrán Yuánchéng of Xiǎnshèng Monastery in Kuāijī, Together with Preface.
Annotated by the Later Scholar, the Śramaṇa Zhànrán Yuánchéng of Xiǎnshèng Monastery in Kuāijī.
A visitor asked about the title of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. He said: "Some explain the single character 'Da' (Great) as Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle;

others explain it as Essence, Attribute, and Function regarding the 'Great Buddha-Ushṇīṣa. Which of these two is correct? I replied: "Essence, Attribute, and Function together explain the single character 'Da.
For Essence is Great, Attribute is Great, and Function is Great. Essence is precisely the meaning of Emptiness, because the true essence is formless."

Because its specific form and appearance cannot be apprehended, "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa) have the meaning of being provisional; they manifest from the essence and are solemnly present as something that can be directly encountered.
"Function" (vṛtti) has the meaning of the Middle Way, for it unites with the preceding essence and characteristics to constitute wondrous activity.

Because the essence is empty and inexhaustible, one cannot find its boundaries or limits; thus it is called the "greatness of essence. Because the wondrous characteristics are inconceivable, even through diligent contemplation one cannot see their summit.

Therefore, it is called "Great in Aspect" (*xiàng-dà*). Its function (*yòng*) is unfathomable; neither Māras nor heterodox teachers can perceive its boundaries. Therefore, it is called "Great in Function.
As for why these three are collectively named "Great," it is because their merit is equal. The three are not three of themselves but are always one; the one is not one of itself but is always three.
To raise the one is to have the three; to speak of the three is to unify them. Whether one or three, whether vertical or horizontal, all may be called "Great. Thus...
It is said: because there is one and not two, it is not central; because it is not central, it is not perfect. Because there are two and not one, it is not central;
because it is not central, it is not perfect. From this we know that they are interconnected with sovereign mastery, unimpeded whether vertical or horizontal.

Because they are unimpeded, they are called "perfect" (*yuan*); because they are perfect, they are called "great" (*da*). The Buddha is the person, and the crown of the head is the metaphor; that is to say, these three dharmas are the Buddha.
That which is revered and honored is likened to the crown of the head. If one attempts to correlate this with the three syllables, the meanings do not cohere;
fearing that this would not accord with the Buddha’s intent, I have not adopted it. Furthermore, one should know that these three dharmas are all reflections of one's own mind.
If one perceives one's own mind, then all three are equally illusory and false. It is said that these three dharmas are what all Buddhas have realized.

To use an analogy, it is like the crown of the head. As previously discussed in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, why do you dismiss it as illusory and false? This contradiction between what precedes and what follows is truly incomprehensible to me. He said: "Do you understand?

When those of the Two Vehicles cultivate emptiness, ordinary beings cultivate the provisional, and those of the Mahāyāna cultivate the Middle Way—do these not all constitute the aspiration for the Way (*bodhicitta*)?
He replied: "Indeed. For example, when Ānanda saw the manifestation [of the Buddha’s power] and gave rise to this aspiration, he shaved his head under the Buddha. That which he generated..."
Is this mind not indeed the mind of the Way? [The Master] said: "It is truly the mind of the Way. If this is so, why did the World-Honored One rebuke them, saying:
'All sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind; they employ various deluded thoughts. Because these thoughts are not true, there is cyclic existence'?
When he says they 'employ various deluded thoughts,' does this not refer to that very mind of the Way they have produced? [The Master] said:

However, the Tathāgata takes that very view from which the mind of the Way was aroused as his object; yet, when sought through the seven points—internally, externally, and in between—it is utterly unfindable.
Just as it is with seeing, so too is it with hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. The Two Vehicles cultivate emptiness [in this manner].
Since the provisional has already been refuted, the same applies to emptiness within the provisional; there is no case where this is not so.

Since they cannot be apprehended through successive investigation, how are they not identical to illusions and delusions? Therefore, because the Buddhas realize this unapprehendability, their wondrous functions unfold with total freedom.
The student falsely recognizes that there is something to be attained, yet throughout their life they fail to achieve resonance with reality. Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"Because one recognizes all 'selves' as nirvāṇa, there is talk of realization and awakening, which is called 'accomplishment. It is like a person who mistakes a thief for their own son."
One’s household wealth and treasures will ultimately never be realized. Thus we know that the "three" and the "one" are both merely images of one's own mind.

If one realizes one's own mind, then [these categories] are found to be utterly unobtainable, identical to illusions and delusions. One asks: "If this is so, why did the Buddha not point directly to one's own mind?
Why did he extensively explain such names and characteristics, causing later generations to become bewildered and unable to enter? Could this possibly be the Buddha's intention?"
Indeed. This is because the Buddha does not speak to the Buddha, but speaks to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). When speaking to the Buddha, his mouth would simply hang on the wall;
however, since ordinary beings are lost in delusion, he provides instruction and revelation so that they may awaken and enter into realization.

It is like a bystander pointing to another person and saying, "There is ink on your face," or "Your eyes have cataracts and visual distortions," or even describing the features of a dragon-like countenance and a phoenix-like nose.
With a tiger’s head and a swallow’s chin—whether noble or base, this is not spoken merely for oneself, nor is it false.

Why? Because that person receives it according to the words; thus, there is nothing therein that is not so. If one wishes to turn back and seek to see it, one will be unable to behold it for the rest of one's life.
If one seeks it outwardly, one will be unable to find it even throughout kalpas. The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise.
It is so. It may be that the darkened mind is in secret accord [with reality]. Yet, if it manifests even in a single stirring thought, one has already missed the mark.

How much more so if one seeks to find a place of rest within names and forms? I fear such a state would not be attained for the rest of one’s life; therefore, I say it is illusory and false. [The interlocutor] says:
"The three virtues and the three great principles are truly perfect and complete, yet you further disparage them as being like illusions and falsehoods. This seems somewhat inconsistent with reason."

I fear this cannot be so. Why? The Buddha refers to "mysterious causes" (mi-yin), the sutras are titled "definitive meaning" (liao-yi), and bodhisattvas are defined by the "ten thousand practices" (wan-xing).
Could it be that there are other things apart from these three dharmas? If you say they are one and the same, why speak of "cultivation and realization"?
Now, as for those who cultivate and realize [the Way], how could they realize that which is illusory and false? The answer is: it refers precisely to these three dharmas.

Because the Buddhas realize that which is unobtainable yet obtainable, their wondrous functions are sovereign and free. Because ordinary beings do not know this, they transmigrate through beginningless time.
As for the Three Vehicles, each clings to one-sidedness and thus fails to achieve further progress. The relative superiority and inferiority among these three can be known by comparison.
It is because all phenomena do not transcend these three, and these three dharmas are fundamentally reflections of one's own mind.
If one realizes one's own mind, then both name and form vanish together. As in the previous analogy of the ink, they can be realized yet cannot be apprehended;
they can be known yet cannot be seen. They exist though they do not exist; they do not exist though they are not non-existent. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says: "The wisdom I have attained..."
Wisdom is subtle and supreme. That ordinary beings turn their backs on the good and head toward evil is because [ignorance] is the profound root of saṃsāra;

that those of the Three Vehicles loathe evil and rejoice in the good is because it is likewise the source of biased views. If one says that greed, hatred, and delusion are [the truth], then ordinary beings would fall into the error of nihilism;
if one says that greed, hatred, and delusion are not [the truth], then those of the Three Vehicles would remain stuck in biased views. Therefore...
Regarding this inconceivable Dharma, it is revealed in a hidden manner. What is meant by "revealed in a hidden manner"? It is as when Ānanda mistakenly entered a chamber of lust;
upon returning to the Buddha’s presence, he requested instruction on the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, subsequently referring to them as the "initial expedient means.
Ānanda clearly understood that these three dharmas depend upon the single mind; if the single mind is awakened to, then the three dharmas manifest spontaneously.
Is it not said that this is "delusion appearing as awakening"? Furthermore, the World-Honored One is like one who tracks down a thief to ruin his house, or applies a wedge to fit through a hole.
He does not investigate the error of falling into lust, nor does he preach the subtle *śamatha* to him; he simply asks about the original aspiration for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
This is because those of the Two Vehicles do not understand their own minds and falsely give rise to joy and aversion, thereby falling into lust.

[The Buddha said: "It is so. The arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) is a virtue. Although transgression and virtue are two, they are identical in their lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).

Since there is no difference in their objective sphere, to feel either longing or aversion constitutes a sickness. The World-Honored One used his own path of self-reflection to question [the monk] seven times, only then realizing that [the aspiration] did not exist.
If your aspiration for enlightenment has no location, then where does the mind that falls into lust reside? One of sharp faculties and superior wisdom may immediately [realize this]."
"Knowing the Return. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "The mind is not within, nor is it without, nor is it in between.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the nature of sin. The two bhikṣus attained sudden and great enlightenment. Although Ānanda did not immediately grasp it, he recognized his own mind;
out of compassion for those who would come after, he raised the question again later. Is such an instruction not called "esoteric"?
To expound the sublime principles: the cultivation and realization of all Buddhas is that which bhikṣus should study; the various sūtras elucidate this as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*);
and bodhisattvas cultivate it as the myriad practices (*caryā*). Now, among the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world, space is the ultimate limit;

among the hundred rivers and many streams, the ocean is the ultimate limit; and among all dharmas, the mind is the ultimate limit. As for the mind, it is the great root of total retention (*dhāraṇī*) and the foundation of all meanings.
This is the wondrous gateway. This sutra directly reveals the eternally abiding true mind. If one awakens to this mind, then all phenomena will ultimately be firm and solid.
Such are the names and meanings; why do you still harbor doubts?
△ Thus have I heard (up to) Mañjuśrī being the principal figure.

The phrase "at one time" is spoken by the compiler himself, stating: "In this manner, I heard this Dharma from the Buddha. This is because he does not dare to claim that he himself possesses the Dharma.
Furthermore, he specifies the time and place so that there may be a basis for verification and it is not considered to be a fabrication. Herein, [the text] proceeds...
The antiquity of this matter is profound. Those who preach the Dharma have never offered incense, and those who discourse on Chan do not speak of their spiritual lineage.

Since there is no basis for such practice, the life-force of wisdom has been severed. Nothing exceeds this in its severity as an act of shedding the Buddha’s blood. If one insists that no reliance on a teacher is required—
If that were so, why did Kāśyapa wait for Maitreya? Why did Dharma come from the West? Why did the Great Sun worry about his lineage being cut off?
And why did Fengxue weep so bitterly? As the subsequent text says: "It is like a commoner who falsely claims to be a king and brings his own execution upon himself."
Those who come later may serve as excellent mirrors [for reflection]. Regarding the summer retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony:

the Buddha ordained that for bhikṣus, the fifteenth day of the fourth month is the morning of the "foot-binding" (*kaṭhina*), and the fifteenth day of the seventh month is called the "unbinding of the discipline.

This was because traveling back and forth on the roads during the height of summer would inadvertently harm insects and ants, thereby resulting in a deficiency in compassion; thus it is termed "protecting the feet. Now, as for what is attained during this single summer retreat:
I have sought clarification from the Buddha regarding this. If there are any transgressions, I shall also confess them myself.

When it is said that even an Arhat is a "beginner," it implies that although an Arhat has already perfected the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), they must still exercise restraint and protection; how much more so for one at the initial stage of the path?

Yet, the śramaṇas of today do not reflect upon the Buddha’s regulations; they wander idly through prefectures and counties, exploring and admiring mountains and waters regardless of whether it is winter or summer, regarding such activities as their primary duty. This is ignorance.
Who among them would not feel pain? As for those Bodhisattvas who consult others to resolve their doubts, those on the lower stages and those with residual delusions are by nature unable to be equal.
If even Great Beings must resolve their doubts, how much more so for beginners and later students? Among the practitioners of the present day, as soon as they have left the household life...
They then study "mastery" (svatantra), yet among their teachers and friends they do not see a single person, nor do they hear a single word of principle.
Even when they happen to stand before a teacher, they never voice their own efforts in hopes of gaining his approval.

When subjected to even a slight interrogation, they feel their hearts pierced through and their bodies exhausted, having no desire to face him again. Compared to such people, how can one measure up to a Bodhisattva? How much more so!

At that time, King Prasenajit was observing a fast for the anniversary of his father’s death. [He] prepared the offerings with solemnity and maintained a dignified demeanor to strictly observe the ritual of the fast.

The king invited the Buddha, saying that he would certainly attend. At the same time, elders and lay devotees were also providing meals for the Sangha; they took turns leading the distribution on the following day.
Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation and did not join the sequence of the Sangha. He returned alone along the way to demonstrate that he had no offerings.
While kings and elders were simultaneously feeding the Sangha, it was known that each had their respective obligations;
however, as butchers, executioners, and those in brothels or taverns lacked the aspiration for the Path and had not been invited, he hoped they would become his final patrons.
"It was because he fell into it by mistake. He asked: "The *mianman* yellow birds still know where to settle;
how could there be sages and worthies who do not know how to choose, yet fall into a chamber of lust by mistake? It is not that they did not know.

Rather, it is because they wish to bring to full completion the immeasurable merit of sentient beings, practicing impartial compassion. Furthermore, we have heard the Tathāgata reprimand Kāśyapa and others for their lack of impartiality."
This is merely a sequential arrangement for the purpose of transcending all doubts and slanders.
At that time, Ānanda, having finished his almsround, returned to the Buddha's presence together with the daughter of Matanga.

To include [the practice of] the sexual seat and the physical caressing of the body clarifies the extreme nature of such coercion. One shall employ mantras to go forth and protect; this is how the Great Teaching arises.
When the fast is completed and one returns, one must expound the Great Dharma; this is why both kings and ministers follow along.
As for what is called "illusory arts," there are sexual mantras, sexual drugs, and sexual powers. In the *Loutan jing* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra), "tan" is written as "lou."

He causes them to burn with intense passion; yet, as they do not yield to lust, he coerces them into entering fire and further subjects them to the constraints of malevolent incantations so that their bodies lack autonomy.
Fortunately, there are no aphrodisiacs, and their minds have not yet become deranged; therefore, it is said that [the precept] is merely about to be destroyed.
When Ānanda saw the Buddha, he prostrated himself in worship and wept with grief... [until] he withdrew to sit silently, receiving the Sage’s instructions.

He realized that because he was afflicted by the demon’s spell, his power of the Way was incomplete; realizing his power of the Way was incomplete, he knew that his extensive learning had been without merit.
I entreat you for the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*, hoping that the power of the Way may be perfected.
○ The Buddha told Ānanda: "You and I share the same vital breath... [up to] "...because this perception is not true, there is cyclic existence."
First, the account of the natural bonds of kinship reflects human sentiment. Second, the inquiry into the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment serves to discern delusion.
Ānanda, having grasped the meaning, reported according to reality, saying that his own vital energy was coarse and turbid, unable to give rise to the supreme, pure, and wondrously luminous state.

Because he could not give rise to it, whenever he encountered desire, he felt deep fear. The World-Honored One then fully instructed him that both delight and aversion are collectively termed [delusion].
Deluded conceptualization. Beginningless birth and death—the source of this illness lies herein. Deluded by this, one wanders through transmigration; it is thus in all seven stations.

If one awakens to the single mind, even Buddhahood cannot be attained [as a separate state]. Ānanda, out of compassion for future generations, entreated the World-Honored One to reveal and clarify this in minute detail.
Only now do I realize that joy and aversion are entirely like dreams and illusions.
○ You now wish to investigate supreme bodhi... (up to) ...therefore I have resolved my mind and vow to abandon birth and death.
First, examine the direct mind to cause one to leave behind flattery and deception. For the Way prizes truthfulness, while the harm wrought by flattery and deception is profound.
Next, interrogate views and attachments; this is like inviting a thief to destroy one's home. To call the mind "the eye" (as Ānanda did) is to mistake a thief for one’s own son.
Both longing and aversion are equally formed by the deluded mind and its false calculations. If one departs from delusion—
As for calculating and deliberating, how could joy or aversion arise? Those of the Three Vehicles do not understand this, and thus falsely give rise to grasping and rejecting.
Since the source of their affliction is the same, it must be discerned. Ānanda merely serves as the head of the assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said... (up to) 'this general must know where the enemy is.
To clarify the true mind, one must exhaust delusive confusion. If delusive confusion is clarified, the true mind will naturally be realized.
Therefore it is said that if one does not know where the heart-mind resides, one cannot subdue the dust of worldly toil. The 'king' corresponds to the aforementioned permanently abiding true mind."
The "bandits" refer to the various deluded thoughts employed previously; "mobilizing the troops" refers to the present investigation of the mind and discernment of the views.
When delusion is exhausted and awakening is perfected, the mind penetrates and phenomena pervade; this is the natural order of things (*dharmatā*), not something produced by forceful artifice.

The World-Honored One has clarified this through both doctrine and metaphor; it is fitting that it should be understood without words. Since Ānanda did not yet deeply comprehend this, it was unavoidable that he had further questions.
"Because you allow your consciousness and mind to wander about, this is your fault" (up to: "Thus, the conscious mind actually resides within the body;
yet you only know that the wandering of your consciousness and mind is your fault, while failing to realize that your entire being belongs to delusion.

Why is this? If this conditioned mind were truly existent, it would have to have a location. Since it has a location, it cannot be without a point of reference. Since there is a point of reference..."
[The Master] showed [it]. "Where is it now? "The ten kinds of ordinary beings' consciousness-minds are within.

This is to ensure there is no discrepancy in the words. "The blue lotus eyes are only on the Buddha's face. This is to ensure there is no discrepancy in the location. Since the Buddha and sentient beings have no different locations, [the principle is established].
"Why is it that my own mind and eyes alone are located elsewhere?
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "As you are now sitting here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall... (omitted)... therefore, while I am in the hall, I am able to see from afar."

Wishing to demonstrate the mind that has no fixed location, [the Buddha] first establishes the views regarding the internal and external. The World-Honored One points to the hall to pose a question, desiring to shatter the notion of a mind existing within.
Ānanda answers according to the question, yet he does not yet understand the reason for the inquiry. Previously, it was said that one observes with the eyes and the mind gives rise to attachment;
this refers to the process from the external to the internal. Now, it is said that [the mind] is "in the hall," as the doors and windows are open.
"To see clearly from afar" refers to that which proceeds from the internal to the external. Between these two contradictory statements, which one is definitive?
At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden arm amidst the great assembly... [up to] "...it is impossible for it to dwell within the body."
To shatter the deluded mind, he first rubbed the crown of [the disciple’s] head to comfort him; this was the height of his compassion.

It was because he feared that those of the Lesser Vehicle, upon suddenly hearing the Great Dharma, might give rise to fear and timidity. Having thus comforted him, he proceeded according to the principles previously explained:
"If your mind were within the body, it should be like you being inside a hall—you would first see the interior of the hall and only then see external objects. Next...
It is exactly so. Why is it that you do not see the internal organs within your body, such as the heart and liver? Even if you cannot see those, the sinews and veins are visible on the surface;
these too should be clearly perceived. Therefore, you mock [the Buddha] by saying you do not see the Tathāgata inside the hall but can see what is outside the hall.
Ānanda himself admits this is not the case; thus, there is yet another layer of error. He asked: "Suppose it were made of lapis lazuli..."
"Can the Bodhisattva Guang see the five viscera within and perceive that the heart is located inside? He replied:
"When he can see within his own body, does this mean that the eye faculty turns back to observe, seeing it because there is no obstruction from tactile objects?

Or does it mean that he realizes it through internal realization with perfect clarity, seeing it without depending on external sensory objects? If the eye faculty were to turn back and the mind-eye were to return..."
If they were both "outside," then if it did not depend on the external objects (*viṣaya*), the liver organ would not be its object.

If it were not its object, who could know it to be the liver organ? Moreover, since "seeing" and the "conditions for seeing" are precisely what the Tathāgata has refuted, how can they be called "inside"?
The mind is like the root, while the eyes are like the branches and leaves; if the root is removed, the branches and leaves wither of their own accord. Therefore—
Previously, both the mind and the eyes were presented together; now, however, the inquiry concerns only the location of the mind.
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha: "I have heard the Tathāgata’s Dharma-sound...
[up to] ...it is impossible for it to dwell outside the body."
Since the mind within has already been refuted, you must then claim that the mind is outside the body. You cite the analogy of a lamp being outside a room, hoping it will clarify the meaning.
However, the World-Honored One used that very analogy of the lamp to refute your error.
If your mind were like a lamp outside a room, then when you alone see the lamp, everyone else would likewise see that same lamp. If this were truly the case, [it would be so].
"When one person eats, are all people satiated? Ānanda replied that this was not so. "The Arhat has already forgotten the grasping at a self; yet even his physical life is not shared by others.
How much less could an ordinary person, who clings to the notion of a distinct self, cause a multitude to be satiated by the eating of one?
The World-Honored One’s intention was this: since you say that physical lives are not shared, then your own body can only be known by yourself. How could there be...
Can a mind external to the body know your body? If you grant that it does know it, then it would be equivalent to the mental measure of another.

If it were equivalent to the mental measure of another, then body and mind would be distinct entities. If they were distinct, then the mind that knows could not perceive the body, and the body that perceives could not know the mind.
If one says each possesses its own cognition, then they are like two separate persons. If one says each lacks cognition, then they are likewise [inanimate].
"Grasses and trees are not like this now. I shall now show you my hand of tūla-cotton.
If your mind were like a lamp outside a room, would it not likewise be outside your body, just as my hand is? Try to examine this:
does this cognizing mind reside by my hand, or does it reside at the boundary of your own body? If it were in my hand..."
"It would be identical to [knowing] another's mind; what concern would that have for you? Ānanda, if it were not your concern, then both your body and your mind would have no location.
If it were located within the boundaries of the body, how could you say it is outside?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said—that because one does not see within [it is impossible]—up to 'it is like two pieces of lapis lazuli joined together;
such a thing cannot exist.

Ānanda, since the mind of both the internal and external has already been refuted, you further calculate that it dwells hidden within the sense organs, like two pieces of lapis lazuli joined. If this were truly so..."
That the latent roots are identical to lapis lazuli applies not only to the ears, nose, tongue, and body;
it is even so for what is seen by the eyes, as well as what is heard by the ears, smelled by the nose, tasted by the tongue, and touched by the body. All are identical to lapis lazuli.
Each of those has its own cognition; with what could they be said to conjoin? That [conjunction] is beyond analogy, yet this [position of yours] is likewise untenable.
How could it be that among the five sense faculties, you alone grant that "seeing" belongs to the mind, while all the others are not the mind?
Ānanda, in truth, you have taken your own fundamental nature as the basis for your inquiry; the World-Honored One’s refutation of this is merely meeting error with error. Why?

Furthermore, sentient beings can verify this for themselves within their daily lives. When the ear hears sounds, they do not abide for even a single moment, yet the nature of hearing remains tranquil.

When the tongue tastes flavors, the nose smells fragrances, or the body perceives touch, there is cognition when these organs are engaged with their objects, but no awareness when they are disengaged.
Only this faculty of knowing and seeing is vividly manifest, ever present before one’s eyes; yet people cling to its partial aspects.

This is important. Thus, when the father and son hesitated, it was solely to refute the faculty of sight. If this seeing is destroyed, then hearing, smelling, tasting, and cognition will naturally be destroyed without even needing to be refuted.

Therefore, the World-Honored One did not use the other faculties as examples to refute it; he merely used the analogy of glass covering the eyes to point out that the dharma and its metaphor were inconsistent.
Why is this? Because when the eyes are covered by glass, although one sees mountains and rivers at that time, in reality—
When one sees lapis lazuli, the mind is hidden within the visual faculty; thus, when seeing mountains and rivers, how could one ever see the eye?

If one were to see the eye, the eye would become identical to its object. If it were identical to the object, there could be no seeing. If there is no seeing, one cannot say that [the mind] follows [the eye].

If one says it does follow, then both the physical eye and the mental eye must possess the capacity for seeing. If this were necessarily the case, then two eyes would have to exist together, joined like lapis lazuli.
"Then lapis lazuli should also possess the capacity for vision. This argument is not tenable; it contradicts both fact and principle. Thus, the dharma and the analogy cannot be equated.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected thus...
[as previously stated] ...that you claim seeing darkness is called 'seeing within'—this is impossible."

Whether refuted from within or without, the latent root is likewise not [the mind]. It is simply that you do not know the mind that is devoid of intrinsic nature, yet you further establish views of "internal" and "external.
Ānanda’s intention was that the viscera and organs reside within, while the orifices dwell without, as if there were some entity moving back and forth therein.
The World-Honored One then interrogated him: "Does this dark object face you or not? If it faces you, then the darkness is right before your eyes; how could it ever have been behind you?"
"Internally. This does not refer to the darkness in a still, dark room; it refers entirely to your own internal viscera. Such an interpretation is incorrect. Ānanda understands this for himself:

it does not mean the darkness facing the eyes, but rather the darkness encountered through inward reflection (*pratyavekṣaṇā*). Since you have already established "internality" through inward reflection, why would you alone not see the face through inward reflection?

If you could see the face, then this mind would reside within empty space. If it were in space, [it would follow that...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
What concern is this of yours? If the void were able to see, and that [void] were your mind-eye, then the Tathāgata seeing your face now would likewise be your mind-eye.
If it were truly so, then because he is able to see your face, your mind-eye would already know it; yet your body would remain without sensation.
This would be identical to the previous analogy of the lamp being outside the room. If you maintain that the mind also exists—
[The Master] said: "I know. The body also possesses sensation. If this were so, then in this dialogue between questioner and respondent, there would not be two people;
it would simply be you alone who would become two Buddhas. The Sūtra says: 'It is precisely the Tathāgata who now sees your face, and that is also your own body. This statement is not tenable. Why?
If it were as the words say, then it would mean that your body already knows [the mind], and thus the union with the mind would not be a matter of sensation. Such is the meaning."
This is not consistent. It should rather be said: "The Tathāgata now beholds your face, as well as the eye of your mind. Your eye already knows; the body ought not to be unaware.
This would be more convenient for the meaning.
Ānanda said: "I have often heard the Buddha teach and instruct the fourfold assembly [up to]: 'Wherever there is a correspondence, the mind exists accordingly;
such a thing is impossible.
That 'because the mind arises, dharmas arise' means that dharmas have no self-substance. That 'because dharmas arise, the mind arises' means that the mind has no self-substance."
Since it is said that they "arise," when there is arising, the mind exists wherever it encounters its conditions.

Since it is also said that they "cease," when there is cessation, the mind is absent wherever those conditions are removed. This being so, how much more is this true for the mind of discursive thought? When following conditions, its arising and ceasing are manifest;
when conditions disperse, both are unobtainable. If even discursive thought is unobtainable, how could it have a location?
Therefore, the World-Honored One raised the objection regarding the existence or non-existence of their substance: "The mind and its objects possess only their names;
they fundamentally lack intrinsic substance. If that which lacks substance can unite, then the nineteenth realm would unite with the seventh sense-object.
Why? Because there are only eighteen realms and only six sense-objects. If the nineteenth realm were to unite with the seventh sense-object, it would be a mere name in vain.

In reality, it has no substance. Because it lacks substance, it cannot combine [with objects]. If it must have substance, then you should try to fathom whether it comes from within or enters from without.
If it emerges from within, one should see the interior of the body; if it enters from without, one should first see the face. Ānanda further explained, saying:
"When I say that the mind follows what exists, I mean only that the mind possesses cognition; I do not mean that it possesses vision. Why is this? Vision is its..."
The eye. The mind knows that it is not the eye that sees; to claim otherwise is incorrect. The World-Honored One challenged him, saying: "If it were the eye that could see, then consider this:
when you are inside a room, you previously said that because the doors and windows are wide open, you can see far into the distance. Is it the door that sees?
Since the eyes of a dead person remain yet they cannot see, how could the nature of seeing ever belong to the eye? [The opponent] asks: "The eyes of a dead person..."
As for those who cannot see, they are like the people inside that room. Previously, it was said that the mind is within the body;
why did the World-Honored One not approve of this? The answer is: a person and a room can be clearly distinguished from one another, but how can the mind and the eyes be separated?

Have you not seen what is stated in the following passage: "When deluded once, it becomes the mind; one is certainly confused into thinking it resides within the physical body, not realizing the nature of the physical body."
Externally, the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth are all things manifested within this wondrously luminous mind. It is further said:
"Empty space arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean; the myriad lands of outflows and subtle dusts are all produced in dependence upon that space."
Therefore, by minutely investigating whether they possess a single substance or multiple substances, and whether they are pervasive or non-pervasive, one finds that they have no location whatsoever.
Thus, one should know that the former false recognition of views such as "internal" and "external" can be eliminated.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha [teaching] with Mañjuśrī and others...
it is impossible that there should be a ‘middle’ between them.
This passage cites the Buddha’s discourse with Mañjuśrī as proof that what was previously discussed is neither internal nor external; however, it does not clarify what this “middle” actually is.

Because there is only name and no actual substance, [the opponent] cites direction as proof. Ānanda himself explains that it is neither the body nor the manifestation, but rather exists between the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*).

He fails to realize, however, that the sense organ is identical to the body and the object is identical to location. Therefore, the World-Honored One refutes this by means of both the "inclusive" and the "non-inclusive" [arguments].
If it were inclusive, then one half would possess cognition and the other half would lack cognition; that which possesses cognition would then belong to—

The sense organ (*indriya*) does not know its own object (*viṣaya*), nor does it exist in between them. If it does not encompass both, it is neither organ nor object; since these two do not exist, where could the middle be?
Furthermore, if it encompasses both, the three characteristics are clearly present; if it does not encompass both, even the one cannot be found.
This meaning is explained extensively in the following section on the twelve bases (*āyatana*). Changshui [Zhixu] changed "the external do not mutually know" to "the external also mutually know."
This great [position] is not so. Why? Furthermore, the mutual cognition between the internal mind and body and the mutual cognition with external things are like two palms joined;

they do not constitute a refutation of the intended meaning. I say: if there is something seen within, yet there is no mutual cognition externally, then because there is no cognition internally, it cannot be established as being within.

If the mind and body mutually cognize one another, then to claim they exist externally is illogical. The absence of cognition refutes the aforementioned "having something seen," and mutual cognition refutes "not mutually cognizing."

The meaning of the text is clear. Why, then, do you change the character "not" (不)? Therefore, by synthesizing each phrase, one sees that because there is no cognition internally, it is not established within;
externally, things do not cognize one another. That body and mind cognize each other is not logically consistent with being external.
My limited view is thus; may the wise correct it. In the commentary, it is stated that while the sense organs and objects lack cognition, the essence of the mind possesses cognition.
This great claim is not so. The sutras clearly state that the eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form (rūpa) is insentient;

when consciousness arises between them, it is the mind that resides therein. Furthermore, the World-Honored One said: "If your mind were to reside between the sense organ and the object, would it encompass both, or would it not encompass both?
As for what is meant by 'encompassing both,' would that not mean encompassing both the organ and the object? How could it be otherwise?"

The eye itself is without cognition; it is the eye that possesses discernment. The object of form (rūpa) is without cognition. Is it not said, therefore, that cognition belongs to the faculty (indriya) and does not belong to the object (viṣaya)?
If one were to conjoin these two, then half would be the same as the faculty and half would be the same as the object; hence it is said that they stand as opposing adversaries.
If they do not coexist, they would neither be faculties nor objects; thus, they would lack the essence of their own nature.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I have previously seen the Buddha together with Mahāmaudgalyāyana...
[up to] ...that there is no such place where the mind that perceives and knows is called ‘non-attachment to all things.’”
Previously, the twelve classes of beings all held that the conscious mind resides within the body.
When it was stated that "wherever the body comes into contact with an object, the mind follows and exists there," this was based on the perspective of ordinary people and posed as a question.

Having been refuted, [the interlocutor] again cited the time when the Buddha and Mañjuśrī discussed the true nature (*dharmatā*), arguing that since it is neither internal nor external, it must exist in between; yet, unexpectedly, this too was refuted.

This is what is to be refuted. Furthermore, herein he cites what was taught to the śrāvakas: since it is neither internal, external, nor intermediate, yet one further establishes "non-attachment to all," this is precisely where the śrāvaka falls into error.

What was stated above—that where the mind follows its conjunctions with objects, it exists accordingly—refers to recognizing the object while being deluded regarding the essence, failing to know that the essence is fundamentally non-existent.
Herein, "non-attachment to all" refers to clinging to the essence while being deluded regarding its function. And...
They do not know that [the mind] originally possesses both essence and function; each adheres to one-sidedness and is therefore refuted.
However, the World-Honored One’s intention was solely to cause them to know that the deluded mind has no fixed location; he did not wish to lead them into confusion regarding essence and function.

Therefore, he pointed to all the objects and phenomena before one's eyes to pose his question. If those [objects] were all dark and indistinct, identical to insentient matter, they would have no [locus].

Discrimination! Who clarifies non-attachment? If all those things are clearly perceived as soon as one lifts one's eyes, and discrimination remains vividly present, how can one clarify non-attachment?
This is precisely what is meant by the following passage: "There are merely verbal expressions; in both cases, there is no actual reality. This is what that refers to.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat amidst the great assembly;
he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I am the youngest brother of the Tathāgata...
[omitted] ...I am thirsting and waiting expectantly to reverently hear your instructions."
Previously, because Ānanda had fallen into lust, he was filled with panic and self-reproach, feeling that his power of the Way was incomplete.
He returned to the Buddha’s presence and specifically requested instruction on the initial expedient means of wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna. The World-Honored One specially instructed him:

"It is because you do not know the eternally abiding true mind and instead employ various deluded thoughts that there is joy and fear. If the true mind were awakened to, both joy and fear would be eliminated. This...

This refers to the initial expedient means of *dhyāna* and so forth. Through these seven successive rounds of inquiry and refutation, one finally realizes that all that was previously studied and identified was merely the deluded mind.
Although one may possess extensive learning, one cannot attain the untainted state (*anāsrava*) and remains subject to the turning of external objects;

this is the error of being deluded regarding the truth and pursuing the false. Regarding the "path" in the context of *śamatha*, it is the path leading to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). As for the subsequent text:
He clearly understood the path by which his family had returned, and he immediately extolled the merit of the instruction revealed therein.
He said, "If this path is made clear, not only will we ourselves be benefited, but it shall also cause the icchantikas to destroy their various evil views."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face (until: ...with palms joined, listening attentively). Regarding the emission of light from the face and the description of it as "various":
this is because the functions of the eyes, forms, ears, and sounds differ. The six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) of ordinary beings are each confined by their own attachments;
their illumination is not clear, and thus they are termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). The six sense organs of the Buddhas, however, are identical...

At that time, they mutually radiate light, illuminating everything without exception; thus it is like a thousand suns rising at once. To manifest that fundamental luminosity must necessarily shatter ignorance (*avidyā*), there are the six kinds of earth tremors.
Since ignorance has been shattered, it is as if the blind have regained their sight; therefore, the land appears all at once.

As the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) mutually integrate, there is no separation between self and other, for all share the same true mind (*tathatā-citta*); hence it is said, "they merge into one."

Regarding the "realms": what is called the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha is the manifestation of the wondrous awakening of one's own mind. As for the bodhisattvas each dwelling in their own lands:

although the six sense faculties are said to be mutually integrated, they are in reality unmoving from the fundamental limit (*prakṛti*). This is because they wish to bring forth their original luminosity.
First, auspicious light appears to awaken the beginner's mind. The wise, having thoroughly understood this through the "elephant" (the phenomenal), proceed to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

What is meant by the manifestation of the elephant? For those such as ourselves, we attain the light of the mind by means of the Buddha’s light; we come to know the noumenal aspect through the phenomenal aspect.
In this way, the light of the six sense organs of all Buddhas is inherently possessed by us. Why is this so? It is just like the eye.

From this, light is emitted. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, shrubs, humans, and animals—the myriad phenomena of the forested and the vast, brightness and darkness, form and emptiness—all are clearly manifest at a glance.
One enters into the most minute details with total penetration; the subtle and the coarse are all clearly discerned, and both the hidden and the manifest are encompassed.

Although the light of the sun is bright, it cannot illuminate a dark chamber; yet the light of the mind is so subtle and wondrous that there is nothing, whether bright or dark, that is not clearly perceived. Thus it is said: "A thousand suns would not [illuminate it]..."
This is sufficient to illustrate its luminosity. As it is with one faculty, so it is with all six;
they are fully present in daily life, without deviation from moment to moment. Among Buddhas and sentient beings, who is not thus?

It is only because we are unable to directly accept this that the sages and worthies laboriously engage in mutual questions and answers, serving merely as banners for the Dharma-gate. Inferring from this, it is still like borrowing from the multitude.
This is the limited measure of birth. If one were to rely on fundamental direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could its quantity be measured?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial... [up to] "...wrongly enter the various realms of existence."
In the preceding text, [the teaching] proceeded from Ānanda to the assembly at large; here, it proceeds from all sentient beings to instruct Ānanda.
This is because they mutually illuminate one another. Why is this? Sentient beings abide in delusion, while the Buddhas dwell in awakening.

Ānanda’s position corresponds to the first fruit of the path, situated precisely between delusion and awakening. To trace one's origins and exhaust the source, there is nowhere else to go than this. Therefore...

The Tathāgata addressed [the assembly] as follows. The text is divided into three sections. Because sentient beings are entirely deluded, their karmic seeds arise spontaneously, like a cluster of akṣa fruits.
Because all Buddhas are entirely awakened, the single path is level and smooth, and they possess mastery over all dharmas. Those who practice the Way dwell between these two states;
this is entirely due to their failure to understand the two kinds of fundamental natures. Although there are said to be two kinds, they are in essence but one mind. Why is this?
This is what is meant. That which is called the root of birth and death is precisely the pure essence of nirvāṇa. Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"The various illusory manifestations of all sentient beings are all produced from the Tathāgata’s perfectly enlightened pure mind. From this, we know there is no separate essence.
Now, regarding the root of birth and death and the pure essence of nirvāṇa, it is said therein that they are the beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa.
"Bodhi" means awakening. However, awakening and non-awakening seem to constitute two states. Therefore, when the Buddhas realize this, they see that birth-and-death is itself nirvana;
thus, their entire being is manifested as the Great Function. When sentient beings are deluded regarding this, they see that nirvana is itself birth-and-death;
thus, whatever thought they give rise to, worldly afflictions arise first. This is why [the teaching] was shown and instructed to Ānanda.
It is difficult to cause practitioners to know what they should select. What are the conditions that arise within the essence of *nirvāṇa*?

It is said that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is opposed to *nirvāṇa*; afflictions (*kleśa*) are opposed to awakening (*bodhi*); the holy is opposed to the ordinary; the correct is opposed to the false;
joy is opposed to aversion; gain is opposed to loss; the deviant is opposed to the right; emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is opposed to existence; and the person...
It faces me; whatever phenomena it faces are all conditions arising from its own substance. These conditions have no inherent substance and do not abide for even a single moment;
therefore, it is said that they "arise in this very place and perish in that very place. Failing to understand these non-abiding conditions, you give rise to false notions of grasping and rejecting.
Thus, Ānanda, seeing a superior form, you gave birth to joy and attachment, and fell into the chamber of lust.
Thus, fear arises. If one knows that these conditions do not reach one another from moment to moment, then Mātanga is but a dream;
who could detain your body? To have been left with this fundamental luminosity and yet to enter the various realms of existence in vain—how truly lamentable!
“Ānanda, if you now wish to know the path of *śamatha*... [up to] ‘this is not my mind; what should it be called? The preceding text asks:
“If the eye were able to see, when you are inside a room, can the door see? Clearly, it is evident that seeing does not belong to the eye.”
Why then do you say, "Your eyes can see; what constitutes the mind? For what reason are the words of the World-Honored One so internally contradictory?
It is because the previous passage cited seeing as returning to the mind, thereby refuting that the eye sees;

whereas this passage reveals that the mind does not see, and thus provisionally points to the eye as seeing. Thus far, seven rounds of inquiry have clarified the distinction between the true and the false.

However, because he knew that Ānanda’s state of doubt was not yet exhausted, the World-Honored One raised his fist once more to test him. Ānanda understood only that the mind consists of investigation and pursuit;
he did not realize that joy and aversion, grasping and rejecting, are all the mind's erroneous calculations. Therefore, the World-Honored One rebuked them all as being non-existent.
This was much like a precious sword swung directly at one's head—such that even Deshan and Linji would have been forced to fall beneath it.
Ānanda feigned astonishment, like a wise general deploying troops to provoke a battle, intending to cause all sentient beings to know their fundamental nature.
That we cannot directly accept this and instead mock Ānanda for not understanding is truly self-deception.

During the Tang dynasty, when An Lushan rose in rebellion, there was an old soldier who fled from the front lines; as he returned along the road, he heard [the sound] from an empty space by the wayside.
The mother abandoned the child’s crying and went to look at him. The child pointed to a cloth bag on the beam; the soldier immediately took it and showed it to him.

When the child saw the ashes, his thought of rice vanished, and he was struck with amazement and slipped away. It was because the mother could not bear to part with him that she had temporarily entrusted the ashes to him as a substitute for rice.
Generally speaking, in the daily activities of sentient beings, the whole body is not understood, even though the whole body is fully present.
Therefore, when the deluded mind dies once and for all, one is liberated and transformed. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "All sentient beings realize perfect enlightenment;
I believe this. Ānanda was not truly incapable of understanding; he simply wished to exhaust the nature of things and fathom their source so that the Great Teaching might circulate.
It was for this reason that he gave rise to this fear of the mindless state.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This is the deluded appearance of false thoughts regarding external objects... [omitted] ...therefore one undergoes the cycle of transmigration.
Above, it was called the path of *śamatha*; *śamatha* means "calm contemplation" (*靜慮*). Now, as for calm contemplation, one should achieve union through a state of no-mind.
Therefore, the World-Honored One, with a single exclamation, categorically rejected it as "not mind. If one realizes no-mind, that is the purity of *nirvāṇa*.
The essence is the path. Ānanda clung to it through conceptual grasping and investigation, unaware that this was precisely the root of birth and death.
Once his view had been shattered by the World-Honored One, he asked in alarm, "What should this be called? To this, [the Buddha] clearly declared: "This is merely a false external object;
how can it be called the original mind? All wandering through birth and death arises from mistaking a thief for one's own son."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am the beloved younger brother of the Buddha... [omitted] ...“...to reveal that which I have not yet awakened to.

Previously, Ānanda had fallen into lust and was struck with fear; he sought refuge at the Buddha’s dwelling and, realizing his own spiritual power was incomplete, requested instruction on the primary expedient means of sublime *śamatha*.
Yet the World-Honored One did not interrogate him regarding the error of his lapse into lust, but instead inquired as follows:

He gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Following several rounds of interrogation and refutation, although he now recognized his error, he remained in a state of apparent realization yet still deluded.

Thereupon, he again described the two minds: the aspiration for enlightenment is the mind that makes offerings to all Buddhas; the perverse mind is that which slanders the Dharma and violates the precepts.
Since the aspiration for enlightenment has been seized, he came to understand that the perverse mind is likewise non-existent. Nevertheless, these two are not the [true] mind.
Thus, I am as heartless as grass and trees. It is not only I who have been struck with terror, but the entire assembly has likewise fallen into doubt;
therefore, I hope for your instruction. For those of the Three Vehicles, in their renunciation of evil and pursuit of good, do not realize that this very "good" is the cause of evil.

To abandon the heterodox and seek the orthodox—how could one realize that the orthodox is itself the root of the heterodox? Once acceptance and rejection are established in the mind, discrimination naturally manifests in thought.
When thought persists, birth and death are vividly present; when the mind is empty, nirvana is equanimous.

Ānanda exerted himself for the sake of the assembly, yet in acknowledging his transgressions and returning to them, he investigated the origins in detail and found that every single instance was rooted in the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One revealed [the truth] to Ānanda... up to: "Who among them has cultivated and realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?
Previously, it was stated that the pure essence of *nirvāṇa* can give rise to all conditions. Yet Ānanda still clung to the conditioned mind, taking it to be his own true self.
Having been thus deprived [of his understanding], he immediately fell into doubt, thinking himself no different from grass and trees. The World-Honored One told him: "All dharmas that arise..."
It is only that the mind of nirvāṇa manifests; there is not even a single mote of dust in the world that does not arise because of this.

Why do you cling to and identify with the conditioned mind, attempting to equate it with annihilation? Because you grasp at the conditioned mind as being real, the practitioners of the Three Vehicles have been unable to accomplish the holy path throughout kalpas.

Ordinary people are deluded by this, and the karmic fruits of beginningless time arise spontaneously. If one awakens to the fact that what arises from conditions has no inherent nature, one will immediately understand.
When the great function manifests in accordance with its essence, one may be said to possess mastery over all phenomena. Ānanda had not yet realized this; his fear and trepidation arose once more.
The World-Honored One earnestly exhorted him again: "This mind of conditions exists only because of causes and conditions. Even if seeing and hearing were extinguished,"

To remain secluded and guard the inner self is still merely a mental object (*dharmadhātu*). It is not that I intentionally reject what you grasp as "non-mind"; you should examine this for yourself within the mind.
If there were a nature existing apart from objects, it could indeed be the true mind; but if conditions cease and there is no substance, then the mind would likewise be subject to annihilation.

If the mind were subject to annihilation, then there would never be a day when the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena) is cultivated or realized. Ānanda, [toward]...
Grasping at the mind that takes objects as conditions, he mistakenly regards it as real and is unable to escape the peril of Mātaṅga; therefore, he requests the sublime *śamatha*.
The Tathāgata pursues him with inquiries everywhere so that he may know this conditioned mind has no existence. Ānanda then concludes that there is no mind at all.
The World-Honored One gradually reveals that this mind has no substance apart from its conditions, which seems perhaps credible. However, if one says "internally"...

To guard against the seclusion and tranquility is still to dwell within the dust of dharmas; this is surely difficult to believe. Therefore it is said: "Apart from this awareness and cognition, there is nothing else.
At that moment, Ānanda and the great assembly were silent, overcome with self-reproach.
Regarding the phrase "losing oneself and remaining silent": previously, he grasped the conditioned mind as his own self;

however, the World-Honored One caused him to scrutinize it minutely, whereby he came to realize that the conditioned mind is not real, and thus he lost himself. Nevertheless, this mind does possess a substance.
It should not be extinguished; that which lacks substance should not manifest. If it were the self, it would not depend on conditions; if it were not the self, it should not be cognizable.
If it were to exist independently and entirely apart from the self, it would be like a fixed post; if it were to follow conditions entirely and spontaneously, it would be like a delusion.
Since these two difficulties cannot be reconciled, [the opponent] remained silent.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "From all those in the world who practice and study [the path], up to those who fail to achieve the fruit of sainthood, their initial words are fundamentally flawed because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind and instead employ various deluded thoughts. These thoughts are not true."
Undergoing these cycles of transmigration can be called a direct path indeed. Fearing that Ānanda might not immediately believe this, I have repeatedly refuted and rebuked him.
Now, having reached this point, he has fallen silent and lost himself; no longer harboring any self-doubt, I have told him clearly:
it was not because you failed to subdue the evil incantations through mistaken recognition that practitioners of the Way fail to achieve the holy path—it is invariably due to this very reason.
When Ānanda heard this, he wept again with deep sorrow... [until] "...awaken my mind of wondrous clarity and open my eye of the Way.
Regarding his weeping and saying "again," there are two reasons: first, because he could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman, he feared that his power of the Way was incomplete;
yet he did not realize that the very mind seeking the Way is precisely the root of birth and death. Second, he had previously thought...
The Tathāgata bestowed upon me samādhi, yet I did not realize that body and mind are fundamentally not interchangeable; this is why I weep with repeated sorrow.

"Leaving one's father and fleeing" is a metaphor for turning one's back on the Truth and heading toward delusion. "Saying one has eaten but remaining hungry" is a metaphor for misunderstanding the samādhi bestowed upon me.
Being entangled by the two obstacles and failing to know the nature of the mind—which is quiescent and eternal—is clarified through the Dharma.

This is a metaphor for the meaning of turning one's back on one’s father. It means to give rise to the wondrous, luminous mind and open my eye of the Way. It seeks to rectify the error of "eating while facing away. As for what are called the two obstacles:
first is the obstacle of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), which perpetuates birth and death; this is precisely the error of turning one's back on awakening and pursuing external conditions.
Second is the obstacle of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*), which hinders right knowledge and vision; it consists of clinging to what has been heard and seen, failing to practice accordingly. This is...
This is the error of regarding extensive learning as being without merit; it serves to further clarify the meaning of his sorrowful tears.

This mind that can return is but a momentary, illusory sojourner, like a traveler. Who is its master? To call this illusorily sojourning mind the "original ground of the heart-mind" is how utterly erroneous!
Ānanda asked again: "If the nature of my mind that hears the Dharma has something to which it may return, then what of the Tathāgata’s speech?
Can that also return? The World-Honored One replied: "That too can return; it returns to the faculty [of hearing].
When there is no faculty, I remain eternally silent. Thus, both speaking and listening each have something to which they return. How then is the wondrous, luminous, original mind?"
"It cannot be returned. The World-Honored One said: "Furthermore, as for the seeing of my seeing, this is fundamentally your own seeing—the luminous source of your clarity.
If you maintain the distinction between subject and object, it is produced by false conceptualization; it is like a second moon created by pressing on the eye, not the actual moon itself.
Although the distinction between subject and object exists, it still cannot be returned. If subject and object are forgotten, this is truly the wondrous enlightened nature of clarity."
When you wish to return, to whom would you return? For this reason, eight kinds of transformed appearances are indicated;

each one returns to its own original source, and as the eight kinds of seeing follow these appearances, they are extinguished. If they were not extinguished, who would know the distinction between before and after?
To what place should the essence of your eightfold seeing return? If it returns to light, then darkness will be extinguished along with it; who [would perceive it]?
You should recognize this as darkness. In this way, those marks arise and perish of their own accord; how could the essence of seeing ever come or go because of them?
Since there is no coming or going, all those returnable marks naturally do not belong to you. That which does not return to you—[is the true self].
If it is not you, then who is? Thus, one knows that your body is pure and eternally abiding. Because of the existence of subject and object, delusion and confusion arise.
Wu-xing says, "There is also something to be returned; it is returned to ignorance. This interpretation is far too circuitous. The *Pòsè lùn* (Treatise on the Refutation of Form) states:
"All sentient beings, in their daily activities, perceive an ox as an ox and a horse as a horse. What the Buddhas perceive is also thus."
It is likewise so. What is the distinction regarding those sentient beings? The answer is:

all phenomena have two kinds of perceptions, namely, the perception of worldly convention and the perception of attachment. The Buddhas possess the perception of worldly convention, but they lack the perception of attachment.
If this is so, how could the sages and worthies ever have lacked vision? Clarity and ignorance have never had two distinct natures;

attachment and non-attachment—how could these be two different people? If you say that ignorance definitely exists and cannot be destroyed, I fear that you will spend your entire life without being able to see the Way.
If you can ensure that the mind does not take objects as its conditions, then naturally every thought-moment will be in a state of quiescent extinction. Thus the World-Honored One said:
When one asks what should be returned, you say that ignorance should be returned; is this not far-fetched?
Ānanda said: "Although I recognize that this nature of seeing has nothing to be returned... [up to] "...you do not truly grasp my seeking for the reality."

Ānanda said, "If this essence of vision is indeed the wondrously luminous, original mind, why is it that the Tathāgata perceives clearly the lands of even the finest dust motes, while we see only up to the first dhyāna, and sentient beings do not exceed the span of a few inches?

If they are one and the same, there should be no distinction between superior and inferior; if they are not, how can there be 'no returning'? Since both positions fail the test, I do not dare to identify them as such."

"It is the true nature. Yet, World-Honored One, you have explained it by means of superior and inferior perspectives. Whether far or near, those who occupy their positions see that the nature of phenomena is without difference.
It is like a person dwelling within a room who sees only the emptiness of the room;
if they go up into the skylight, they see the emptiness of the skylight; if they go outside the door, they see the emptiness of one direction; and if they stand upon a mountain..."

At the crown of the head, the ten directions are penetrated through and through; suddenly, there is no obstruction. It is not that space has distance or proximity, nor is it that the nature of vision has magnitude or smallness.

Because one is constrained by physical form and location, the vision is divided into superior and inferior. Yet the nature that is able to see has never been different; how could there be any distinction?
From the celestial palaces above down to the great earth below, everything in between is surveyed, including all things and the self.
They appear as they are; objects are inherently distinct, yet how can the nature of seeing differ? This undifferentiated nature is your own nature of seeing.
Previously, it was the objects that could be returned, but the nature could not be returned; here, it is the objects that are distinct, while the nature has never been distinct.
If you suspect this nature is the same as the objects, then you should also be able to see my seeing. When I see an object, [and...]
You also see this object; therefore, it is called "common seeing. If I were devoid of the object at the time of non-seeing, why would you not see the place where I do not see?
If you claim that when you do not see, that is precisely the place where I do not see, then why is it that you see?
You can only know it for yourself; how could it be the place where I do not see? Such being the case, your true [nature]—

The nature [of things] is clearly discernible; how could one not know it? If you claim that subject and object are indistinguishably blended and this and that cannot be differentiated, then when you see an object, the object would likewise see you—how could such a state be established?
During the Tang dynasty, there was the Tripitaka Master "Large-Ears" (Daili), who claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.
Emperor Xianzong requested National Teacher Huizhong to test him. The National Teacher asked: "I have heard that you have attained..."
"Does he possess the supernormal power of knowing others' minds? Zang replied, "He does. The Master asked, "Tell me, where am I right now?
Zang said, "The Master is the teacher of the entire nation; how could you be at Tianjin Bridge watching monkey tricks?"
He asked again, "Where do you say this old monk is right now? He replied, "The Master is the teacher of an entire nation;
how could he be standing by the river watching people cross? He asked again, "Where do you say this old monk is right now?
Huizang did not know how to answer. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Wild fox spirit! Where is your power of knowing others' minds?"
As for the locus: when an ordinary person perceives form, it is known through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eye-faculty;

what the National Preceptor asks about, however, is the object of the mind-faculty (*manas*), which ordinary people do not see, yet the Tripitaka Master is able to see. This is truly different from that of ordinary beings. This reached its third instance.
The mental consciousness does not take it as an object; this is not merely the case for the Tripitaka Master—it is the same even for the Buddha-eye.
Therefore it is said: "If you see the 'not-seeing,' that is naturally not the characteristic of that not-seeing. If this is so, then the Tripitaka Master can only know it himself;
how then could the National Teacher see what another person does not see? As for myself, you, and all the world...
It is solemn and distinct, never becoming confused or disordered. What you perceive can only be known by yourself, and what I perceive can likewise only be known by myself.
This nature is wondrously luminous and universally mirrors all existence; why do you not immediately verify this for yourself, instead of seeking the truth through me?
"How could this be considered wisdom? Nevertheless, because the World-Honored One possesses great compassion, he spoke these words as if descending into the weeds of common parlance.
Had this occurred under the gate of a Patriarch, when the student asked, 'How can one know that this is my true nature?

the Master would have immediately administered one hundred and twenty blows of the staff—not a single blow less—so as to make him personally realize his own pain and itching. Yet, as for this Ānanda..."
It cannot be that there is no inquiry. Why? If there is knowing, this "knowing" is deluded cognition;
if there is no knowing, this "knowing" is neutral (avyākṛta). Therefore it is said: "If this is it, you are adding a head to a head; if this is not it..."
It would be like cutting off one's head in search of survival; were it not so, even the World-Honored One would find it difficult to provide an explanation.
He was skilled at interpreting discourse, using objects to lead others toward self-recognition.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, if this nature of seeing is necessarily mine and not that of others...

[and] is universally able to contain the lands of the ten directions,” he continued, “I previously did not know why there were differences in distance and proximity, or superiority and inferiority, as perceived by the holy and the ordinary; how can this now be known?”
"This is my true nature. Yet the World-Honored One extensively cited examples from above and below, surveying all things on land and in water, causing him to choose for himself;

thus he came to know that the substance of things and the self are distinct, and he remained silent, gaining confidence within himself. Within this, [the Master] further argued that since one directly perceives the nature of the self, how could there be inequalities such as large or small, broad or narrow?
All such [distinctions] arise from pursuing sensory objects and give rise to views, resulting merely in these false conceptualizations. The World-Honored One said:
It is said: "Large and small, distant and near—each belongs to the preceding sensory objects (*viṣaya*). There is no need for exhaustive inquiry. This is why emptiness is cited as a metaphor.

Now, emptiness has no inherent directionality, yet it assumes squareness or roundness according to its vessel. The nature of seeing has no inherent nature, yet it manifests as large or small according to conditions.

If one observes emptiness by removing the vessel, how could squareness or roundness exist? If one perceives the nature apart from sensory objects, then both 'large' and 'small' are non-existent. Thus it is."

Why speak only of "seeing one's nature"? The six sense organs and the four great elements are, from the very moment they arise, interfused; they merge indistinguishably within the realm of sensory objects.

Thus, the thousand-fathom body of Śākyamuni is not large, and the *jiaoming* insect dwelling in a mote of dust is not small. Swallowing and disgorging world-systems—such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). To apply even a slight degree of discursive thought is already inadequate.
If one can awaken to this essential principle, body and mind are, in this very moment, fundamentally empty. Should one persist in clinging to prior conditions...
"Then even throughout kalpas of exhaustion, how could one ever perceive one's nature?
