Ānanda said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if this essence of seeing is necessarily my wondrous nature...
[down to] ...its subtle and minute illumination is nothing other than seeing. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Ānanda followed up his previous inquiry with four sections. First, he asked:

"My mind-nature has various points of return, yet the wondrous, luminous, original mind spoken of by the Tathāgata—how can it have no point of return? The World-Honored One, guiding sentient beings to discern their vision, said:
"All things that can return are naturally not you; as for that which does not return to you, if it is not you, then who is it? Next, although...
He realized he was not yet a non-returner (*anāgāmin*). He thought that the Tathāgata’s vision and his own were of different caliber;

suspecting that there must be another way to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood, he asked, "How can I know which is my true nature? To this, the World-Honored One extensively cited various phenomena and images.
He caused him to choose for himself and distinguish between self and other, even saying: "If you do not see the ground where I do not see, it is naturally not a thing;
how could it not be yours? Ānanda did not understand that the seeing of non-seeing is the true nature;

he remained stuck in the sensory objects before him and doubted whether his own vision had magnitude, breadth, or narrowness. Thereupon, the World-Honored One cited space as an analogy to clarify that there is no breadth [to it].
Narrow indeed! Furthermore, while phenomena (*dharma*) may be reversed, nature (*prakṛti*) cannot be reversed; phenomena are inherently differentiated, yet nature is without differentiation;

phenomena have distance and proximity, yet nature is neither distant nor near. Through such an exposition, the distinction between phenomena and self is clearly adjudicated; it may truly be called "lucid."
Why did he ask again? This wondrous nature is now before me; seeing it must be my true self. What, then, are my current body and mind?
It seems there is an error here. Because, although a semblance of understanding has given rise to true faith, it has not yet been clarified.
Among the great assembly gathered there, none were without doubt. Therefore, Ānanda requested again that they know where this error lies. All...
This is simply because one has not realized that body and mind are fundamentally empty. As the preceding text states:

"I shall investigate and pursue [this] to take it as my own mind," to which the World-Honored One rebuked, saying, "This is not your mind. Had one been able to sever this at that moment, why would there have been need for so much questioning and answering?
Failing to grasp this point, you still persist in investigation; thus, seeking the delusion with the delusion, you are like someone who sends off a thief only to catch him.

The thief has no end. Furthermore, what are this body and mind? Yet the World-Honored One says that the body, the mind, and the vessel-world (the physical environment) are all equally illusory conditions, produced by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
If one is free from false conceptualization, then both subject and object are empty; when illusory conditions do not exist, they have never existed from the beginning.
If one can set aside the vessel to contemplate emptiness, one will realize that emptiness is neither square nor round; by discerning emptiness through the vessel, one understands its true nature.

Yet it is difficult for those present in this assembly to immediately believe; for their bodies and minds are fundamentally based on illusory existence. How could they not harbor doubts when you distinguish that which is false and conditioned by sensory objects?
As previously stated, "When one is deluded, it becomes the mind," and one is certainly confused into thinking it resides within the physical body.

One does not realize that everything from the physical body outward—to the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—is all a manifestation within the wondrously luminous Mind. Although [this has already been explained]...
Although the truth has been revealed, Ānanda still remains in doubt; it is only after Mañjuśrī initiates the discourse that he finally believes there are no two moons.
Thus, Ānanda asks: "The nature of seeing is truly the self, yet the body is not the self. The World-Honored One then replies: "This seeing is not seeing; it belongs entirely to the external objects.
That which is called 'self' or 'not-self' is all merely illusory matter. Apart from the body, no self can be found; apart from the objects,"
There is no name by which it can be designated; what, then, is this thing? It is precisely like turning one's back on the ocean and becoming lost in a bubble.

It stands right before me now, yet it is as if I were looking at a bubble and taking it for the ocean. However, we who are practitioners of discourse should resolve each and every point within ourselves.
Failing to understand that things arise through conditions, everyone speaks only of the realm of the sages and worthies.

At that time, the assembly, consisting of those who were not yet free from training, heard these words of the Buddha and was utterly bewildered, unable to understand the beginning or end of their meaning...
[until] it was able to cause you to point out what is "pointing" and what is "not pointing."
"Not those beyond training" (aśaikṣa) excludes the sages who have reached the stage of no-more-learning.

Indeed, these saints of no-more-learning, like the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, abide in samādhi and clearly understand that both the seeing and the objects of sight, as well as all that is conceived, are identical to flowers in the sky.
Having realized them to be like flowers in the sky, they do not hinder the functioning of these very things; thus, this seeing and its objects are fundamentally...

The pure essence of Bodhi is such that within it there is neither "is" nor "is not. This assembly before me, being not yet those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), cannot penetrate and awaken to their original mind;
they still rely on the deluded body and deluded mind to give rise to subject and object.

Hearing that the subtle seeing and the emptiness of form are not two separate things driving one another away, they become bewildered and lose their composure. Since this is not something known by ordinary people, there is no way for them to ask about it.
The World-Honored One simply uses his own reality—which is non-deceptive and non-false—to settle his mind.

As for Mañjuśrī, within the assembly of the Original Teacher, he serves as the eye for discerning the Dharma. Having assumed this responsibility, he saw that the multitude was at a loss; therefore, he rose from his seat to request a definitive resolution.
The World-Honored One first declared: "That which is seen by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas is fundamentally non-existent, yet ordinary beings falsely cling to it as such."
This is not what constitutes an obstruction; therefore, Mañjuśrī alone was used to interrogate the matter of right and wrong.
Mañjuśrī then replied, "I am truly Mañjuśrī; how could there be the dual characteristics of right and wrong? Since the question and answer were thus explicit, there was nothing further to conceal.
I have once had someone look for themselves: "Am I truly this person A? Is there no such person A? Why is this?
If there were such a person, there would be two persons A. Yet today, I am not without being person A; within this, there is truly neither the mark of "is" nor "is not.
If one can look in this way, the meaning will manifest of itself. How can you completely attribute this to the sages and worthies? If you can personally realize it...

The self is not something that exists apart from both [subject and object]. Once "is" and "is not" have been discarded, then the self, the views, and their conditions are all manifestations of the wondrous mind of bodhi.
Failing to understand these manifestations, one is deludedly turned by form and emptiness, giving rise to interpretations of "is" and "is not.

This is like the appearance of two moons caused by pressing on the eyes; it is not because there is some other entity present. When the pressure is released, the two moons were originally non-existent. Thus, when one is free from delusion—

If one calculates in this way, then both "is" and "is not" are non-existent; yet, failing to awaken to the original mind, one follows all that is seen and heard, which is entirely termed deluded thought (*vikalpa*).
One cannot escape from such "is" and "is not" unless one awakens to the mind, for awakening naturally enables one to transcend the distinction between the finger and what it points to.
Is there not the analogy of using a horse to illustrate that a horse is not a horse? If one uses "not a horse" to illustrate that a horse is not a horse, applying it to this text, I fear—

Not so. That [text] merely equalizes all things by directly asserting that there is neither right nor wrong. The meaning here, however, is that when one is stuck in conditions, right and wrong are vividly present;
when the mind is awakened, right and wrong cannot be found. Comparing this with that, the latter is mere frivolous discourse (prapañca).
Students should understand this.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, it is truly as the Dharma King has taught, from ‘the conditions for awakening’ up to ‘how one sees light.
Ānanda then described this himself: ‘It is profoundly still and eternally abiding; its nature is neither arising nor ceasing. This is the realm of my own silent realization.’”
It cannot be compared by means of the names and signs of conceptual proliferation.

Those non-Buddhists [assert] twenty-three principles, such as *sattva*, *rajas*, *tamas*, and *mahat*, which are successively produced from one another; the twenty-fifth is called *pradhāna* (the Primal Darkness).
This *pradhāna* is profound, obscure, and indistinct—seeming to exist yet being non-existent. Ānanda has personally seen that the nature of awakening is serene, neither arising nor ceasing.
How could this be conflated with the *amṛta-tattva* (the principle of the obscure)? Regarding the true self and non-self: because it is non-self, it harmonizes with all phenomena.
The *ātman* (self) of the non-Buddhists is established as a substantial entity; while it appears similar to this [Buddhist concept of] serene permanence, it is in fact false.
Therefore, I request that you resolve my doubts. Because they wish to conflate [the two], they cite what was said by Mahāmati on Mount Laṅkā regarding the non-Buddhists themselves.

"However, that which I speak of as causes and conditions is not within their realm. Now, when one contemplates the self-so-ness of the nature of awakening, what difference is there from the 'self-so-ness' of the non-Buddhists?
If there is no difference, then the Tathāgata should not have used the characteristics of causes and conditions to refute them.
If there is a difference, where exactly does this distinction lie? As for the 'self-so-ness' of the non-Buddhists, they merely calculate that all phenomena are self-so."
Nevertheless, one forcibly establishes conventional names and phrases. Thus, that verse says: "Who dug the lakes, seas, and mounds of mountains?

Who trimmed the thorns and painted the birds and beasts? Fundamentally, there is not a single dharma that can be produced; therefore, it is called *svabhāva* (nature/spontaneity). Ānanda has already said:

"I now observe that this nature of awareness is spontaneous and stands apart, inherently distinct. How much more so when observing that the nature itself is spontaneous—this is beyond verbal expression.
This may be compared [to the following]: Is it not said that one who understands superficially yet harbors doubt is such a person? Yet the World-Honored One’s intention was this:

when I speak of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to refute that which is spontaneous (*svabhāva*), I am precisely stating that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and are not spontaneous;

I do not speak of the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*). If one were to speak of the nature of awakening, then words and thoughts would be severed, and the sphere of mental activity would be transcended—beyond both spontaneity and non-spontaneity.

Neither can be apprehended. As previously stated regarding "seeing" and "not seeing," etc., if you claim that there is a fixed, inherent [faculty] that can be apprehended on its own, you must clearly distinguish it:

does it have an inherent essence? If light constitutes its essence, then in darkness the faculty of seeing would perish; if darkness constitutes its essence, then in light the faculty of seeing would be extinguished.
In such a case, the preceding conditions would constantly contend and supplant one another—how could this be considered inherent? Furthermore, if it were independent of light and darkness...
Regarding the aforementioned conditions: as for that which is "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*), it does not establish itself by itself, just as the eye cannot see itself and the mind cannot know itself.

If one does not know [it], how can it be called spontaneous? If one insists that there is definitively no spontaneous nature, it would be like a person without hands—the fist would ultimately cease to exist;
yet, for a person without eyes, seeing is not entirely non-existent. As the subsequent text states:
Since all verbal expressions are equally devoid of substantial meaning, one must not allow the conventional designations of externalist sophistry to confound the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).
○ Ānanda said: "If this wondrous nature of vision is not self-arisen" (extending to) "...it follows your grasping."
The nature of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) has already been refuted. Furthermore, you now doubt the existence of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It is simply that you do not realize that the "spontaneity" established by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) resides within all phenomena; therefore, it was refuted by means of causes and conditions.

Since it has been stated that "nature is not spontaneous," and this distinction has already been settled, how can you take "nature" as a model for "characteristics" and interpret them as being caused and conditioned? As for the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists, it is like, for example:
A person in life is blind in their eyes. The non-Buddhists say: "This is simply natural blindness; it is not due to any other cause.

The Tathāgata refutes this, saying: "It is indeed due to causes and conditions—conditioned by the sinful karma of past lives and caused by the physical endowment inherited from one's parents—that one experiences such a deficient form."

If one encounters a divine physician who administers elixirs and medicines, and the cataracts are thereby removed so that one regains the vision of one's nature—yet if this were merely spontaneous, the physician would be unable to cure it.
Since the physician is indeed able to effect a cure, how could this not be due to causes and conditions? Truly, as you have argued, it must be due to causes and conditions.
However, this is not so. While the blindness and clarity of the eyes seem to pertain to causes and conditions, if this nature were likewise a product of causes and conditions, then [the conditions]—

When extinguished, its nature ceases to exist. Just as when a jar or basin is broken, the nature of the jar or basin no longer exists, even a divine physician could not restore the essence of seeing to its original state, because its nature does not belong to conditions.
Because it can manifest by following conditions, and because it can follow conditions, it is able to be free from all marks while being identical to all phenomena;
this is the mastery of both identity and detachment, not a mere harmonious fusion. If one wishes to use worldly...
To confuse and compare names and signs with the true nature through frivolous discourse is exactly like grasping at empty space; it is merely a waste of effort.
Ānanda said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, [from] 'it must be the wondrous enlightened nature'... [up to] 'the wondrous path to Bodhi.'"

Ānanda, having previously suspected that the wondrous enlightened mind was confused with the "natural cause" (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists, and since that [view] has already been refuted, he now further cites the Buddha’s own words in hopes of once again conflating them.
He fails to realize that what the Buddha taught was precisely intended to refute such worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, all worldly phenomena arise from causes and conditions; if they were separated from these conditions, they would likewise not exist. The non-Buddhists...
The Way does not reach through causes and conditions; yet you grasp it as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

You construct such frivolous arguments (*prapañca*), yet the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither caused by conditions nor uncaused by conditions, neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous; therefore, it is called "wondrous. Ānanda did not understand its wondrousness, and thus he could not help but harbor doubts.

Furthermore, this nature of seeing should possess nine conditions, namely: space, light, the sense organ, [the object, the mind, attention, the root of consciousness, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of volition].

The objects, mental attention (*manasikāra*), discrimination (*vikalpa*), and the seeds of defilement and purity are present here. Now, possessing only the four minds, these constitute the seeds, mental attention, discrimination, and the defiled and pure [factors].
The eye is the faculty (*indriya*); space and luminosity are the objects (*viṣaya*). By mentioning these four, the nine are complete; thus, the meaning is fully established.

The World-Honored One’s intention was this: "When I speak of causes and conditions, it is for the purpose of shattering worldly views and not from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Thus, that very essence of seeing (*darśana-śakti*) is able to perceive light when conditioned by the sun, moon, or a lamp; it perceives darkness when separated from them. While light and darkness differ from one another, the nature of seeing remains without distinction."
Because there is no difference in seeing, both are called "seeing. What is it that is not seen? Since the nature of seeing is omnipresent, there is nothing that is not seen.

Furthermore, emptiness, light, and so forth, must be different in their preceding and succeeding moments; yet because the consciousness of ordinary people is coarse, they falsely perceive them as a single thought-moment.
When a Bodhisattva observes with subtle wisdom, they see nine hundred births and cessations within a single kṣaṇa. Those births...
Cessation is its own cause and condition. To know this arising and cessation is fundamentally called "seeing the nature.

Since the nature is neither arising nor ceasing, when one sees light, that seeing is not itself the light. These four principles are established; when applied by analogy to all phenomena, there are none that are not thus.
Furthermore, when one sees the seeing, that seeing is not itself seeing. Seeing is already detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. This is because it conditions sensory objects.

The perception of objects is not true; the perception that is detached from objects is likewise delusive. One must simply forget both subject and object simultaneously before words and thoughts can be severed.
To make this clearer now, let us substitute "eye" for "perception": at the moment of seeing forms, the eye is not the form;
at the moment of seeing the eye, the seeing is not the eye. Seeing is already detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. Xuánjué said: "If one uses knowing..."
Knowing stillness: this is not a knowing that lacks an object. It is like a hand grasping an *añjali* (wish-fulfilling jewel); it is not a hand that lacks the *añjali*.

Using the analogy of the seeing that perceives form, if one uses knowing to know knowing, it is likewise not a knowing that lacks an object. It is like a hand forming a fist; it is not a hand that is not a fist.
Using the analogy of the seeing that perceives seeing, it neither knows the knowing of stillness, nor does it know itself as knowing. It is not.
This is ignorance; yet through knowledge, it is made clear. By using the analogy of "the seeing of seeing," that [text] speaks of "knowing-knowledge" while this speaks of "seeing-seeing.

That speaks of "clarity," whereas this speaks of "non-attainment. This may seem credible; however, one must further understand that the meaning of the text is interconnected, and one must not hold to a partial interpretation.
At the time of seeing form, form is not itself the seeing. Even the "seeing of seeing" is still merely a name.
Seeing. If seeing were separate from seeing, seeing could not reach it. Therefore, the preceding text refined the vision of the emptiness of form, transcending "is" and "is not.
If one clings to external objects, all various manifestations are termed deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*).

Only by awakening to the luminous nature of true enlightenment can one transcend the distinction between "pointing" and "not pointing. Within this, true seeing is non-seeing; thus, seeing is the object, and the non-object is non-seeing.
All of these are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed for us the teaching of causes and conditions (up to) how much more so the discrimination that 'it is neither the lamp nor the seeing'."
Ānanda previously asked how one may know the true nature of the self. The World-Honored One then elucidated this point by point:
it is neither superior nor inferior, neither distant nor near, neither caused nor conditioned, nor is it spontaneous; it is neither form nor seeing, nor even the seeing of seeing.
When delusive conditions are completely dispelled, the true nature manifests before one. Yet, being unable to believe it immediately, he again became deeply confused and distressed.
It is not that I do not believe it; rather, I simply wish to thoroughly investigate the subtle details for future sentient beings until they reach a state free of doubt.

For instance, when one person sees a shadow, it appears quite different from what others see, which might seem plausible. However, if an entire nation collectively witnesses a portentous calamity, the case is otherwise.
Faith is truly difficult to attain; therefore, one must advance and retreat in harmony with clarity before beginning to realize that true nature is devoid of seeing.

For instance, when a person with a single visual impairment sees the five colors of a lamp, one cannot say they do not exist; yet if it were not for that impaired person, they would see nothing at all, and thus one cannot say they do exist.
For example, an ordinary person perceives the physical body with its faculties, the vessel-world of mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
Yet, to those Tathāgatas of the ten directions and Great Bodhisattvas who dwell in samādhi, these things are utterly non-existent, like flowers in the sky.
If this seeing-faculty were inherently present as the object of perception, why would the sages not see it? If this [seeing] were caused by conditions upon a naturally existing realm...
It is inherently existent. Why, then, do the sages also not perceive it? If this perceived object were itself the seer, then the act of seeing would have already become the object;
who then would be the one seeing that seeing? If this perceived object is not the seer, then when we now see mountains and rivers, what does this clarify?

It shows that our failure to understand is a false conceptualization, like a person with a cataract grasping at shadows. If one realizes there is no [independent] seer, then one is identical to the true seeing of the sages.
...Thus it is.
○ What is meant by "shared delusory vision" (tongfen wangjian)? [From here to] "because its nature is not that of an eye disease, it is not called 'seeing'.

"Shared" (tongfen) refers to the calamitous phenomena seen collectively by a nation. To apply this principle, one may consider the sense-faculties and bodies perceived within the six realms of existence.
The vessel-world is entirely a product of false conceptualization. Furthermore, the mountains, rivers, and great earth are perceived identically by all beings within the six realms of existence;
yet the Buddha taught that they are fundamentally non-existent, like flowers in the sky. Consequently, the entire assembly was struck with alarm and found it difficult to believe immediately.

Therefore, [the Buddha] took the false vision of a single person and advanced it as an analogy for the false vision of an entire nation, and used the calamitous omens of a nation to draw back and illustrate the optical illusion of a single person’s cataract. This seemed easier [to comprehend].

Explanation: This is to know that distinct objects exist because they manifest a commonality (*sabhāgatā*). If one understands that the visual impairment of a single person is an illusion, then one knows that the portents of calamity affecting an entire nation are not real.

By this analogy, the mountains, rivers, and great earth perceived by those in the six realms of existence—the perception itself, the conditions for perception, the causal conditions, spontaneity, the perception, and the perception of perception—are all equally termed false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). Fundamentally, they do not exist at all. Why?
Furthermore, as for the images perceived by one person or one nation—all being ordinary beings—those others who perceive nothing at all are all designated as sages.
Thus, advancing and retreating in accord with clarity, the faculty that can see the mountains, rivers, and the great earth is called "luminous awareness" (*jue-ming*).

This is identical to a phantom image. If one awakens to the fact that phantom images are fundamentally empty, then this so-called "luminous awareness" is not true luminous awareness. Therefore it is said:

Awareness is not within the cataract; it is truly called the seeing of seeing. Awareness does not establish itself; if it were to establish itself, it would become dependent, and thus it would not be true awareness.

If this seeing is removed, then the clarity of awareness cannot reach it. Since the clarity of awareness does not exist within the fundamental luminosity, how can it again be called awareness, hearing, knowing, or seeing?
Therefore, the perceptions of ordinary people are all equally the clarity of awareness; they are all, in fact, the cataract of seeing.
As for those who abide in samādhi, their true essence is not an optical aberration; therefore, it is not called "seeing.
○ Ānanda, it is like the common deluded vision shared by sentient beings (up to) the false arising through combination and the false death through combination.

The former advances the distinct karma (bipākakarma) by taking it as an analogy for the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga); this [latter] retreats from the homogeneous class by merging it with the distinct karma.
Therefore, it is said that "advancing and retreating are explained together. The obstruction of evil is merged with eye disease; the calamitous phenomenon is merged with the circular shadow.

Although they differ in magnitude, their deluded karma is fundamentally the same. Thus, it is said: "Both are produced by the beginningless delusion of vision; both are falsely conceived within the non-existent."
Because they are seen to exist: from one person, it is extended by analogy to one country; from one country, to Jambudvīpa; from Jambudvīpa, to the four continents;
from the four continents, to the Sahā world-system; and from the Sahā world-system, to the impure lands throughout the ten directions.
From the minute to the manifest, from the near to the distant, this progressive illumination reveals that all are equally the wondrous clarity of awakening.
The mind, failing to understand its own fundamental wondrousness, falsely conceives itself as luminous awareness, thereby creating these illusory conditions for affliction.
Furthermore, what is perceived by one person or one nation—seen as existing here and non-existent there—may perhaps be believed;

however, from this Sahā world up to all the impure realms throughout the ten directions, it is difficult to gain conviction that they all equally perceive an illusory manifestation. Therefore, this analogy is employed for the subsequent text.
It says: "The void arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea. The lands of conditioned existence, as numerous as motes of dust, all arise depending upon the void.
When the bubble perishes, the void was originally non-existent; how much more so the various realms of the three worlds?
If this were not used as an analogy to illuminate that point, it would surely be a futile discourse.
If one can distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction (up to:
the pure fundamental mind and fundamental awakening abide eternally), then that which is called "awakened clarity" is deluded clarity, while the "taintless wondrous mind" is true clarity.

Because these two types of conjunction cannot be precisely discerned, there arise the two kinds of deluded vision—common and individual. Perceiving the existence of subject and object becomes the cause of birth and death. If...
One can penetrate the delusion; "reality" (zhen) is likewise a forced designation. This is because delusion arises from reality, and reality is manifested by depending on delusion.
If one does not cling to reality, then delusion is also non-existent. Therefore it is said: "By speaking of delusion, all realities are revealed; delusion and reality are both equally delusions.
Since they are neither real nor unreal, how can there be a seer and that which is seen? Know that when these two are distanced, then both union and non-union arise.

Death is not birth-and-death; all are unattainable. If one understands this unattainability, then the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing is perfected, and one attains the eternally abiding fundamental mind.
"Ānanda, although you have previously awakened to the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment... how can you distinguish between what is reasonable for union and what is unreasonable?
That same principle applies to darkness and openness, as well as to all various obstructions."
The various phenomena of the world adhered to by non-Buddhists are all held to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*). The World-Honored One refutes this by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Ānanda says, "I see that this nature of awareness is spontaneous; I fear it is the same as the view of the non-Buddhists. The World-Honored One then clarifies the matter through actual events: [Ānanda] knows it is not spontaneous, yet suspects it is not due to causes and conditions.
The World-Honored One then instructs him to describe the causes and conditions of his seeing; [he replies that] it exists because of the sun, the moon, and lamps.
As for that seeing: if there is no object, one does not see. The World-Honored One told him: "Seeing that perceives an object is identical to dependent origination;

seeing that is detached from an object still belongs to deluded clarity. As for reaching a seeing that is itself detached from seeing—how should this be named? Therefore, Ānanda addressed him, saying:
"Regarding natural causes and conditions, their harmony and lack of harmony, my mind has not yet attained awakening; how much less could I understand 'seeing the seeing' upon hearing it again?"

It is not seeing. By means of this, the two kinds of deluded vision—distinct karma and commonality—are further elucidated through their mutual relationship, so that both the seer and the seen are revealed to be mere false imaginings.
These arise falsely in conjunction with the True Mind; they arise falsely as life and die falsely as death.

If one can distance oneself from them, then neither can be apprehended. Furthermore, as stated previously, the wondrous clarity of True Awakening is neither caused by external conditions nor produced by itself.

However, this is not to say it is not spontaneous. Fearing that one might doubt that the nature of the wondrous mind is spontaneous because it arises through the natural conjunction of those causes and conditions, the World-Honored One explained:
"If this wondrous mind were to conjoin with the preceding objects, then in such a conjunction they would be one and undivided.
If they were undivided, then light and darkness, form and emptiness would fundamentally have no boundaries. If seeing were to conjoin with light..."
It is like water mixing with flour: once the flour is kneaded, the water loses its flow. When clarity comes to mix with seeing, it is like space mixing with a vessel:
once the vessel is formed, space loses its emptiness. If seeing is full, it is like water not mixing with fire; where could clarity mix?
If clarity is full, it is like the sun not mixing with the stars; where could seeing mix? If clarity...

If seeing were necessarily distinct [from its object], where would the mixture occur? If there were a mixture, there would be two entities; whether both perish or do not perish, there must be a boundary between them.
If they were conjoined, they would adhere and not separate; if they did not separate, then as light ceases, seeing would cease—how then could one see darkness?

Since their conjunction results in a single unity, light would not be self-illuminating—how then could one see light? If light were conjoined with seeing, then seeing would not be self-perceiving. How [could it perceive itself]?

Regarding the nature of seeing: if seeing were not in conjunction [with light], then seeing and light would necessarily have distinct boundaries. As for this seeing and this light, what would serve as their demarcation?
The Sūtra states: "Neither in conjunction nor in non-conjunction. This is likely a scribal error; it should read: "Neither in conjunction nor in non-conjunction.
The first two sections clarify that it is not in conjunction, while the final section clarifies that it is not in non-conjunction.
Combined. This is of the same intent as the previous statement that [the nature] is neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous.
○ Ānanda, you have still not yet understood that all floating, mundane, illusory, and transformational phenomena (up to the point where one realizes there is nothing to be attained).
Thus far, we have investigated the mind and distinguished the nature of vision, arriving at this point. Why is it that these are described as being like floating dust and illusory transformations?
Ānanda, having fallen into lust and panic, returned to the Buddha’s presence and requested instruction on the initial expedient means of wondrous *śamatha* and so forth;

yet the World-Honored One did not first interrogate him regarding the error of his lust, but instead inquired about the resolve for the Way he had generated, continuing through seven rounds of questioning.
He then said: "This is not your mind; it is the delusive appearance of false thoughts regarding external objects that obscures your true nature.

Have I not already stated that the deluded mind and false thoughts are identical to the external objects before one's eyes? This is fundamentally different from the teachings heard by the followers of the Lesser Vehicle in the past.

Therefore, Ānanda wept profusely with grief and asked further questions in great detail. [The Buddha] then used his fingers to flick a light, causing [Ānanda] to realize that the nature of seeing is immovable. [King] Bimbisāra...
"I ask: do you perhaps understand that the nature is without arising or ceasing? Why, then, do you tell us that we have lost our true nature?

World-Honored One, you raised your finger to test for delusion and showed us the cause of that delusion, declaring that the obscuration of darkness constitutes emptiness and the binding of darkness constitutes form, thereby causing us to realize that body and mind are not real.
Yet Ānanda still recognizes only the conditions of sensory objects; this is why he has not yet dared to recognize them as his own fundamental mind-ground."

The World-Honored One again cited the analogy of the finger pointing at the moon; there, the subject and object are clearly distinguished. He analyzed the eight returns of seeing, showing that the conditions and the mind are inherently distinct.
If this non-returning were my own mind, why would what is seen by the sages and the common people differ in quality?
To claim that there is a separate nature capable of attaining Buddhahood—how can one know this is the true nature of my own attainment of Buddhahood? Thus, the World-Honored One spoke extensively...
The appearances perceived in the upper and lower realms may differ, yet the nature that perceives them is perfectly equal and without distinction.

If even the perception of objects can be considered identical, then as for the perception apart from objects—who else could it be but you? Ānanda again doubted whether the seeing had dimensions of large and small, or distance and proximity;
the World-Honored One replied that these all belong to the external objects. To seek emptiness apart from its vessel is like seeking squareness or roundness [apart from the vessel].
"How is this possible? Ānanda, you have clearly perceived the nature of seeing before you, yet you instead doubt what the body and mind are.

The World-Honored One pointed distantly at the myriad phenomena of form and emptiness, instructing you to choose between them; yet there was neither 'seeing' nor 'not-seeing. Where, then, could there be 'self' or 'non-self'?
Consequently, the entire assembly was bewildered, which is why Mañjuśrī resolved it for them. Since it is said that this is the original..."

There is neither "self" nor "non-self. Where else could there be "this moon" or "not this moon"? If you awaken to the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous nature that is spontaneous, it will cause you to transcend these designations of "pointing" and "not pointing.
Ānanda, the nature of faith is not subject to arising or ceasing; yet you have again confused it with the obscure principle of *māyā* (the principle of primordial ignorance).
The World-Honored One has examined each point to clarify them, so that you may know that the seeing of seeing is not seeing, and he further applies the same analysis to the karma of discrimination.
Advancement and retreat are both clearly understood. Since there is neither "conjunction" nor "non-conjunction" in the interim, where else could there be "harmony" or "disharmony"?
Therefore, the vessel-world, the sense organs, and the physical body are all termed illusory transformations. The essence of these illusory transformations is fundamentally true in its nature.

If this is the case regarding seeing, it is no different for hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing. Extending this principle broadly, it applies to the five aggregates and the six sense bases as well.

The twelve bases and eighteen realms are false in appearance but true in essence; they remain unchanging while following conditions. Where the delusive and the real intermingle, principle and phenomena are as they are (*tathatā*).
There is no birth-and-death to escape, no nirvana to realize, no afflictions to sever, and no enlightenment to attain.
If you are willing to accept this, you may simply let the mind rest. Fearing that residual delusions have not yet been eliminated, I trouble you once more with this instruction.
Ānanda, why are the five aggregates fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Prajñā is termed the "five skandhas. "Skandha" (aggregate) takes the meaning of accumulation; "skandha" (aggregate) is named after its function of covering and obscuring.
From form arise sensation and perception; this is called accumulation. Pursuing delusion and turning one's back on the Real is called covering and obscuring. Yet these five aggregates—

Taking the apprehension of the six sense-objects as its essence and the arising of consciousness as its function, it extends from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness up to phenomena (*dharma*).

Within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, each should possess six aspects; furthermore, they arise sequentially, each with its own distinct characteristics. The *Sāṃkhyāvikrīḍita-sūtra* states:

"The five aggregates are themselves the world, and there are three kinds: namely, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), and the world of wisdom and correctness (*jñāna-samyak-loka*)."

This awakens one to the world. If one takes what is perceived by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the eye-faculty—from form to consciousness—and regards the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) as the perceiving subject, it gives rise to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "Due to movement there is sound; grasping sound, the faculty is formed. This refers to that.
If one takes what is perceived through the inference (*anumāna*) of the mind-faculty—from consciousness to form—and regards the world of sentient beings [as the basis]...

The mundane world acts as the objective condition (*ālambana*) that gives rise to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). This refers to what was previously described as "aggregating conditions within and surging outward.
If one understands the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) according to their true nature (*lakṣaṇa*), this is precisely the wisdom of perfect enlightenment regarding the mundane world;
therefore, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous and true nature of *tathatā*.
“Ānanda, it is like a person with clear, pure eyes... (up to)... you should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is likewise so.
As for the aggregate of form, it refers collectively to the sense organs, the physical body, the receptacle world, the faculty of seeing, and the objects of that seeing.

If a person, prior to the arising of a single thought-moment, wondrously discerns its source—like pure eyes gazing into space where there is nothing at all—it is for this reason that the ten directions...”
The Tathāgatas and the great Bodhisattvas understand that these perceived conditions are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. Even the slightest form or thought is not real;
it is like the illusory vision of floating flowers produced by the fatigue of staring into space. To say that the fatigue arises from "staring" is a misconception;
the fault truly lies within oneself and cannot be attributed to another. Therefore, it is said that because there is no cause, there is no movement. This is used as a metaphor.
Awakened clarity becomes empty and dull; by staring fixedly, weariness arises. Thus, through mutual dependence, they form a vibration.

From this, earth, water, fire, and wind gradually form the faculties, the body, and the vessel-world. Within this, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is likened to flowers before the eyes of one suffering from ophthalmia.
Furthermore, all the various chaotic non-characteristics are likened to the seeing-faculty and its objects. The ancients used these metaphors for the forms of the nine realms; this [text] fears...

This is not so. The preceding passage states that what the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattva perceive while abiding in their own samādhi—namely, the perceiver and the perceived objects—are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
How could this not be a distinction made from the four noble ones? On what basis, then, could it be conflated with the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?
"Ānanda, these floating flowers do not come from space, nor do they emerge from the eyes... (up to)... the aggregate of form is empty and false;
fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature."

It is like the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*): it does not exist through causes and conditions, nor does it arise from the mind. If it existed by virtue of conditions, then since there would be coming and going, it could not be without a location.
Now, when we examine phenomena (*dharma*), what is their actual nature? Since conditions do not exist, how can arising and ceasing be possible?
Therefore, they are likened to "mad flowers" (*keśoṇḍuka*): they do not exist due to space. If they were to arise from the mind, then since they arise from the mind, they ought to possess cognition.

If there is a knower, having departed from the object of cognition, one must then turn back to the locus of consciousness. If there were such a locus, there would be an additional entity within the mind.

If there is no knower, then having already become an object of cognition upon departure, what could possibly exist upon returning? Furthermore, at the time of perceiving an object, there is no absence of discrimination;
why then is it only when there is no discrimination that the nature of the mind is termed "quiescent and eternal"? Therefore, this is likened to delusory flowers and is not [the true nature].
Because of the eyes, there is the mind; because of false grasping, there are the eyes. Because the two delusions of cataracts and optical defects share the same root, the analogy is apt.

Since they do not arise from empty space or the eyes themselves, they are not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); since they appear only when one is fatigued, they are not spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

"Ānanda, it is like a person whose hands and feet are at ease... [up to] ...the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous.

'The hands and feet are at ease' means that, for example, original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) has no sensation. 'Because there is none, they rub against each other' means that, for example, it arises suddenly."

The mind gives rise to painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings. Now, as for these feelings: they do not arise from the object alone, nor do they arise from the sense organ alone;
they require the conjunction of the organ and the object before false feeling can arise. It is like the illusory sensation of touch that arises when two hands come together.

When the organ and the object are in their suchness (tathatā), one fails to perceive the stirring of thought; therefore it is said that, being without [awakening], one is able to obscure right mindfulness.
This is termed the "aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*). If this aggregate of sensation arises from an object, then the object itself must possess sensation, independent of my cognition.

Furthermore, when many people perceive the same object simultaneously, they all experience sensation at once; it should not be that some experience sensation while others do not. It is like the moon traveling through the sky:
to a nobleman, it is a source of joy; to a thief, it is like a grievance. How could there be such a selective process on the part of the objective realm?

[The feeling] arises from this. If these feelings of suffering and pleasure exist because of the sense faculties (*indriya*), then the faculty itself must possess the feeling; why then would it need to depend on conditions to give rise to feeling?
If they necessarily exist because of the faculty, then as when the eye sees a form, once the object has been seen, one should see the faculty upon returning [to it].

If there are those who perceive it, it appears as if a single entity were moving back and forth within the body. Yet the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has no substantial reality; it is likened to illusory contact.

If one realizes that illusory contact is not real, then one awakens to the fact that sensation is without sensation. Since both the sense faculties and their objects are empty, it is not the case that it is known only through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
nor is it something that exists spontaneously.

"Ānanda, it is as if there were someone speaking of sour plums... [up to] the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is empty and false, fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously.

The preceding aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) was entirely one's own delusion; therefore, it is likened to the fatigue of the eyes. The aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) depends upon conditions; therefore, it is like two palms. This.

Regarding the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) within the middle [five aggregates]: its entire substance has no basis. It is provisionally established through the apprehension of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), thereby forming this empty perception. If the six sense objects were absent, the substance of perception would be entirely non-existent.

A plum is a sense object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*); "plum" is said to be a sense object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*); sourness is a sense object of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*). When the person before me speaks of the plum...
The mind takes as its object the realms experienced in the past; these are precisely the mental objects (dharmas).

If the essence of perception were a single entity, it would be impossible for this single perception to arise by taking form, objects, sound, and taste as its objects simultaneously, such that water would only emerge from the mouth. Conversely, if the essence of perception were diverse [for each object], [the aforementioned phenomenon would not occur].
It would follow that there are multiple cognitions. [If] the mouth can emit water, the ears should likewise do so; the plum should flow out on its own. Why do you say it has no taste?
If the cognition of sourness must exist because of speech, then that person [the plum] should naturally flow out. If it does not depend on speech, how could water emerge from the mouth?
[If one] thinks of treading upon a precipice, [one must] supplement the two objects of touch and mental phenomena (*dharmas*), for the object of fragrance (*gandha*) is missing. The plum should...

The section on "Possessing Fragrance" is abbreviated in the text. Because perceptions arise from encountering sensory objects, they are not spontaneous; because there is no source from which they come, they are not produced by causes and conditions.

○ Ānanda, it is like a violent torrent (up to): the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has no fixed form; it changes and shifts subtly, never remaining still for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), and is thus likened to a flowing stream.

As years and months pass by, the transition from youth to old age occurs without deviation, and this is likened to the waves. Its true nature (*dharmatā*) suffers no diminution, and is thus likened to the water itself. Such is the aggregate of formations.

If it must be that my nature exists, then observe by means of that very nature: what is the form of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)? If it must exist as emptiness, then emptiness itself undergoes flux; how could it concern me?
If it were identical to my nature, then as the aggregate of formations flows and moves, my nature should likewise flow along with it.

Yet, why is it that the body undergoes childhood and old age, while the seeing-nature remains unchanging, limpid, profound, empty, and still? It would follow, then, that this is not the essence of my nature. If it must be that it is not my nature, then [the Perfect Mirror...]
As for coming and going, what substance could they possibly be? If they were not false and illusory, why would there be no location for their ultimate arising and ceasing?
Because they flow without flowing, they are not spontaneous; because they do not flow while flowing, they are not produced by causes and conditions.

If the nature were necessarily to flow, then what would this perfect brightness and wondrous stillness be? If the nature were not to flow, then what would these transformations that respond to conditions be? Therefore—
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is itself empty; the wondrous nature is eternally real. Only water somewhat resembles it, and thus it is used as a metaphor.

Ānanda, it is like a person who takes a *piṅgala* jar... [up to] ...the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is illusory; fundamentally, it is neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.
Consciousness relies upon the four great elements, just as a jar contains space. The arising of views of existence and non-existence is like blocking two openings.

Recalling the past or the future from afar is likened to a long journey; the false grasping of those objects is like sending provisions to another country. Yet this aggregate of consciousness does not come from that [object], nor does it go here.
If it were to come from there, it would be like a person remembering Beijing—the place of recollection would not be devoid of its multitude [of impressions].
People say: "How is it that one does not see [the object] coming here from the capital? If it were to go there, the objective realm would appear before one;

how then can this body still remain upon the bed? Formerly, there was a venerable elder who, with a mind full of desire for a courtesan, dreamed of having intercourse with her one day and discharged impurity.
He then thought to himself: "Since she did not come here and I did not go there, yet the act of lust was accomplished."
"The Buddha’s teaching that 'all is but mind' does not deceive me. With this, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, realizing arhatship.
He then understood that the five aggregates are all the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness, and he believed it.

An ancient master used the metaphor of casting off one body to receive another to illustrate a long journey: the present aggregate is this country, and the future aggregate is another country. This does not connect with the preceding passage.
This is likely not the case. The continuous flow of present consciousness and perception can be verified moment by moment; why then must one look back so far to the subsequent aggregates?
Since it goes where it does not go, it is not spontaneous. Since there is no basis for either [the preceding or succeeding states], it is not produced by causes and conditions.

△ Furthermore, Ānanda, how is it that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous true nature of Suchness? [This continues] until: the sense base of the eye is illusory;
fundamentally, it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

In this context, although the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are contrasted, the primary analysis concerns the faculties. By means of the first five aggregates—which are subsumed within the single aggregate of form—one analyzes how all five aggregates are empty;
yet one does not realize that the other four aggregates, such as sensation (*vedanā*), all arise in dependence upon the six faculties and the six objects.
Therefore, it must be extensively refuted. Previously, you designated the clear and bright eye as "real" and the frantic, weary flowers as "delusory.

Yet, these very things—the pure eye and the cloudless sky—are themselves but delusory objects. Thus it is said that both the eye and the fatigue are equally the manifestations of weariness produced by staring.
Why are the pure eye and the cloudless sky given the same name, "manifestations of weariness"? Was it not stated previously: "Form..."?

They are a mixture of deluded thoughts; taking the characteristics of these thoughts as a body, since they are already the marks of deluded thought, how could the six sense organs not be the marks of deluded thought?
Furthermore, it is said: "From the physical body outward to empty space, mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind.
Are these not likewise like floating flowers that appear in dependence upon the mind? Therefore, the six entrances are identical to the eyes.

This arises from the symptoms of fatigue caused by staring. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To falsely identify the four elements as the characteristic of one's own body, and the reflected shadows of the six sense-objects as the characteristic of one's own mind.
While that text speaks of "false identification," it does not yet reveal the reason why they are falsely identified; herein, this is clarified.

This may serve as a complementary clarification to that [previous point]. Now, the nature of seeing is fundamentally without sight; it manifests due to the presence of sensory objects (*viṣaya*). When the objects cease, seeing perishes, leaving no trace or location whatsoever.

Within light there is no darkness, and within darkness there is no light. Whether seeing darkness or seeing light, the nature of seeing remains non-dual. Thus, one knows that this seeing does not arise from the objects.
If it were necessarily produced by the sense organ (*indriya*), then when separated from those objects such as light and darkness, what would it depend upon?
[If you say] it sees: if seeing arises from empty space, since space is fundamentally without cognition, how could there be seeing?

If there must be seeing, and it can see external objects, why does it not see its own face? If it can see its own face, then this is simply the cognition of space; what concern is it for your faculty of sight?

These three locations are fundamentally non-existent; how can they not be false? Seeing exists in dependence on objects; it is not spontaneous. Since the locus of seeing has no origin, it is therefore not caused [by the eye].
Conditioning.
○ Ānanda, it is like a person who uses two fingers to tightly block their ears... [until] ...the ear enters into falsehood;
fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature.

In the preceding passage, because the eye-faculty grasps objects with sharpness, seeing involves attachment; it does not depend on other conditions, directly confronting the faculty and its object—both of which are equally marks of exhaustion.

Herein, the ear-faculty is fundamentally perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-gati*): in a single instant (*kṣaṇa*), no mark of arising can be found; in a single instant, no mark of cessation can be found.
If it were not non-existent, what would one point to as delusion when the ears are plugged? If it were to be confused with [the ordinary], [it would be so].
This is a false conceptualization. Fearing that people might fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), the World-Honored One skillfully employed analogies to bring it to completion;
this is truly what is called unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*). Now, as for the fact that arising and ceasing cannot be apprehended in a single moment:

when the faculties and their objects are perfectly dissolved, it is not only that the sphere of sound is entirely non-existent, but the spheres of the faculties themselves are likewise unapprehendable. For this reason, he specifically selected this as the path of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). Thus, even when the ears are plugged, sounds are produced.
It never ceases throughout the day. Because the locus of sound is impermanent, the faculty of hearing is also impermanent.

It exists where it does not exist; it is constant where it is not constant. How could it be anything other than delusion? Thus we know that both the faculties and their objects are equally manifestations of weariness.

If this nature of hearing were produced by sound, then when the faculty of hearing is silent, hearing would be manifested because of sound; when the sound ceases, hearing would cease. If it were to cease, [then...]

Furthermore, upon encountering another sound, you should no longer hear [the previous one]. If you do hear it, then hearing does not cease because of the sound. Since it does not cease because of the sound, how could it possibly arise because of the sound?
If hearing were produced within the faculty (the ear), what would its mode of hearing be when separated from that auditory object (sound)?

If it were produced in empty space, then empty space itself would hear; what concern would that have with your sense-faculty? Since there is no hearing in any of these three locations, it is not produced by causes and conditions. It arises from fatigue...
Because it produces sound, it is not spontaneous.
○ Ānanda, it is like a person who pinches his nose hard... [until] the nose enters into falsehood; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is its nature spontaneous.
Question: Since the faculty of hearing was shown to achieve perfect penetration (*avivarta*) by using a physical obstruction to manifest its weariness (*klama*), this is indeed logical.

Why, however, are the three faculties of the nose and so forth all manifested as delusion by means of false weariness? What is the reason? Answer: Because the three faculties of the nose and so forth are dull in their apprehension of objects, they are constantly in resonance with the *dharmatā*.
Without employing false weariness, there would be no way to manifest their delusiveness. Why is this? It is because the three faculties of the nose and so forth...
When in contact, one perceives objects; when separated, there is no cognition. If there is no cognition, then not only is the object unknown, but the faculty itself is also unknown.
Since both the faculty and the object have thus completely detached, what thing can be pointed to as being delusory?

Because that [object] is absent, one suddenly contracts [the faculty], resulting in the exhaustion of contact. Due to this exhaustion, obstruction and penetration are manifested; penetration is manifested because of obstruction, and obstruction because of...
Notification: When the channels are open, one perceives fragrance; when they are blocked, one does not perceive it. These arise alternately and are both termed "contact through exertion.

To know cold and know chill is called "touch"; to perceive fragrance and perceive stench is called "smell. At the time of smelling, there is no touching; at the time of touching, there is no smelling.
Since these two states do not coexist, they possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*). If they lack an inherent nature, how could they arise from sense objects? Nor are they...
It emerges from the sense organs. If it emerged from space, space itself should hear it. Since it arises through contact produced by exertion, it is not spontaneous.
Since there is no cause in many locations, it is not produced by causes and conditions.
“Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who licks his lips with his tongue... [from] the tongue’s entry into falsehood, it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of spontaneous nature.
The nature of blandness is constant;
yet the tongue does not taste itself. It is through the exertion of labor that consciousness arises, manifesting sweetness, bitterness, and blandness. Blandness is not bland of itself.”
It is through bitterness that the bland is revealed. Bitterness is not bitter in itself; it is known as bitter by contrast with sweetness. They depend upon one another, just like light and darkness.

When there is bitterness, there is no blandness; when there is blandness, there is no bitterness. Since the nature of bitterness does not exist, what shape could the tongue have? Since the sense organ does not exist, [how can there be a perceiver?]

This cognition is merely a false awareness. Thus, both the faculty and the object are equally the result of staring-induced fatigue. If this cognition of taste were necessarily real, it must have a location.
Since it has a location, it cannot be without a specific indication. If it arose from the tongue, the tongue itself could not taste its own sensation.

How can it know taste? If taste were produced within the tongue, the tongue itself would have to know it; what concern would that have for your faculty of the tongue? If it were produced in empty space, what connection would the tongue and taste have with it?
Since it exists in neither of these three places, it is not produced by causes and conditions. Since consciousness arises from the exertion [of the faculties], it is not self-existent.
“Ānanda, it is as if there were a person who, with one cold hand, touched another warm hand... [until] the body enters into falsehood;
fundamentally, this is neither due to causes and conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.”

The body is suchness (*tathatā*); it must depend on conditions to be manifested. When combined [with conditions], there is cognition, whereby one perceives cold and heat; when separated, there is no awareness.

Its nature is equivalent to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Nevertheless, the enumerations of the name "contact" (*spraṣṭavya*) are quite numerous, as extensively illustrated by examples such as illness, itching, smoothness, and so forth.

Thus, when the six sense organs encounter their objects, there is nothing that is not contact (*sparśa*). Herein, the mention of "cold" and "heat" as forms of contact is merely intended to provide a general illustration.

Now, as for contact: when it is in cold, it is identical to cold; when it resides in heat, it is identical to heat. It exists when joined and is absent when separated—where, then, does its inherent nature reside?

Because contact manifests the body, yet contact has no location, what form could the body possibly have? Therefore, know that both the body and contact are equally the result of staring into exhaustion; they are devoid of that [separate self-nature].
The two objects (dust) are ultimately without substance. If this cognition of touch necessarily arises from an object, then when it is hot there is no cold, and when it is cold there is no heat;
since the object itself does not exist, how can it produce touch? One knows the body by means of touch; yet if touch is not truly touch, the body is likewise not truly a body.
The body does not touch itself, and touch is not produced by the body. If it were produced in empty space, what would it have to do with the body and touch? [It must] depend on their conjunction.
Only then do we know that it is not something spontaneous; since it ultimately has no source, it is not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). As the text says:

"If it were established through the convergence of forces, it would depend on the contact of toil. This is also an error in carving [the woodblock]; it should read: "If it were established through the convergence of forces, there would be toil and contact as its cause."

The meaning is this: [the appearance] exists because it involves labor; if there were no involvement, it would not exist. If you say it is due to contact with labor, then there must first be contact with labor before there can subsequently be mutual involvement.
This would be identical to the case of the laborer who sees flowers; I fear this is simply not so.

"Ānanda, it is like a person who falls asleep when exhausted... (up to)... the faculty of mind enters into falsehood; fundamentally, it is neither caused by conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.
The faculty of mind has no form and is not like the eyes and other organs; it is dark and indistinguishable, like seeing in a dim room, relying upon the states of waking and sleeping."
This is used to discern that [the waking state] is not real. Generally, common sentiment regards the waking state as real and the dream state as false;

therefore, one first discerns that the dream is unreal, and subsequently argues that the waking state is likewise not true. Why is this? What is seen within a dream does not differ from what is perceived in the waking state.

Because it flows and passes away in moments (*kṣaṇa*), one’s memory cannot reach back to it, leading one to falsely claim it was forgotten. How could one know that it was originally non-existent? It is simply that one does not understand its original nature.
There is none. That which is called the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) has no real form; how then could it possess any real dharma?

Therefore, it merely takes as its object the five sense-objects that have already passed away and fallen into oblivion, falsely claiming to see and hear them. It forms concepts of arising and ceasing, which is termed the nature of cognitive awareness. Its entire substance is utterly false and illusory.
This is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If one realizes that objects are fundamentally non-existent, then consciousness and the sense faculties are likewise non-existent.
Thus, one knows that both faculties and objects are equally the result of visual fatigue. This nature of awareness arises during both waking and sleeping.

While it may seem plausible during the waking state, if one examines the dream state, neither the body nor seeing and hearing exist as even a single thing. Since the dream does not exist, how could the waking state be real? [Such is] the nature of awareness.
Dreams are not real, yet people often believe them; since one does not perceive them while dreaming, how could it be otherwise? This exists here but is absent there—whence does its nature arise?

If it arises from the mind (*manas*), why does it not arise by itself? It is called "mind-born" because it relies on the remnants of the other five sense organs after they have ceased their functions.
Seeing belongs to the eye, hearing belongs to the ear; each of the five organs has its own specific domain. Apart from these five, what is there?
Furthermore, what is this thing that can produce cognition? Since dreams occur due to sleep, it is not spontaneous; since they ultimately do not exist, it is not produced by causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the twelve bases (āyatana) fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?
Previously, it was explained that while the objects (viṣaya) are what enter the faculties (indriya), the refutation was directed primarily at the faculties.

Herein, since the faculties are the locus where the objects reside, the refutation is directed primarily at the objects, while simultaneously refuting the ultimate faculty (paramārtha-indriya). This is because the physical eye is the ephemeral faculty (bu-chén gēn), whereas the act of seeing is the ultimate faculty.

They enter by borrowing from one another to gain their names; they dwell by relying on one another to establish their titles. Their grasping at roots is firm and solid, making them intimate with the nature [of reality].
By employing metaphors to illuminate this, one only then realizes they are delusions; therefore, they are refuted first. The floating dust is easy to discern;

it is pointed out directly before one's eyes to cause one to recognize its emptiness and falsity, and thus it is refuted later. As stated previously: "If the eye were able to see, then even those who are already dead..."
The eye exists; why then does it not see? All say that seeing does not belong to the eye, mistakenly taking the nature of consciousness to be real.
Herein, both seeing and form-emptiness have no location. Thus one knows that the ultimate truth is not something truly existent;

only the faculties and their objects, along with the perceptions of knowing, seeing, and hearing, are like illusory flowers—originally non-existent. If one awakens to this non-existence, then all seeing and all hearing are entirely as they are.
The wondrous true suchness-nature of the ālayavijñāna; subsequent passages will follow this pattern.
○ Ānanda, you should now observe this Jeta Grove and its various springs and ponds (up to:
that both form and seeing are two locations of falsehood, fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor arising spontaneously.
If you claim that seeing must be real, does it arise from the sense organ or from the object?

If it arises from form, then it is just like the trees, forests, ponds, and marshes before one’s eyes, which are clearly perceived as soon as one looks. Since it arises from form, it would be identical with form;
if so, one should not see empty space. If you say that because it arises from form, form cannot see itself, then this precisely accords with seeing empty space and the forests and trees before one.
Regarding a pond or pool: there should be nothing to look at. If that form and emptiness were both observed by the same seeing-essence, one would know that this seeing does not arise from form.
If it arose from the sense organ, then form would arise from the eye and be one with the eye; emptiness would not be produced [by the eye], and thus one should not see emptiness.
Why then are emptiness and form so clearly perceived, without partiality? How could the characteristics of form be perceived in such a biased manner?
Does it arise from the eye? If you claim that this seeing does not arise from form, then during the dark fortnight when there is no form, why is there no seeing and no cognition of form?

If you say it does not arise from the eye, then since the visual faculty does not reach other lands or foreign countries, why is there no cognition of those two places as being non-existent, such that one sees them like flowers in the sky?
The wondrous mirror of the mind reflects all phenomena, never encountering obstruction; how could it be...?

It is not the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā). Because seeing is manifested through form, it is not spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Since both form and seeing are non-existent, they are not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Ānanda, listen further to this: from within this Jeta Grove... [until] you hear that both the location of hearing and the sound are false.
It is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously.
The nature of hearing is inherently wondrous, perfectly transcending arising and ceasing; therefore, when the eight musical tones play together, each is heard distinctly.

Although they are heard simultaneously, they follow one another in succession without ever becoming confused. If this nature of hearing were something that comes from the sounds to the ear, [it would not be so].
Ānanda has heard that there is no sound in other places; why then do the entire assembly hear it simultaneously? Could it be that the sound of the bell responds individually to the ears of others?
If it were divided, the bell would possess consciousness; if it were not divided, they hear it at the same time, meaning it does not come solely to Ānanda’s ear.
If it certainly does not come [to his ear], how is it that he hears it when near, but does not hear it when far? Furthermore...
If the ear were to travel to the location of the sound, Ānanda’s ear would have already gone to the place where the drum is; there would be no ear in other locations.

Why, then, are the various sounds of bells, elephants, horses, and so forth heard clearly and simultaneously? If they are heard simultaneously, then the ear does not travel to the location of the sound.
If it certainly does not travel there, then just as a person who has not entered Beijing would not hear the sounds within it, why is this sound not heard? Therefore, one knows that the ear—
Whether sounds are heard or not heard, both are illusory and false. To realize that there is no reality here is the fundamentally wondrous mind.
Question: When distinguishing the states, you speak of "hearing" (*wen*); when concluding, you speak of "listening" (*ting*). What is the difference between listening and hearing? Answer:

Hearing is the original state, which does not arise or perish. Listening, however, involves deliberate mental effort (*manasikāra*). Because it involves deliberate mental effort, it is dismissed as illusory and false. It is like...

The previous [discussion on] the eyes and so forth was of this nature. Because hearing is manifested through sound, it is not self-existent (*svabhāva*). Since both sound and hearing are non-existent, it is not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Ānanda, you again smell this sandalwood in the incense burner... (up to) "...thus, smelling and the fragrance are both false in two respects."
This is neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature.

The nose perceives its object through contact; such perception necessarily depends on conditions for its arising. Because it depends on conditions for its arising, the sense organ alone does not produce it.

If it were necessarily produced by the organ itself, then when the nose comes into contact with fragrance, why would it require another object such as wood? If it certainly does not require another object, then the nose [would perceive] by itself.

[Objection: It is said that "hearing" is not the actual object. One perceives fragrance through hearing; fragrance belongs to the external sense-field (*bāhyāyatana*). Because it belongs to the external sense-field, the nose does not produce the fragrance.

If it were produced within the wood, the wood would possess the fragrance inherently, and one should perceive it immediately upon contact. Why then must one rely on burning smoke to perceive the fragrance?

If the fragrance necessarily resides in the smoke and the wood, then at a distance of forty *li*, where there is neither smoke nor wood, how could one perceive the fragrance? If it is certainly not [in the smoke or wood]...

Wood. If you burn wood other than that [which you claim produces fragrance], why do you not perceive its scent? If it were certainly not the nose that perceives it, why would the eyes or ears not smell the fragrance?
To say it is neither the nose nor something else, nor both, is to say it is nothing at all. In truth, it is like a phantom flower; there is no basis for further interrogation.

Such is the wondrous nature of things—how could it have a cause? If it were produced from empty space, then space would be without interruption; what need would there be for smoke from burning? Thus, there is the perception and the non-perception.
"Ānanda, you constantly hold the alms bowl amidst the assembly during the two times [of meal]. (Up to: ... that which tastes the flavor and the flavor itself—both are equally false and illusory;
they are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously."
The nature of blandness is eternal and constant; yet the tongue does not taste itself, and thus it cannot even recognize blandness—how then could it recognize flavors?
