If the nature of flavor were known, it would necessarily arise dependent upon the tongue. Sweetness, bitterness, pungency, and acidity each have their own primary cause; when one receives food, sweetness and bitterness are vividly present.

When separated from food, what flavor does the tongue produce? A single tongue cannot possess multiple flavors; when examined from all perspectives, they are found to be non-existent. If this is not false, what else could it be?
If you say that the perception of flavor must not arise from the tongue, then why is it that sweetness, pungency, saltiness, and blandness are not perceived when the body touches food?
This tongue is not the tongue; it is equally named an illusory flower. That which is not the tongue is itself the tongue; its original name is the nature of the treasury (tathāgatagarbha).

If this nature of taste must arise from food, yet the food is not self-aware—if the food were aware, it would possess mind-consciousness. If it possessed mind-consciousness, [it would be a sentient being].
The taste is produced by the food itself; what concern is this for Ānanda? If this nature of taste were not caused by the food, why would vinegar not be salty, and why would honey not be bitter?
If it were produced from empty space, then eating space would be flavorless; yet if taste were not born from emptiness, then emptiness itself would possess flavor.
If it were salty, it would always be salty; the head and face would experience that saltiness, becoming like a sea fish. How could empty space selectively maintain saltiness?

Your tongue and the flavor combine to give rise to the nature of the cognition of taste; therefore, it is not spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Since there is no fundamental basis upon which to rely, it is not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
“Ānanda, when you habitually rub your head with your hand in the early morning... (up to)... thus both the body and the tactile sensation are equally illusory;
fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they of a spontaneous nature.”
Contact has no fixed location; it is only known when there is conjunction. Thus, by citing the rubbing of the head, one reveals that cognition and sensation exist:
the body acts as the agent, and the hand acts as the object. Yet, the body does not touch itself; it relies on the hand to perform the rubbing, while the body becomes the object of the rubbing.
Since neither the agent nor the object can be definitively established, how could this not be illusory? When the hand rubs the head, it becomes one with the head. If [the hand] were to rub...
When the foot is active, the head is without cognition; how much more so for the four limbs and hundred bones? As one presses here, one perceives there, yet there is no fixed location.

If each part were individually devoid of it, then everything would be dark and unconscious; what, then, could be called "contact"? If each part possessed it individually, there would be many contacts; which contact would be yours?
It is not the case that there is some separate entity outside the body that acts as your contact, waiting for contact to manifest itself.
Because it is known, it is not spontaneous. Because both body and hand are absent, it is not produced by causes and conditions.
○ Ānanda, that which you constantly take as an object within your mind (up to the point mentioned) is such that both the mind and its objects are equally false;
fundamentally, they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they spontaneous in nature.
The mind has no separate object; it takes as its norm the remnants of those five sense-faculties that have already passed away and ceased.

What constitutes this norm? It is because both the wholesome and the unwholesome possess a fixed rule. If these wholesome and unwholesome norms were separated from form, sound, odor, and taste, they would utterly not exist;
they would be purely neutral (*avyākṛta*). As for this norm, if it is identical to the mental factors (*caitta*), [then...]
[The opponent asks: "The dharma is the mind itself. How can it be called a 'dharma-object' (dharmāyatana) by taking the five sense-objects as its object?

If it were separate from the objects, what would the mind look like to be called a 'dharma-object'? If it existed in a location distinct from the mind, it would not be without a specific reference point.

Color, sound, fragrance, and taste each correspond to their respective five faculties; which among these is the dharma separate from the mind? Even if one were to grant that such a dharma exists, [what would be] the self-nature of that dharma?"
As for its nature: is it known or unknown? If it were known, it would be the same as that of others; what concern would it have for Ānanda?

If you say it is identical to the dharmas and identical to the mind, why then is the mind divided into two? If it is not known, then the brightness, darkness, forms, and emptiness before one’s eyes are clearly and vividly reflected;
apart from these, what further thing could there be that is called a "dharma"? If you allow that such a thing exists, it cannot be non-manifest.
[The Master] said: "How could there be any object outside of emptiness within the human realm? This mind is not the mind; it is apart from phenomena and yet identical to phenomena.

It has no location whatsoever. How could it not be illusory? When conditions are encountered in opposition, they form sensory objects; therefore, it is not self-existent. As for phenomena, they are fundamentally non-existent."
Therefore, they are not causes and conditions.
Furthermore, Ānanda, how are the eighteen *dhātus* fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness?

The faculties and their objects are suchness (*tathatā*); fundamentally, there is neither subject nor object. Consciousness abides between them, establishing the views of "internal" and "external"; thus, they are called *dhātus*.

Now, consciousness is intimately close to the mind; it is truly difficult to discern its delusions. Therefore, one first destroys the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), with consciousness being dealt with last. Why is this?

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute the illusory substance of a single lifetime and serve as the basis for the six sense organs. Objects have no self-awareness; they manifest their characteristics because of the organs.
The organs likewise lack cognition; consciousness relies upon them therein, and thus there arises discrimination. If one can [dissolve] these four great elements...
If [the self] does not exist, the six sense organs produced by it likewise do not exist. Since the organs do not perceive their objects, what could the objects possibly encounter?

With neither organs nor objects present, even if consciousness were to exist, what would it have to employ? Thus we know that when the Tathāgata destroys the false to reveal the true, he establishes a sequence within that which is without sequence.
"Ānanda, as you have understood it, visual consciousness arises with the eye and forms as conditions... (up to)...
thus the eye, forms, and the three elements of the form realm are fundamentally neither causes and conditions nor of spontaneous nature."

This was previously explained as the conditions for the arising of the sense-faculties and the body; now, the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is revealed, which is entirely different from what was said before.

This is done to address previous doubts, hence it is said: "As you have understood," referring to the seven inquiries mentioned above, within what I have taught, it is not these two types [of causes].
With the eye and form as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; the eye possesses discrimination, while the object of form is devoid of cognition. Thus, consciousness arises.
In that case, the mind would reside therein. The World-Honored One cited this to refute [your position]:

"Regarding your statement that consciousness abides between the sense organ and the object, does it arise because of the eye, or does it arise because of the form? If it arises because of the eye, the eye does not know itself, apart from those external objects."
There is nothing that can be differentiated. If you say that differentiation occurs without depending on external objects, then as for your visual consciousness:
is it blue, or is it yellow? Since there is no indication, from what basis could its boundaries be established? If it were produced from form (*rūpa*), then consciousness would be form;
when form ceases, consciousness should also cease. If it ceases, who would know whether it is empty or form? It is just like [the case of] consciousness itself.

When it is empty, one knows that form undergoes its own transformations; what coming and going can there be for consciousness? Since consciousness neither comes nor goes, from whom could the realms be established?
If you insist on seeing consciousness as arising simultaneously with the sense organs and their objects, then half would belong to the organs and half to the objects;

when combined, they become one, and the nature of consciousness itself becomes detached. When it is in form, it is form; when it is in the organs, it is the organs—what then is this consciousness that you designate as a realm? It is detached.

Thus, the two unite. If one knows [the mind] returns to the faculties but does not know it returns to the objects, what would consciousness (*vijñāna*) look like? At what location could it be said to exist as a "consciousness-element" (*vijñānadhātu*)?

If these are not combined, then there are neither faculties nor objects; the characteristics of an element would naturally not exist. Since the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is entirely absent, it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Because it falsely relies on the True to be established, it is not something that exists spontaneously (*svabhāva*). To realize that the false has no existence is the Treasury (*ālaya*).
The nature first exists.
○ Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand: with the ear and sound as conditions, the ear-consciousness arises (up to:
then the ear, the sound, and the sphere of sound—these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature).
The preceding passage used the two bases of the eye and visible form to refute the meaning of "non-element" (*adhātu*).
Herein, there are further three bases: the ear and sound. "Element" (*dhātu*) has the sense of delimitation; it is so named because it reveals that the ear and sound are distinct from one another.

If these two exist, it is admitted that consciousness arises based upon them. If these two were fundamentally non-existent, what would be called "consciousness"? This concludes the entry into the text of the preceding section.

Specifically, it was refuted that the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) do not exist; now, we provisionally rely upon the organs and objects to determine that consciousness cannot arise from them.

If this consciousness were to arise in the ear, then just as with movement and stillness, the ear would not hear itself. If it does not hear itself, it would not know [the sound]; what form, then, would the ear have?
If it were to arise in the hearing [itself], hearing would not hear itself. If hearing necessarily heard itself, then those things such as movement and stillness should not be external.

Objects have no form or appearance; the ear is merely an object of touch. How could they intermingle to produce the realm of consciousness? If consciousness were produced from sound, then sound would know itself.
If sound possessed consciousness, what would it have to do with your hearing? If you do not hear, you likewise cannot know where the sound is located.
Even if you were to know the sound, it would not mean that consciousness exists within the sound. If you truly do not know it, then [the situation remains the same].

Regarding grasses and trees, one falsely conceives that consciousness arises; therefore, it is not spontaneous. Since they were originally non-existent and cannot be relied upon as a basis, it is not through causes and conditions.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand—namely, that the nose and fragrance serve as conditions to produce nose-consciousness (up to the point where it is said)—then the nose, the fragrance, and the fragrance-element:
these three are fundamentally neither of the nature of causes and conditions nor of the nature of spontaneity.
First, determine the location of the nose. Consciousness arises dependent upon the nose; yet even this producing nose has no name.

How, then, could the consciousness produced by it have any realm? Next, distinguish to which category this cognition belongs: it is neither flesh nor empty space, nor is it the cognition of fragrance.
If cognition itself does not exist, from what could the element (dhātu) be established? If it arises because of fragrance, fragrance does not know itself;
who then knows the consciousness of fragrance? If it knows fragrance, it does not arise from fragrance; if it does not know it, it cannot be called "consciousness.
Since fragrance does not know fragrance, on what basis is the element established? If consciousness does not know fragrance, then the consciousness-element is not established by reason of fragrance.

"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you have clarified— that the tongue and flavors act as conditions to give rise to tongue-consciousness (up to)— then the tongue, the flavors, and the tongue-element,
these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature."
If this nature of consciousness arises because of the tongue, why does it depend on things such as sugarcane or sour plums to be called "knowing taste"?
If taste were necessarily not produced from sugarcane and such things, then when you taste your own tongue, would it be sweet or bitter? If the tongue were bitter, it should not taste itself;
who would know it to be bitter? If it were truly bitter, it would be one with bitterness and thus should not [be tasted].
If it knows sweetness, how much more so for bitter, pungent, and salty? Since it can mutually know both existence and non-existence, even this "knowing" is not fixed;
what, then, is this consciousness produced by the tongue? If such consciousness does not exist, on what basis can the sense-field (dhātu) be established?

If consciousness must necessarily arise from taste, and taste itself possesses the knowledge that discriminates between sweet and bitter, then it would be identical to the tongue of another person—what concern would it have for you? Since it has no concern for you, who [is the knower]?
One knows that this is taste and not non-taste. Taste is not a single entity, yet the tongue does not possess multiple bodies. If they were combined into one, there would be no discrimination;
because there is no discrimination, one would not even perceive taste—how then could consciousness arise? If discrimination is clearly present, then consciousness does not arise from taste.
If consciousness arises from the union of the tongue and taste, and ceases when they are separated, how can this be considered the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*)?
"Ānanda, furthermore, regarding what you understand— that body-contact serves as a condition for the arising of body-consciousness (up to)— then the body, contact, and the body-element,
these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature."
If this consciousness necessarily arises in dependence upon the body, the body itself should experience contact; what need would there be for cognition through conjunction?

Since cognition occurs only through conjunction, when separated, cognition would be absent. What, then, would the body cognize? If [cognition] were produced because of contact, then prior to the conjunction, your body should not exist.
How could there be consciousness without a body capable of knowing contact? A solitary object is devoid of cognition; thus, cognition does not arise from contact. The sense organ is not self-aware;
thus, cognition does not arise from the body. An object does not touch cognition, yet the body’s cognition possesses touch.

These two opposing sides appear to constitute a boundary. However, when one realizes that the body is itself contact and contact is itself the body, and neither side exists independently, then no boundary remains.
[This] is established. When combined, there is cognition; it may then be called "the body. When separated, there is no awareness;

how then would it not be identical to empty space? Cognition and non-cognition are indeterminate from moment to moment; from where, then, could your bodily consciousness arise? Since consciousness itself does not even exist, [how can there be a body]?
For what reason are the elements established?

○ Ānanda, furthermore, regarding that which you understand—the mind and mental objects acting as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness (up to the point mentioned)—then the mind, mental objects, and the mind-element:
these three are fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.

If it arises from the mind (*manas*), its arising cannot be without an object-condition (*ālambana*). With volition (*cetanā*) as the condition, consciousness (*vijñāna*) exists; apart from conditions, volition has nothing upon which to deliberate.

Since volition itself lacks the act of deliberating, how can it give rise to consciousness? Even if it were capable of giving rise to it, what would consciousness be used for? Mind, intellect, and consciousness are one essence with three names;
there have never been three distinct dharmas. Yet, when differentiated, the three dharmas are perfectly distinct. If [volition] can give rise to consciousness, why does it not give rise to itself?

The mind is thus; mental consciousness is likewise. When they are identical, it is called "mind" (*manas*), which is precisely the "intention" (*manas*). Since mind and consciousness are fundamentally non-existent, what is there to be called "mind"?

And what exists as "consciousness" or "intention"? Consciousness is also like this: they exist in relation to one another and do not exist in isolation. They are merely false names and have never possessed substantial reality.

Since their essential nature is unreal, from whom could the realms (*dhātu*) be established? Whether they arise due to phenomena, or whether they are immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*), the five sense objects appear with clarity.

Regarding the five sense faculties, what is it that is called "mind" (*manas*) and "phenomena" (*dharma*) which can give rise to consciousness? Therefore, it is asked: what is the nature of phenomena?
If they are merely objects of inference, then since past moments do not endure, what phenomenon could be present before the mind for consciousness to arise from?

If you say that it is precisely those [past] things arising and ceasing that are called "consciousness," then when there is arising, it is the phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) that arise; when there is cessation, it is the phenomena such as form that cease. Which of these is [the object]?
Consciousness arises and ceases together with them; consciousness is identical to dharmas such as form. When it arises, empty form is manifest;

when consciousness is identical to dharmas such as form and ceases, discrimination is entirely absent. Since there is no discrimination, what form or characteristic can consciousness have? Because consciousness has no form, the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu) is not established.

How then can there be the dharma of consciousness? If [consciousness] were produced by the union of the sense-faculties and their objects, then since the five objects already confront the five faculties, why...
This refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*). When meeting with its corresponding object, consciousness arises.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has often spoken of the principle of combined causes and conditions...
[up to] ...the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, the dharma free from conceptual proliferation.”

Since Ānanda has already stated that the causes and conditions of combination are all worldly transformations, he seems to understand that the eternally abiding true mind is not a product of such combination.
Now that he knows it is not a product of combination, why does he again conflate "causes and conditions" with "spontaneity" to raise this question?
This is likely because he considers the sense organs, the body, and the physical world to be divided into two categories—the intimate and the remote—and thus the meaning of the sense organs...

The "Self" has already been refuted above. Since the meaning of the "receptacle world" is more remote, I hope you will further elucidate it; therefore, I must request this again, which is not a mere repetition.

The previous statement—that one does not know that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, space, and the world, are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind—although it simultaneously refutes both the two divisions of the "root-body" (the faculties) and the "receptacle-world," the primary point of refutation lies in the root.
The body. These—the earth, water, fire, wind, space, views, and consciousness of the lower realms—are also refuted by means of two parts.

While the object of refutation is primarily the vessel-world (the physical environment), although their meanings appear to be interconnected, they are distinguished by their degree of intimacy. If one were to ask by conflating the present with the past, [it would be a confusion].
Thus, Ānanda was truly ignorant. Why? Because in the preceding passage, the Buddha stated, "I have spoken of worldly causes and conditions;
they are not the ultimate truth," clearly indicating that this was so. Why, then, did he ask again?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "You previously expressed weariness with and detachment from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas...
(up to) 'it is like a whirling firebrand, never resting.
Above, it was stated that the nature of wondrous enlightenment is neither cause nor condition; why then do you constantly say it possesses the four kinds of conditions? And yet, in the world..."
The Venerable One said: "I have spoken of the various worldly laws of causes and conditions, which are not the ultimate truth.

Not knowing what constitutes the ultimate truth, I therefore asked about worldly causes and conditions. The World-Honored One then clearly informed me: 'You previously sought detachment through the Śrāvaka vehicle;
though you were learned, it was of no avail, for you could not escape the peril of the Mātanga woman. Thus, I entreated the Tathāgata for his wondrous *śamatha*."
Since [the elements such as] earth and so forth are the primary skillful means, I have elucidated that the nature of the storehouse (ālaya) is utterly distinct from the mundane world.

Why, then, do you again confuse it with causes and conditions or spontaneity, thereby falling into self-doubt? This is because, though the true medicine is present before you, you fail to recognize it.

Indeed, the characteristics of the mundane world are stubborn and obstructive, lacking integration; yet if you insist on their non-harmony, they would be like space, which does not harmonize with anything.

If form were [absolutely] so, the world could not be established or sustained. If one were to dogmatically insist on their combination, then light and darkness, form and emptiness, could not be distinguished.
If they were both combined and separated, then birth and death, and death and birth, would have no interval or cessation; by what cause, then, could there be liberation?
Furthermore, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is not like this, for it is able to follow conditions without changing; thus it is identical with form...
Emptiness appears to be a composite; yet when one seeks its substance, it cannot be found. Because it remains unchanging while following conditions, it is neither form nor emptiness.
It appears not to be a composite, yet its great function manifests before us. Those who wish to eliminate conceptual proliferation should investigate this.
○ Ānanda, it is like water forming ice, and ice returning to water.
Ice originally depends upon water; it has no external substance of its own. Water, congealed by the wind, becomes functional. This serves as a metaphor for all dharmas.
All are based upon the *tathāgatagarbha* as their substance. This nature manifests according to karma, giving rise to the appearances of the world.

In this way, the entire appearance is identical to the nature; it is not something else joined with it. Since it is not a conjunction, it is not produced by causes and conditions. Because it manifests according to karma, it is not spontaneous.
That the nature is thus is the true reality (*tathatā*), not a forced assertion. If one wishes to speak of a blending or a harmonious union, it is like water becoming ice.
How could it be that [the elements] combine with one another to form ice? Nevertheless, the meaning of "beginning" and "end" must be distinguished.
Initially, due to non-awakening, earth, water, fire, and wind arise, forming the phenomena of the world. The ignorant outsiders designate this as "spontaneity."
World-Honored One, by means of causes and conditions, one breaks through that notion of spontaneity.

Taking non-awakening as the cause and the movement of thought as the condition, that which is not caused by a cause exists where there is no existence, like water forming ice due to the seasons and conditioned by the north wind to take on its form.

Sentient beings cling to these forms and are deluded regarding their true nature, thus needlessly undergoing the cycle of saṃsāra. Therefore, the Buddha appears in the world to point directly to the fundamental source.
This matter serves to cause one to recognize the fundamental nature. It is like pointing out that ice is itself water; there are no external causes and conditions that combine to form ice.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) seek water apart from the ice, while those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) cling rigidly and fail to realize its melting unity. Herein it is revealed that the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world are entirely the single *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Throughout vast eons, there has never been any other substance; who, then, undergoes birth and death? Therefore, this is not the same as mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Observe the nature of earth: from the coarse great earth down to its subtlest form, it is merely a verbal designation and lacks any real substance.
When water freezes into ice, it is clearly not a case of [new] combination; yet when dust forms into earth, the appearance of combination is manifest. Analyze it further and further."
Their essential nature is entirely non-existent; with what, then, could they be joined? Dust and earth are both merely different names for the element of earth (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*).
They are no more distinct in essence than ice and water. Since there is no difference, they cannot be said to "join. When analyzed, one perceives emptiness and does not perceive form;
since form itself does not exist, what substance could combine to form a minute particle (*paramāṇu*)? When joined, one perceives form and does not perceive emptiness; [yet] emptiness...
Since they are not even seen, with what could they be joined? Thus one knows that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is harmonious without being blended, and joined without being conjoined.

For the conscious mind to calculate this as natural causes and conditions is entirely termed frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Why? If one were to dogmatically insist that it is not blended, [it would be a false attachment].

In reality, this earth element is formed from the aggregation of atoms. If one dogmatically insists that it is a composite, then upon analyzing it down to the point where no form remains, there would be nothing left to combine.
If it were necessarily spontaneous, why rely on the aggregation of atoms? If it is not spontaneous, then who piles up the mountains and peaks?
If it were not due to causes and conditions, how could it be called "non-awakening"? If it were necessarily due to causes and conditions, its nature would be identical to annihilation.

Thus, when the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha remains unchanging while following conditions, the three dharmas are clearly manifest; when it follows conditions while remaining unchanged, even a single dharma cannot be found.
Nature and characteristics are fused as one; essence and function are sovereign. Therefore, *Nirvāṇa* is called the "Secret Treasury.
Thus it is said: "There are only words, but no real meaning at all. Not only was there no gate where Ānanda asked his question, but even the World-Honored One’s answer lost its way.
Who can understand and take up this principle that transcends the narrow path?
"○ Ānanda, the nature of fire has no self; it relies upon various conditions... (until) there are only words and explanations, but no real meaning.
The ancients drew the hexagrams and said that the 'void within Li' is the image of an empty mind and the absence of self.

Now, as for 'having no self,' there is nothing that is not the self; therefore, earth, water, and wind all possess the nature of fire. Although this nature is inherently present, it must depend upon conditions."
It arises like fire within wood: when drilled, the fire appears; like fire within stone: when struck, sparks fly; like the waters of the great ocean:
stirred by the wind into flames; or like fire in the sky: dependent upon tinder and a mirror. Since it depends on these various conditions, it is neither a blending nor a joining.

Yet, it cannot arise from nothingness on its own; thus, it is also not a case of non-blending. This is merely the mind of consciousness engaging in false conceptualization and asserting it with force.
[Such] attachments result in error. If one is free from verbal expression, then all that is conceptualized is empty. Why is this?

If it were due to the sun and a mirror, since these are situated in different directions, there would have to be a visible trace of the fire’s coming and going. If it were not due to the sun and a mirror, yet one sought fire by facing water, fire would not arise.
Therefore, as stated in the preceding text: it is neither through causes and conditions nor not through causes and conditions; it is neither through conjunction nor not [through conjunction].
The harmonious union is a realm difficult to conceive; only the Sages know it. To engage even a slight amount of discursive thought has already delayed [the realization] by eight *kṣaṇas*.
○ Ānanda, the nature of water is not fixed; its flow and stillness have no constancy... (until) ...there are only words and explanations, but they possess no real meaning whatsoever.
The nature of fire is called "non-self" because it follows wherever it dwells; water is said to be "indeterminate" because it conforms to high and low.
If it flows constantly, then from humans to devas, all would be submerged and drowned; if it were always still, then the myriad things of the world would have nothing to sustain them.

To be wondrously attuned to the requirements of the moment—is this not the hidden nature (*tathāgatagarbha*)? If they must necessarily combine, the moon ascends in the heavens and the pearl is held in the hand—[yet] heaven and the abyss remain distinct.
Separated as they are, how could they meet and produce water? If it were necessarily from the sky, humans should be able to see it; since it cannot be seen, it does not descend from the moon.
If it were necessarily from the pearl, the pearl should flow forth of its own accord; yet the pearl does not flow of its own accord, so for the pearl to produce [water] is illogical.
Nevertheless, it is not that it exists spontaneously without a cause, nor is it produced without the coming together of conditions. It is just like the act of recollecting.
When those who have passed before feel pity or resentment, tears flow from their eyes; when they think of sour plums, water issues from their mouths;
when they recall precious treasures, their bodies become lustrous. Such watery natures pervade the entire Dharma-realm and are accomplished according to thought;
how could this not be following one's karma?
"Ānanda, the nature of wind has no substance; its movement and stillness are not constant... (until) there are only words spoken, yet they possess no real meaning.

Awareness is luminous, while space is dark; their mutual dependence creates agitation. Thus, the great element of wind exists. Now, as for this great element of wind: when there is movement, wind arises."

If it does not move, it does not exist; therefore, it is said to have no substance. Furthermore, Ānanda, when the robe moves and the wind brushes his face, the wind does not emerge from the robe, nor is it produced from the face.
Space is quiescent and does not intermingle with them; thus, it exists in neither of these three places. Its essential nature is fundamentally empty.
Ordinary people, with their coarse consciousness, claim that it is "wind" that moves mountains, roars through trees, flattens grass, and stirs up waves. Yet, if one examines it minutely...
Contemplate this: when the world moves, observe the movement and stillness of the body; observe the movement and thoughts of the mind. There is nothing that is not termed the wind-element.
Outwardly, it sweeps through the entire realm; inwardly, it is the movement of every thought within the multitude of beings. Following karma is thus; what fixed location can there be?
To harbor thoughts regarding form is merely to fall back into delusive conditions.
○ Ānanda, the nature of emptiness is formless; it is manifested through form... (until) there are only words and explanations, entirely devoid of real meaning.
The extent of what is excavated reveals the depth of the void; this is what is meant by saying that the void is manifested through form.

The four great elements, such as earth and so forth, are the particulars, while the great element of space is the universal. The universal and the particular encompass one another, and all are uniformly termed the "five greats.

They pervade everywhere and contain one another, existing nowhere not present; therefore, they are called "great. Because they mutually displace, mutually contain, mutually conceal, and mutually manifest—precisely because they mutually conceal—[they are so designated].
The entire earth is contained within empty space, yet one does not realize that empty space is contained within a single mote of dust.
Because they manifest one another, when the earth is excavated, space is revealed; such is the nature of their principle. How could it be subject to exhaustive inquiry? Therefore it is said:

"There are only words and explanations, but no substantial meaning. If [space] is revealed because of excavation, then the excavation itself emerges from the earth; space does not arise of its own accord. Its emergence—
When earth is seen as empty, their natures appear contradictory; yet this emptiness does not emerge because of digging—it is the solid, vast earth. Where, then, can one see emptiness?
If they are separated, form and emptiness stand as two, each with its own boundaries. If they are merged, form and emptiness are both forgotten, each lacking an inherent nature.
Only this nature of emptiness encompasses the ten great elements; thus it dwells within the four great elements and the six sense organs, governing both the sentient and the insentient.
Within the realm of emotion, because there is no birth yet nothing that is not born, the earth emerges and reveals the void. Although things arise, they have never truly arisen;
thus, the excavation naturally brings forth the earth. The followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this; desiring to abandon birth in order to seek non-birth, they fail to see the truth.

How could one know that birth is itself non-birth? Thus, the analogy of emerging from the earth is applicable. If it is so for the insentient realm of the vessel-world, how could it not be so for the sentient root-body?
Abiding between the two—space and earth—one illuminates the Perfect Equality.
“Ānanda saw that awakening is devoid of cognition and exists only because of form and space” (up to) “there is only verbal expression, but no real meaning.

From the time the seeing was analyzed through the eight returns, until Ānanda himself confessed that he could not distinguish this seeing from non-seeing before the myriad objects and images, the entire assembly was bewildered. Mañjuśrī then requested: “These various objects and images, and this...”
"What is this essence of seeing? The World-Honored One replied: 'Its original nature is the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind.
Ānanda had conflated it with spontaneity, causes and conditions, and their combination. The World-Honored One explained each of these in detail.

Although Ānanda understood that the nature of seeing was thus, he feared he might not yet be able to extensively infer its application to the aggregates, sense bases, and elements; therefore, [the Buddha] expanded upon it."

The explanation becomes even more clear. Ānanda had thoroughly realized the nature of the sense organs and the physical body, yet he had not yet fully integrated his understanding with the external world of vessels. He therefore requested further instruction once more; thus the text proceeds in connection.
Previously, the inquiry moved from the sense organs and the body outward to the world of vessels; hereafter, it moves from the world of vessels inward to the sense organs and the body.

These elements mutually support one another, so that the *tathāgatagarbha* nature is revealed as clearly as pointing at one's own fingers or palm. This refers to what is known as the sentient and the insentient.
It is one with true reality. Above, it was said that one cannot discern what is seeing and what is not seeing; yet it was not known why this was impossible.
Now, the World-Honored One points to seeing, form, and emptiness, examining them together: they do not constitute a single entity, and even when reduced to their essence, they remain divergent.
Whether identical or non-identical, different or non-different—this is truly what is called the severance of the path of words and thought, where the movements of the mind find no place.

All these insentient things are equally named the six great elements; they fully encompass the faculties of sensation and hearing and embrace the ten dharmas—all are the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Since neither "this is seeing" nor "this is not seeing" can be apprehended, how could there be names such as "identical substance" or "different substance"?
If one can awaken to this essential meaning, one has attained Buddhahood prior to kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; even if one has not yet realized it, it is simply a matter of falling into...
Prince Mo’s nature was such; this is not a matter of forced rhetoric. If one directly accepts it as it is, how could there be anything that is not realized?
○ Ānanda’s cognitive nature has no source... (up to) ...there are only words and explanations, but they possess no real meaning.
Vision is triggered by objects; appearances arise because of the sense organs. Since both appearance and vision lack inherent nature, they are like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another.
This precisely points to the nature of consciousness, which has no source. A single organ does not manifest cognition, and a single object does not manifest appearance.

Consciousness dwells between the two, functioning through discrimination. Yet when its essential substance is investigated, it cannot be found at all; therefore, it is said to be "without source. The mutual correspondence of the organ and the object is fundamentally...
Suchness is beyond analysis. Within it, consciousness sequentially points and designates. If separated from the sense organs (*indriya*), consciousness has no place to abide;
if separated from objects (*viṣaya*), consciousness has nothing to cognize. If there were necessarily no cognition, who would distinguish between color and emptiness?

If light and darkness had no place to abide, what would constitute the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue? If there were necessarily no sense organs (*indriya*) or objects (*viṣaya*), this consciousness should emerge from empty space. If [it were] necessarily...
When emptiness emerges, it is neither characteristic nor perception. If there is no perception, who is it that cognizes empty-form? If there is no characteristic, what establishes awareness?
Without cognition and without awareness, how could it not be equal to empty space? If there were cognition and awareness, it should not be identical to material phenomena.
If there were truly no cause, one should be able to cognize other objects independently of conditions; yet seeing relies upon characteristics, and characteristics are projected toward objects.
What is the form of consciousness? If it must have a form, it should be something that can be pointed out. Apart from the sense organs and their objects, what is this consciousness?
If nothing can be pointed out, its substance is fundamentally non-existent; how could it not be the hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha)?

If one awakens to the fact that the nature of consciousness is originally non-existent, then one will know that seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving—along with the preceding earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as all phenomena—are each in accord with the true nature.

All-pervasive and perfectly complete, Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed do not obstruct one another. In the preceding passage, "perceiving touch" and "perceiving cognition" collectively encompass the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).
Here, "seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing" collectively encompass the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*). In the previous text, the earth and the five organs were both described as "pure";
here, the conscious mind possesses the function of discernment, and is therefore termed "wondrous enlightenment. If we discuss [the principle of] following karma, first—
If one seeks water, fire, or wind in a single location, they appear in that one location; if one seeks them throughout the entire Dharma-realm, they appear throughout the entire Dharma-realm.

The consciousness-mind follows karma, and there is nothing that does not conform to it; therefore, all are equally called "Great. The nature of the sensory faculties, the physical body, and the vessel-world is thus:
there is no birth-and-death from which to escape, and there is no nirvana to be realized. This is the definitive teaching of the Buddha. Those of the present age should...
To wish for the east while facing west—abandoning this and grasping that—is how utterly erroneous it is!
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the subtle and wondrous instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata... (up to)...
spoke verses before the Tathāgata to praise the Buddha.

It begins with the examination of the mind and the discernment of views and concludes with the universal integration of the seven elements. Throughout the intervening sections, through methods of affirmation and negation, refutation and critique, it elucidates the true mind and the nature of the treasury.

This is termed the "subtle and wondrous revelation. Previously, one clung to the notion that the body exists apart from the self; now, it is understood that even the "true" is identical to the "delusory.
Reaching this point, truth and delusion are fused together, and right and wrong are both extinguished. The mind becomes coextensive with the pervasive presence of the seven elements.
Therefore, it is said that the mind pervades the ten directions. The seven great elements all arise as illusions based upon the true mind;

hence it is said that empty space and the worlds are all like objects held in the palm of one's hand. Since they arise as illusions based upon the mind, the entire totality is the mind itself; thus it is said that they are all identical to the wondrous mind.
The world arises as an illusion based upon the mind, and the physical body, in turn, dwells within the world; therefore, the world is empty...
Space, compared to a leafy object, is appropriate; the physical body, compared to a mote of dust, is likewise so.

What was previously stated—that one did not know that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous true mind—is only now realized.
As the subsequent text says: "Empty space arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the sea; the minute dust-like lands of the outflows are all [likewise]."
It arises dependent upon emptiness; when the bubble ceases, emptiness itself is fundamentally non-existent. How much more so for the various realms of the three worlds? This is what is praised here.
Nevertheless, we teachers of discourse should examine ourselves: does our body and mind at this very moment exist outside of emptiness?
Is it within empty space? If you have not yet attained such resonance, by all means do not speak of what has already passed.
*“The Wondrous, Profound, Total Retention, Immovable Honored One”* (through to) *“Without passing through kalpas, one attains the Dharma-body.”*
"Sublime and profound" refers to the Prajñā of the ultimate truth; "total retention" refers to the liberation of the conventional truth;
and "Immovable Honored One" refers to the Dharma-body of the Middle Way. First, Ānanda requested the initial expedient means of sublime śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.
When the World-Honored One investigated the mind and distinguished the seeing, he specifically took the clear realization of the eternally abiding true mind as the primary expedient means.

Since the time of the *Āgamas*, the principle of the three truths that had been heard was not yet unified with the true mind; having undergone gradual cultivation and progression, it was not called ultimate or firm.
Now, since the mind has been realized and the true and the delusive have merged, they are equally termed the "storehouse nature. Therefore, [it is] one.
When all matters reach this point, they become ultimately firm and solid. The single mind and the three truths are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, sovereign and free like a king.
What was previously unheard is now heard; therefore, it is called "rare.

What was previously heard involved cultivating one portion of the three virtues, realizing one portion of the *dharmakāya*, and severing one portion of ignorance; this is merely the common discourse of the Buddhas.
Now, in a single thought-moment, the inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas are suddenly extinguished; without relying on incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one attains the Dharma-body.
Is this not truly rare? An ancient said: "Ānanda’s understanding was through intellectual realization, not through actual attainment.

Some have said that it was for the sake of the entire assembly and not for Ānanda alone. Others have said it was a temporary vision granted by supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). I say this is not so. Fundamentally...
The nature of existence is seen once and forever seen; how could it be seen for a mere moment through supernatural power?
Since it is said that each and every one knows their own mind pervading the ten directions, how could it be that one attains it while another does not? Ānanda later advanced to the second fruit;

his advancement occurred within the state [of realization], for the Dharma-body does not undergo increase or decrease. Furthermore, the Dharma-body possesses realized virtues, which, once realized, are realized forever.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a prince born by natural right, fully endowed with his status. While his father remains on the throne, he is temporarily lodged in the Eastern Palace;
how could he be compared to one who seeks office as a subject? Furthermore, it is like a scholar: the principle to which that young student proceeds is equal to that of the Three Dukes.
Those who advance to office do not do so merely for the sake of literary composition; if one were to obstruct the principle because of rank, one would perish for kalpas.
There is none. For one who perceives the nature [of reality], to use principle to dismiss the stages would cause the entire assembly to fall into the error of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).

As the subsequent text states: "Although the principle is realized all at once, the obstacles are eliminated simultaneously with that realization; yet in practice, gradual cultivation is required until the causes are exhausted through successive stages.
This may serve as clear evidence.
"May I now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King... until the *śakara* [vajra] mind is unshakable.

Because the Dharma-body possesses the virtue of realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it is said that he "attains" it; because the Wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*) possesses the virtue of retribution (*vipāka*), it is said that he "becomes" it;

and because the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) possesses the virtue of great grace, he delivers beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Since the Dharma-body has already been realized but the Wisdom-body is not yet perfected, he gives rise to this vow.
In Sanskrit, this is called *Vairocana*; here it means "Perfected in Merit. Because his benefit and salvation are inexhaustible, he is termed the "Jewel King.
His emanations pervade lands as numerous as atoms, universally responding to the nine realms; these are his transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).

These three bodies respond perfectly, neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor separate—this is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*). Such a profound mind cannot be known by others; only the Buddha can bear witness to it. Not...
To abandon evil and seek purity, one must practice by means of that very evil; therefore, he vows to enter the evil age in order to deliver sentient beings.

"May I become a Treasure King" is the vow that the Buddha-way is supreme and shall be accomplished. "Deliver those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges" is the vow that sentient beings are boundless and shall be delivered.
"May I become a Treasure King" implies that one must certainly study the unsurpassed Dharma-gate; having vowed to deliver sentient beings, one must certainly [practice].
I shall sever boundless afflictions. Having fulfilled the four great vows, this may be called the profound mind. I vow thus;
I further entreat your compassion to provide subtle instruction so that I may swiftly achieve the indestructible nature of emptiness.
Even if all else might perish, my resolve shall remain firm and can never be shaken.
△ At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (up to) the sound of the Dharma he had preached still left room for lingering doubt and regret.

Although Pūrṇa had previously expounded the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths and was ranked by the Buddha as foremost therein, the present subtle and wondrous exposition provides a further revelation.
Even the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) cannot yet be seen, let alone heard. To use a metaphor, it is like a deaf person.

The Buddha’s original intention was to lead me to awakening, yet I did not realize this and instead increased my confusion and distress. If even we who are among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) still harbor lingering doubts and regrets, how much more so for Ānanda, whose residual taints (*vāsanā-āsrava*) have not yet been eliminated?
This is because within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the myriad phenomena of the world are described [in a limited manner].
All these things are impermanent, arising from the conjunction of causes and conditions.

Now, hearing that the nature of the treasury is primordial, being neither cause nor condition, neither a conjoining nor a combining, and that all dharmas are truly eternal—this is utterly different from what was previously taught. Therefore, I make this request.
If we rely on the principle of inner secrecy and outer manifestation, every single point is nothing other than a model established for future generations.

"World-Honored One, although all the sense organs and objects in the world (through) undergo successive transitions, ending and beginning again in an endless cycle, Pūrṇa has already realized true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) but is not yet familiar with wondrous existence (*prabhāsvara*).
Because of this true emptiness, it is logically consistent that [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure."

If one does not yet know that wondrous existence, one will be able to follow [the truth] through phenomena; thus, there is the error of clinging to principle while being deluded regarding phenomena, and conversely, there is the profound mystery of transcending entanglements within phenomena themselves.
As the preceding text states: "The wondrous enlightenment is serene and still, pervading and encompassing the Dharma-realm, swallowing and exhaling the ten voids."
"Manifesting according to karma" can be said to fully reveal both phenomena and principle, and to be complete in both negation and affirmation.
Pūrṇa (Manzhi) bases his request upon the actual realization present before him, desiring that the principle be illuminated through the very facts so that there may be no further doubt.
Formerly, Master Changshui had doubts regarding this point and specifically asked Chan Master Langye Jue: "If the fundamental nature is pure and still, why..."
"Suddenly mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise. Jue asked, "Since it is fundamentally pure and still, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Changshui attained great enlightenment; furthermore, the question and answer were non-dual. What did Changshui realize?
Let those everywhere who possess the eye of discernment examine this. Those who have not yet passed through the barrier must not let it be consumed by mere words.
Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said regarding earth, water, fire, and wind [up to] "they thirst for the unsurpassed compassionate teachings of the Tathāgata":

in the preceding passage, the nature of grasping was challenged by means of their characteristics; it was shown that they are fundamentally pure and thus should not suddenly give rise to mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

In this present section, the characteristics of grasping are challenged by means of their nature; empty space and form cannot coexist, and water and fire do not harmonize. How, then, can they all equally be called the Store-nature (ālaya-dhātu), which is omnipresent?

There is no obstruction. Indeed, grasping at characteristics makes it difficult to realize the nature; they appear as incompatible as water and fire. Yet, if one uses the nature to dissolve characteristics, what room is there for form and emptiness?
It is like the four great elements already inherent within a piece of wood: when drilled, fire appears; when wrung, water comes forth; when shaken, wind arises;
and when burned, it becomes ash. If one seeks them before they have been brought forth, they cannot be found; yet the nature itself is all-encompassing.

How could there be any contradiction? If [the elements] exist as distinct entities after they have already formed, then water, fire, wind, and earth would each possess their own distinct capacity for contact.

If one claims they do not merge, then there should be visible boundaries of water and fire within wood. If they were definitively merged, then the world would be indistinguishable from empty space and form.
Therefore, it was said previously: "There are only words; there is no real meaning at all. How could it be that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra did not understand this? It is simply...
I wish to distinguish these matters with subtle clarity so that future generations may surely believe them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa [until] they reverently listened to the Buddha’s voice, silently receiving his instruction.
There is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and there is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Śrāvakas shatter existence to enter emptiness, thereby realizing the ultimate truth.

Therefore, the preceding passage states: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, while abiding in their own samādhi, perceive that the seer, the conditions for seeing, and the characteristics of what is conceived are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. For this reason, those who are still in training...
He could not help but feel utterly bewildered. Since Pūrṇa had already attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), his vision was identical to that [of the Buddha];

thus, it is said that "the fundamental nature is pure. Because he did not understand how things arise in accordance with conditions, he asked: "How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly come into being?

By clinging to the substance while remaining deluded regarding its function, the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is established based on this. For those of the Hīnayāna only know how to shatter existence to realize the Truth; they do not know how [phenomena] proceed from the fundamental substance.
When functioning arises, how could one know that the nature of true ultimate reality is originally thus? Therefore, one falls into the error of clinging to a fixed nature.

Those who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness—referring to the śrāvakas who have already realized the two kinds of emptiness regarding persons and phenomena, but have not yet realized that persons and phenomena are not non-empty—are unable to turn toward the Mahāyāna because they have [only] attained emptiness;
therefore, the question asks about "pure and original suchness," as they have not yet attained non-emptiness.

Therefore, the question is asked: how can mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? If one can thoroughly comprehend the meaning of emptiness and non-emptiness, then both the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits will accord with the One Vehicle.

The Buddha said, “Pūrṇa, regarding what you have said—that it is fundamentally pure (up to) ‘the nature of awareness is profound stillness and luminous essence’—as for ‘the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous,’ this luminosity is not luminosity.
As for ‘fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous,’ where there is no [discursive] awareness, that is true awareness.”
Because its true substance is ignorance, there is nothing it does not illuminate; because its wondrous function is non-awakening, there is nothing it does not perceive.
Such are its substance and function; they cannot be forcibly named. You have now asked me, "How did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

as if you wished to give them a forced name. Therefore, it was said above: "Now, observe closely: what is the form of each and every dharma? And below it says: "When one person gives rise to [a thought]..."
Truly returning to the source, the worlds of the ten directions would all vanish away. Thus we know that when Pūrṇa asked his question, the Tathāgata rebuked him for wishing to apply a forced name.

Since you wish to apply a forced name—referring to what is called "awakening" and what is called "clarity"—is it that the nature is inherently clear and thus termed "awakening," or is it that the nature has nothing to clarify and must depend on an object of clarity to manifest itself?
Is that which is capable of awakening called "clarity"? If its nature were inherently clear, it would be utterly detached from subject and object;

since there would not even be a "clarity" that clarifies, how could there be an "awakening" that awakens? Since both subject and object are absent, what thing could be pointed to as the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?
To say that "the awakening is not clear" precisely points to the painful spot of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. Therefore, Pūrṇa also took the point of the World-Honored One’s interrogation as his question.

If this true nature were not luminous, there would be nothing to be illuminated. Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "You say that if it were not luminous, there would be nothing to be illuminated;
yet because you have something to be illuminated, I ask: how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?

If there were nothing to be illuminated, who would be called 'mountains, rivers, and the great earth'? Because there is something [to be illuminated], it is not called true awakening. If there were nothing..."
When illumination is examined, both illumination and non-illumination are unattainable. This is because illumination and non-illumination are merely provisional names used to dispel them.
If both illumination and non-illumination are cleared away, then the nature of the profoundly still and luminous awareness is likewise unattainable.

Therefore it is said: "By speaking of the false, the various truths are revealed; yet since the false and the true are equally two kinds of falsity, that which is neither true nor false—how can it be called real?"
"To see what is seen" is precisely this meaning.
○ "The nature of awakening is necessarily luminous; delusion constitutes the awareness of luminosity" (up to) "thereby establishing once more neither sameness nor difference."
This explains and establishes that the aforementioned absence of "that which is illumined" (so wu suo ming) constitutes the delusion of the awakening to ignorance (wu ming jue).

That which has "something illumined" is not the illumination of the inherent nature of awakening (xing jue). If there is nothing illumined, then not only is there neither illumination nor ignorance, but the nature of the awakening's profound clarity (jue zhan ming xing) [is revealed].
Then it cannot be apprehended. Why is it unapprehendable? Because its nature is inherently luminous; fundamentally, there is neither subject nor object.

It is because of the establishment of a deluded subject that a deluded object comes into being; thus it is called "luminous awareness. Since awareness is fundamentally luminous, how could it be manifested by means of an object of illumination?

It is awakening (*bodhi*). Because of the deluded subject (*viṣayin*), the deluded object (*viṣaya*) is established. Since the object is established because of the subject, the subject is in turn established because of the object.
Because the true and the deluded are contrasted, the true essence is taken as the same and delusive thought as different.

Because the subject and object are contrasted, that which establishes [the object] is taken as the same and that which is established as different. That which establishes is precisely awakening-illumination; that which is established is precisely [deluded] illumination.

Awakening. In the following text, they are likened to space as being the same, and to worlds as being different. In the true essence of the nature of awakening (*prakṛti-avabodha*), there is fundamentally neither sameness nor difference.
When one turns away from the truth and follows delusion, then [the world] blazes forth into difference. Because the nature of original awakening (*mūla-avabodha*) is eternally one, it is "same";

because the characteristics of that which is awakened to are eternally distinct, they are "different. Since the clarity of awakening differs from the clarity of what is awakened to, one establishes "sameness" based on "difference" in order to encompass both.

By dispelling identity and difference, one establishes the clarity of the awakening to intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said that there is neither identity nor difference. All of these exist because there is something to be clarified.
Because there is that which is clarified, there arise clarity, non-clarity, and the nature of the profoundly clear awakening.
If there were nothing to be clarified, then there would be neither clarity nor non-clarity, nor would there be the nature of the profoundly clear awakening.
○ Thus, through such mutual disturbance and dependence, weariness arises (until: "therein, neither identity nor difference exists; truly, conditioned phenomena do not exist").

In the true nature (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no subject (*grāhaka*) or object (*grāhya*). Yet, subject and object are falsely established; therefore, disturbance is produced. Because the subject depends on the object for its establishment, and the object depends on the subject for its formation, they arise reciprocally.
Thus, through mutual dependence, weariness arises. This weariness has no cause, just as the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) has no [external] cause.
Therefore, when one remains motionless and stares for a long time, fatigue arises; consequently, one perceives distinct, delusory appearances of flowers within empty space.

This turbidifies the pure eyes and gives rise to worldly toil, creating views of existence and non-existence. One regards empty space as non-existent and uniform, while regarding the world as existent and differentiated.

Having simultaneously discarded both sameness and difference, one further posits "neither same nor different. This is just like discarding both the real and the false, and then establishing that awakening.

The profound name "clarity" (*zhan mingzi*) refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). All of these arise because there is something to be illumined, thereby giving rise to such mutually dependent, delusive names.
If there were no object, it would not even be the nature of the profoundly clear awareness; how then could there be illumination or non-illumination?

First, dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; subsequently, empty space and the world manifest. This is what is meant by "the subject establishing the object. The three types of characteristics [are explained] in the following text.
Continued: Regarding "first, the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness," these constitute the capacities established by causes; therefore, they are called "mutually dependent.
From "the mutual dependence of the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness results in agitation" up to "by these causes and conditions, the world continues."
The wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally luminous; originally, there is neither subject nor object. Because of the obscuration of emptiness, subject and object arise in mutual dependence.

Thus, based on the capacity to perceive, the perceived luminosity is established; conversely, based on the perceived luminosity, the perceiving capacity becomes manifest. These two depend upon one another, both relying on ignorance. Though unmoving, they move; therefore, wind arises.
Since the nature of wind has no substance of its own, it depends upon movement and stillness: when there is movement, wind is produced.
When still, the wind ceases; because of movement, wind arises. This principle must necessarily be so. Initially, movement gives rise to wind; as movement persists, it becomes obstructed.

When wind arises, the clarity of awareness and its object depend upon one another; when obstruction is formed, clarity and awareness establish solidity. Thus, the subjective capacity is abandoned for the sake of the pure object, which is grasped with firm persistence and remains unmoving;
therefore, the Golden Wheel is formed. As movement persists, it becomes solid; as solidity persists, it moves again. Because it moves, wind is produced once more.
Wind belongs to wood; wood can produce fire. As for wind and metal rubbing against each other, it is like obtaining fire in the world by drilling wood with a fire-drill.

Fire overcomes metal, yet metal can produce water; therefore, there is a water-circle (*āpa-maṇḍala*). Because fire and metal possess the relationship of husband and wife, they are able to produce offspring.
Water is produced from metal, and its nature is to moisten from below. Fire is produced from wood, and its nature is necessarily...
It ascends; therefore, it is called "mutual emergence. Gold belongs to the category of Earth (*pṛthivī*); its solidity and dryness form the continents and lakes.
Water is characterized by its fluidity, forming the great oceans. When vapor causes gold to produce moisture, water then receives the pneuma of fire and gold;
thus, fire appears within the sea. Earth receives the pneuma of gold and fire. Since gold can generate water, rivers and streams constantly flow. The trigram *Kǎn* represents water.
The position of the male belongs to Yang; Li represents fire and is the position of the female within it. The husband is strong and the wife is weak;

as the Yang energy is vigorous and abundant, it forms high mountains, which is the principle of fire ascending. Earth occupies the position of Kun, belonging to Yin where Yin is strong and Yang is weak;
thus the Yin energy ascends and manifests as grasses and trees. Therefore, when struck, it produces flames.
When melted, it becomes water; when burned, it becomes earth; when squeezed, it becomes water—none of these destroy the constituent essence of the vapor.
Metal, wood, water, and fire mutually overcome one another, yet they also mutually give rise to one another, serving as seeds for one another’s succession;

thus the world continues in an unbroken stream. As the preceding text states: "Within the state of dark obscurity, darkness coagulates to form matter. However, it was not yet known by what means this occurs.
Regarding form (*rūpa*), herein it is minutely and clearly distinguished that its arising has a cause; thus, this is no empty discourse.

Although the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism speak of the principles of the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) regarding generation and overcoming (*sheng-ke*), they do not know why these five elements arise.
Zhuangzi designated them as "spontaneity" (*ziran*). Formerly, there was a Daoist who questioned Mahamati on this matter, yet Mahamati was unable to answer. Later, [the Daoist] read...
At this point in the sutra, [the Buddha] leaned on his desk and sighed deeply, first expressing his admiration for this Daoist who had so skillfully investigated these principles.

Furthermore, Pūrṇa, [you have explained that] delusion is not caused by another, [extending through to: "bound together by common karma, their union and separation form the transformations of the world."
The delusion of luminous awareness—how could there be any other error? The error lies in the luminosity of awareness; this is called "the cause establishing the object.

Why is the luminosity of awareness considered an error? It is because Pūrṇa did not understand that the fundamental is luminous and fundamentally wondrous, yet he reckoned there to be a "capable of illuminating" and an "object illuminated."

Once the objective realm has been falsely established, a false subjective capacity arises in response. From this, the eye can see, the ear can hear, and so on, up to consciousness being able to discern.
When expanded, there are six; when condensed, there are only four: seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, knowing with the tongue, and feeling with the body.

The nose is also called "hearing," and the mind is also called "knowing. These achieve transformations, each restricted to its own specific function, entangling those of similar karma as they pursue their objects.
Regarding their categories:
○ When seeing light and color, the manifestation of light gives rise to the perception of seeing (up to: "by these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession").

This is not inherently limited, yet it becomes limited; therefore, when one sees the color manifested by awareness of light, this is also the case where the subject (the capacity) perceives the object (the perceived). It is not [inherently] seeing.
Yet they are seen; thus, the "object" (so) once again becomes the basis for the "subject" (neng). Both subject and object are delusions;
this is to pursue delusion with delusion. From this, hatred and love arise. Furthermore, since hatred and love are equally conceptualizations, why speak only of the "flowing of love" as the seed?

Is it that hatred does not constitute a seed? It is simply because [love] is more prevalent that it is mentioned. Thus, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings, from the beginningless..."
At this juncture: because there are various forms of affectionate attachment and craving, there is saṃsāra.

Since hatred does not desire coexistence, the passage below describing those who die and become sheep shows that hatred also constitutes a seed [of rebirth]. Thus, we know that the previous statement refers only to the majority of cases.

When discussing the four modes of birth (*yoni*), it is said that "womb-birth arises from emotion" (*qing*) and "egg-birth arises solely from thought" (*xiang*); these can be described in terms of love and hatred. "Moisture-birth" arises through contact...

This is indeed a matter of emotional response; how could it not be a case of biased attachment? Transformation occurs through separation and response, which truly stems from joy and aversion. Thus, while transformations involve change, separation, and response, these merely discuss the general outline.
The ancients used what is perceived during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to explain this passage, but I fear this is not necessarily the case.

Rather, it was because the World-Honored One, in response to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s question regarding how the mountains, rivers, and great earth could suddenly arise from that which is fundamentally pure and serene, [addressed this].
This directly narrates the causes for the arising of the root-body, the sensory faculties, and the objective world. At that time, no manifest aggregates (*skandha*) can be found;
of what, then, could one speak as being the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Pūrṇa’s conceptualization and craving bind together... (up to) ...by these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession.
The terms "parents" and "offspring" encompass all four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*); they do not refer exclusively to the human realm. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"Egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—all take lustful desire as the cause for the formation of their nature and life. One should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root."
This text states: "Greed is the root. This accords with that [previous teaching]. They propagate their seeds one after another, rooted in lustful greed; this constitutes the notion of attachment.
They devour one another in succession, rooted in the greed for killing; this constitutes the notion of aversion. Humans become sheep, and sheep become humans, repaying one another in turn.
Although rooted in the greed for theft, it is in fact the mutual interaction of aversion and attachment that serves as the seed. When attachment reaches its extreme—
From hatred, love is produced; extreme hatred becomes love. Sexual misconduct is also called theft, and killing is likewise theft, as detailed in the Vinaya.

Regarding lust, killing, and theft, taking one implies the other three, like the *akṣa* fruit cluster, for they must be categorized together. Greed, hatred, and delusion are spoken of as three yet are one.
Therefore, life after life, one remains perpetually bound in fetters.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds [of afflictions]—from here until "therefore, due to this falsehood, they end and begin again"—summarize the continuity of the three types [of delusion].
This clarifies that delusion is not from another source; the fault lies in the luminosity of awareness (*jñāna-prakāśa*). Because of the luminosity of awareness, one establishes further luminosity.
To fully understand "nature" is to realize it is luminous awareness (*vidyā*). From this luminous awareness, the deluded capacity arises; this is the manifestation of phenomenal characteristics.
Because of the existence of this deluded subject and object, one falsely perceives the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—confined where there is no confinement, and seeing what does not exist.
From beginning to end, these are nothing but a single state of deluded sentiment.
Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous awakening is fundamentally wondrously awakened and luminous... (until) when would it ever arise again?
His intention was that fundamental wondrous awakening and luminosity are no different from the Buddha. Since there is no difference, there was originally nothing;

yet through deluded movement, these mountains, rivers, and the great earth arose. If this is so, then prior to such movement, [all sentient beings] were of one essence with the Buddha. All sentient beings—

All have realized the purity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*). Because of deluded movement, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise. Although the Buddhas have now already realized this, they still share in the deluded movement of sentient beings.
If it were not for this deluded movement, how could the pure original enlightenment be divided into distinct entities?
When sentient beings move their thoughts, a world arises; when the Buddhas move their minds, how could a world not likewise arise? If it truly does not arise, then [the world] would never arise.
How could the Buddha not be without difference? If they were necessarily not different, when would mountains and rivers ever arise again?

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra uses the Buddha-nature within the bonds of affliction (*saṃsāra*) to challenge the Buddha-nature beyond the bonds. Now, Buddha-nature is likened to gold ore; that which the Buddhas realize is like the pure gold extracted from the ore.
Although it passes through ten thousand kalpas, the nature of the gold does not change. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Once perfected, it is eternally so."
The golden essence never again becomes ore. Although it was originally gold, it must ultimately be refined through smelting to achieve its perfection.
The delusion of sentient beings is like gold within ore; they harbor many kinds of misconceptions, the first being that they do not believe there is gold within the ore.
First, there are those like the icchantikas who do not believe that ordinary beings possess Buddha-nature. Second, although they hear of it, they fail to discern it;

they pick up common stones and laboriously smelt them, yet even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they never obtain gold—just so, those non-Buddhists ultimately do not perceive their nature.
