Third, although they believe in ore and stone, they cannot distinguish between them at all, nor do they know how to refine them.

This refers to those ordinary persons who practice blindly; fourth, although they are able to identify [the gold], they do not know how to refine it through the application of fire so that it may be perfected, and thus they do not obtain the gold.
This refers to the Śrāvakas who analyze [phenomena]; as stated previously, they are unable to achieve unsurpassed Bodhi.

This refers to those who separately become śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or celestial Māra-kings. Fifth, although they understand the smelting with fire, they do not comprehend the balance of the civil and martial [methods];

these are the bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional. Sixth, they skillfully understand the civil and martial methods of the firing process and employ the wisdom of the Middle Way to smelt and refine it until a small portion of gold is produced;
these are the bodhisattvas of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*). Thus they progress further, up to the fifty [stages].
Only after undergoing repeated smelting and refinement does one obtain pure gold; only then does one realize wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra did not understand this sequence and thus raised this question. Indeed, it is a vital inquiry. Furthermore, this doubt is not unique to the Śrāvakas; Bodhisattvas also possess it.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* records, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha asked: "If all sentient beings are originally enlightened Buddhas, why..."

Therefore, there is further the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*). If this ignorance has existed in sentient beings from the beginning, for what reason and by what causes and conditions does the Tathāgata further say that they have been enlightened since the very beginning?

Furthermore, if ordinary beings in the ten directions were originally enlightened in the Buddha-way and only later gave rise to ignorance, when would all the Tathāgatas ever again give rise to all afflictions (*kleśa*)?
[In this case,] the question is concise while the answer is exhaustive; the answer is exhaustive while the question is concise.

[The preceding section is] abbreviated. [The subsequent section on] "influence" (*yǐngxiǎng*) may be read together with this. Hereafter, five parables are cited in succession to clarify the intent of the question;
it may be said that this represents the height of compassion.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "For example, like a person who is lost... (up to)... awakening (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa are also like this."
The original direction does not shift; it is only those who are deluded who erroneously cling to it. If one awakens to the original direction, one will naturally repent of one's own folly.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas, by virtue of their abiding in *samādhi*, see that this world fundamentally has no existence, being like flowers in the sky.
Sentient beings falsely identify with the clarity of awareness and cling to the existence of luminous cognition, thereby giving rise to the appearances of the mundane world.
However, these various characteristics do not exist because of delusion; they are like a direction that does not shift or move because of one's confusion.
Nor are they non-existent upon awakening, for while these characteristics are fundamentally non-existent, they are established as existent through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If one is free from false conceptualization, they can never be found—just as the direction one is confused about is fundamentally neither south nor north, yet is conceptually designated as such; if one is free from that confusion, [the designation of] south...

The north is clearly present; that which was previously mistaken is now known by oneself to be an error. Thus, it is not only that the Buddhas certify it as being fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*);
when sentient beings were deluded, how could it have ever existed? This answers the question of how things could suddenly arise from a state of non-existence.
If one can attain wondrous awakening, then what is this world where various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) suddenly arise from a state of non-existence?
Next, regarding the analogy of the flower seen by one with cataracts: it answers the question of how the conditioned outflows (*āsrava*) could ever arise again.

Now, emptiness originally has no flowers; they are the delusion of the disease of cataracts. Failing to realize this delusion of cataracts, one falsely recognizes arising and ceasing, taking this to be real—this is madness.
To desire further rebirth is to be both mad and deluded. This analogy has three parts: first, due to the defect of cataracts, seeing arises where there was no seeing; that which does not exist...

There is. This is like ordinary people who are deluded regarding fundamental awakening (*mūlajñāna*) and perceive the signs of the world. Next, it is like when the cataract is removed and the flowers vanish;

yet, failing to realize the fault of the cataract, they calculate that the flowers have already ceased to exist. They perceive a cessation where there is no cessation, seeing as "non-existent" that which is not non-existent.

This is a metaphor for the various *śrāvakas* who falsely cling to the attainment of the cessation of worldly signs. Third, it is like having seen the flowers vanish and then desiring them to arise again, while [the vision] is perfectly full and complete.

Regarding what Maitreya asked, the World-Honored One employed parables to lead him to speak for himself; thus, a single response resolved both points. This may be called a skillful and indirect revelation.
The Dharma-body possesses the virtue of realization (*vidyā-guṇa*), like gold within ore; Nirvāṇa possesses the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), like wood turned to ash.
Therefore, regarding these two upper metaphors, the principle must be realized instantaneously; through this realization, they are simultaneously resolved. As for the two lower metaphors...

In this matter, phenomena are gradually eliminated and their causes are exhausted in succession. If the former analogy were absent, then non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) would incur the fault of harboring long-standing false views;
if the latter analogy were absent, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) would fall into the error of nihilistic denial.

Regarding those with long-standing false views, the non-Buddhists believe that Buddha-nature originally does not exist and is only attained through cultivation—like one who fails to recognize ore and instead smelts other stones, passing through kalpas without [finding anything].

As for those who deny the existence of the seeds: although ordinary beings know that Buddha-nature is inherently present, if they do not rely on cultivation, it is like holding ore and mistaking it for gold—it will ultimately be of no practical use.
If one were to claim that there is no nature of gold within the ore and that one must smelt other stones to obtain it, why would gold not be produced?
Although the nature exists within the ore, it must be obtained through smelting; if it is not refined, the ore-stone will never [become gold].
It becomes gold. If ordinary beings lacked Buddha-nature, their cultivation of merit and refinement of conduct would ultimately be in vain.

Although it is inherently present, it is defiled by afflictions; therefore, it must be realized through cultivation. Thus, whether it is bound within the fetters or released from them, it is the same yet appears different.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s questions are twofold: first, he asks how it is that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise;
second, he asks how earth, water, fire, and wind can coexist without conflict. Having finished answering the first question, the following section answers the second.

"Pūrṇa, furthermore, as to what you asked regarding how the fundamental natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused (up to) 'therefore they give rise to affliction and the phenomena of the world':
space is one, while the various forms are different. This manifestation of unity and difference does not obstruct one another, nor do they become confused."

Because it is unobstructed, when the sun shines, there is light; when clouds gather, there is darkness. Because it is unmixed, this and that are clearly distinct, and the sky and the sun remain vividly as they are.
While the shifting and competing of various forms never ceases, empty space remains quiescent and eternally abiding.
Because they mutually contain one another, both are fully manifested: "This is a mountain," "This is the earth," and "These are the myriad phenomena arrayed therein."
Reaching from the mundane to the supramundane, all dharmas are fully manifested in a single thought-moment, appearing exactly like Indra’s net.

Because they mutually negate one another, light is not darkness and darkness is not light. Because they mutually encompass one another, by raising a single instance of empty space, the ten thousand phenomena are complete;
and among earth, water, fire, and wind, by raising any single dharma, each is individually and completely contained. Why do they manifest together? At such a time, people—

All that is seen is said to be empty space, formless, vast, and unobstructed; therefore, it can universally contain all things. Material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), however, are solid and obstructive—how could they manifest simultaneously?
Thus, the World-Honored One cited the sun as an illustration. Furthermore, although the sun is a single entity, it appears according to the perceptions of those who behold it.
Two people see the sun differently, and when ten thousand or a million people see the sun, each sees it according to their own particular variation. Extending this reasoning broadly...

The people of the four continents all say that they see the sun directly facing them. Even within rivers, streams, the Huai, the Ji, the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the seas, and the canals and ditches, everyone sees a sun;
yet the sun is but a single wheel, though what each perceives differs. If one were to claim these are separate, it would be so.

In the sky there is but one sun; how much less could there be ten million? If it were necessarily not divided, yet that person sees its reflection in various places such as the east and west, in ditches and streams—what would you call this?
If one wishes to discern the reality by means of the conscious mind, even if one exhausted the supernatural powers of a Tathāgata, one would know nothing of its cause.
How can it be said that all are encompassed? It is empty and vast, containing all phenomena within it. Man...
It may be credible that the substance of form (*rūpa*) is solid and obstructive, yet it is difficult to believe that it can contain and encompass [other elements].

For instance, the substance of wood is solid and obstructive, yet it can fully contain the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): when drilled, it produces fire; when twisted, it flows with water; when shaken, it generates wind; and when burned, it becomes earth.
Even such a solid and obstructive form can still fully accommodate the great elements of water, fire, and wind; there is nothing that is not so. Whether they are mutually accommodated or not, each...

Manifesting simultaneously, they are all beyond the reach of thought or deliberation. When essence follows function, form and emptiness contend and supplant one another, and the myriad dharmas manifest together.
When function accords with essence, form and emptiness are equally extinguished, and the single path is serene and level.
Thus, the mind cannot conceive it, and speech cannot discuss it. Pūrṇa had no way to pose his question, and the World-Honored One likewise found no ground for a reply. Constantly...
Abiding in the true mind, one perceives this therein.
"I, by means of wondrous clarity—neither extinguished nor arising—unify with the Tathāgata-garbha... [omitted] ...thereby giving rise to the wondrous, enlightened nature of true thusness."
Ānanda, because the characteristics of form and emptiness contend with and supplant one another, while the Tathāgata-garbha manifests according to karma, there appear the phenomena of the world.
This was used to answer Pūrṇa’s question: "How could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Herein, non-arising and non-ceasing accord with the Tathāgata-garbha;
thus, the wondrous, enlightened nature of true suchness (tathatā) is manifested. This was used to answer [the question]: "When will this wondrous emptiness become bright enlightenment?"

Furthermore, the mountains, rivers, and great earth arise again. Because the Tathāgata has realized wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), with respect to all phenomena, there is neither arising nor non-arising.
Because there is no arising, there is only the luminosity of wondrous enlightenment; because there is no non-arising, it perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*.
Because of this perfect illumination, the essence is its function: the one becomes the infinite. The essence is its function: the infinite becomes the one.
The small manifests the large, as the eye encompasses the world; the large manifests the small, as Mount Sumeru contains a mustard seed.
Without moving, they pervade one another, free from mutual obstruction. That the body contains the ten voids means that each and every thing mutually accommodates the others.

That the dependent manifests within the fundamental, and the fundamental manifests within the dependent, all arises from the power of extinguishing dust and merging with awakening; it is not a forced assertion. Furthermore...

There is mutual concealment and mutual manifestation, mutual relinquishment and mutual sublation; they are mutually identical and mutually inclusive, accomplishing both self and others, as extensively elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
○ Yet, from the "Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind" (up to) "using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
When principle is fused with phenomena, all things are simultaneously "neither. When phenomena are fused with principle, all things are simultaneously "identical.

When both phenomenon and principle are clearly illumined, ordinary beings and sages appear distinct. When both phenomenon and principle are equally extinguished, how can there be birth or Buddhahood? Ānanda clung to delusion and was confused about the truth, giving rise to false joy and fear.
The World-Honored One spoke to him of the non-existence of self and other and the eternal abiding of the true mind, then personally questioned him.
The mind discriminates views, as well as the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.

[The Buddha] uses the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness, to demonstrate their essence, asserting that all of these are "neither this nor that. Fumuci did not understand how they arise in succession;

he asked, "How is it that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the four great elements suddenly arise, and how is it that they contain one another without obstruction? The World-Honored One replied:
All arise from the two kinds of delusive confusion—awakening and clarity—and thus there are three modes of continuity to demonstrate their characteristics;

that is to say, all things are simultaneously identical. If one awakens to the true mind, then the path of speech and thought is severed, the sphere of mental activity ceases, and there is a perfect, harmonious illumination.
One may then either abandon or establish [phenomena] as one pleases; this is what is meant by "leaving both identity and non-identity," being "identical yet not identical. Directly...
Entering the inconceivable realm of the Middle Way is not something known by those of the Two Vehicles.

As for what is called "using worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it was once said that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot know this; yet nowadays, those who engage in study and exposition [claim otherwise].
There is none that does not hit upon their illness.
○ For example, as in the case of the *qin*, *se*, *konghou*, and *pipa* [lutes]... (up to) "cherishing the Lesser Vehicle and being content with a small attainment.
The previous passage stated: "To employ worldly language to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is not so. Nevertheless, it should not be entirely discarded. Ordinary people—

Those who cling to existence are deluded regarding emptiness; those of the Two Vehicles destroy their clinging to existence by grasping at emptiness. Each attains only one extreme and is not called the Middle Way;
both are termed worldly discourse. If it is that which is spoken by the Tathāgata, it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither not existent nor not non-existent, and neither real nor false.
It is neither non-false nor false; neither spontaneous nor non-spontaneous; neither caused by conditions nor not caused by conditions.
It is revealed in this manner as the definitive meaning of the inconceivable Middle Way, through which one enters and realizes the Buddha Vehicle;

few do not proceed by this path. Therefore, it cannot be compared to worldly discourse. Why is this? Because Buddha-nature is inherently present. If it were not revealed in such a way, by what means could it be realized?

And thus one attains the Buddha-vehicle. It is like a lute or similar instrument: although it inherently possesses a wondrous sound, if there are no finger-movements [to play it], by what means could that sound be produced?
Thus we know that words must not be entirely discarded. That which is called "wondrous sound" is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings; it exists equally in both living beings and Buddhas.
Because the Buddha has mastered the method of fingering, he produces the wondrous sound; sentient beings cannot do so, and their efforts result only in disorder.
[The Master] snapped his fingers. "Thus, you should abandon worldly discourse and study the Middle Way. Do not cling to narrow views and give rise to complacency.
He exhorted and admonished them earnestly. "Such is the Buddha’s grace; how can it be repaid?"
Pūrṇa said: "I and the Tathāgata’s precious awakening—perfectly luminous, truly wondrous, and pure mind—are non-dual and complete.
[He continued] until: "This person’s mind is deranged; there is no other cause."
Pūrṇa first asked: "How is it that mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? He then asked: "Earth, water, fire, and wind cannot coexist.
Furthermore, regarding the seven elements, he noted they "manifest according to karma" and "accord with the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of what they know.
Fearing that the assembly present might not yet understand the reason for "manifesting according to karma," he raised this third question. The World-Honored One answered by means of...
The two kinds of deluded conditions—awakening and the clarity of awakening—give rise to the three types of continuity that constitute the world.

If one awakens to the fundamental mind, then all these are seen to be unreal. If it is as you have explained, then the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world are equally deluded conditions formed by ignorance;
yet prior to this state of delusion, they were never different from the Buddha’s original awakening. Sentient beings, for no apparent reason, suddenly...
Delusion. There are appearances of the world, yet it is not known whether the Buddhas also experience delusion and give rise to afflictions at times.
If the Buddha were not deluded, why would sentient beings suddenly become deluded? If sentient beings suddenly become deluded, why do the Buddhas not become deluded?

Thus, the World-Honored One cited the example of a deluded person losing their sense of direction; this does not mean that the directions have shifted, but rather that the deluded person is at fault themselves. The Knower is ever constant.

Awakening is non-delusion. If a deluded person attains enlightenment by means of a finger-pointing, they will never again fall into delusion. Yet, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra further maintains that delusion has causes and conditions;

therefore, he raises this question. His intention is to say: "If I and all sentient beings are identical to the Buddha’s original awakening, being equally perfect and without duality, then we know that we undergo the cycle of rebirth due to delusive ignorance and madness. However, we do not yet know what cause gives rise to this."
This is false. The World-Honored One cited the delusion of Yajñadatta regarding his head as a metaphor; how could there be any real cause for it?

It was solely due to madness that he came to love the head in the mirror and, reproaching himself for having no head, ran about in a frenzy. As for the head in the mirror, there are two aspects: namely, joy and fear.

The text appears to be incomplete. To see the Tathāgata’s mass of purple-gold light as supremely wondrous and peerless, and thereby to yearn for and follow the Buddha into tonsure, is like someone who, out of love for another's head and resentment at their own lack of a share, runs about in a frenzy.
Because he fell into a brothel and was coerced by Mātangī, he gave rise to panic and fear; this is like resenting another's head while envying one's own.
Yet they wish to flee and escape from it. Unaware that all this is merely their own mind, they pointlessly give rise to grasping and rejecting, and suddenly experience joy and fear;
these are all equally called "mad running. Ānanda questioned further and further, and the World-Honored One revealed the matter with subtle detail;

there was none who did not discern this head within the mirror. This applies even to the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve entrances, the eighteen realms, as well as the seven elements.
The entire circumference is the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; what is there that it does not encompass? Yet one deludedly gives rise to grasping and rejecting.
Thus we know that both hatred and love are merely the loss of the mind and running about in madness; how could they have a fixed cause?

Furthermore, the reason Pūrṇa was made to offer his own testimony was to ensure he would certainly understand the absence of cause. Therefore, Dongshan said: "An elderly woman who has lost her way encounters an ancient mirror."
A mind of resentment and aversion arose; he simply gave this head of affection back to him. Mazu said:
"Whatever forms you see are the seeing of the mind. The mind is not the mind by itself; it is through form that the mind is revealed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"To know all phenomena as the self-nature of the mind is to accomplish the body of wisdom, which does not depend on another for awakening. The preceding passage states: "If one can transform objects, then one is identical to Suchness."
Furthermore, it says: "From the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, all are objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind.
If one does not attain clear awakening, who is not wandering about in madness?"
The Buddha said: "Wondrous awakening is bright and perfect; fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous. (Up to: "How could the nature of delusion exist?
Wondrous awakening is bright and perfect; fundamentally perfect, bright, and wondrous. This refers to the perfection of the non-duality of essence and function. Because it is wondrous awakening.

It does not hinder one to follow conditions, for since the fundamental is perfect, how could it ever suffer any deficiency? Now, the false depends on the true for its existence, yet the true does not give rise to the false.
Because it does not arise, how can there be a cause for it? If there were a cause, how could it be called "false"? Although the false has no cause, it nonetheless arises based on delusion.
As it is said: "The falsity of clarity is not due to anything else; the fault lies in the clarity of awareness. Thus, that which is depended upon establishes the dependent.

Once that which is falsely conceived has been established, it gives rise to your false capacity [to perceive]; thus, the capacity also arises because of its object. Therefore, it is said that they are mutually dependent upon one another.

When a single delusion becomes the mind, one becomes resolutely confused, taking it to be within the physical body. One then distinguishes between self and other, and though kalpas as numerous as motes of dust pass, there is no turning back.
To thoroughly understand the cause of delusion: because of delusion, consciousness arises; yet this consciousness that deludes has no cause, and thus both arising and ceasing are unobtainable.

To thoroughly understand that which is unobtainable—is it not like a person who has awakened speaking of a dream? Delusive causes exist because of delusion; when one awakens and realizes this is delusion, both delusion and its falsity are non-existent.
How could the wondrous mind of original enlightenment have ever been lost? It is like the case of Yan Rudu, whose head was originally...

It is not lost; it is only through delusion and confusion that one says it is lost. One runs about in a state of frantic terror—how could it be that one merely regains one's head when the madness ceases?
At the very moment of that madness, how could the head have been lost? If one recognizes the error of the delusion, one will naturally repent of one's own folly.
"O, you need only not follow after the discrimination of the world (up to: 'what need is there for arduous toil or the cultivation and realization of subtle refinements')?
What is meant by the term 'madness'? It is precisely this discriminating mind.

If one does not discriminate, then all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds, of self and others, and all names and characteristics—whether great or small—are unreal, like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent."
There is. What is there to cultivate and realize? If this were so, then Ānanda’s various questions would all be manifestations of madness.
If you recognize this as madness, then the three causes and three conditions will not arise in your mindfulness. How could the supremely pure and wondrous mind be obtained from another?

As for the three causes: the emptiness and darkness constitute the cause of the world; craving constitutes the cause of sentient beings; and killing and stealing constitute the cause of karmic retribution.
All this is due to delusion and ignorance. If one realizes this delusion and ignorance, then such madness and confusion can no longer be found.
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within their own garment; only upon returning home does he realize that the divine pearl was not obtained from without.

The preceding metaphors have reached their conclusion; therefore, I exhort you not to follow discursive conceptualization. Thus, one knows that original enlightenment (*bodhi*) is inherently present and is not obtained from without.

Fearing that those who have not yet awakened might stubbornly insist that *bodhi* must necessarily be attained through cultivation, [the author] notes that while other sutras all state that realization is achieved through cultivation over kalpas, this [text] claims it does not rely on cultivation or realization—these being self-contradictory, it is truly difficult to inspire confidence. Therefore, he cites [the following] once more:
The "pearl in the garment" serves as the primary metaphor for this. For instance, Ānanda beheld the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and, filled with yearning, shaved his head to become a monk.

He further remarked, "I thought the Tathāgata would bestow samādhi upon me so that I need not labor at cultivation; only now do I realize that body and mind are fundamentally independent of one another.
If I do not practice, it is as if I had never heard [the Dharma]. This teaching seems to stand in direct opposition to what has been revealed here.
Contemplate the meaning through the text. Ānanda was filled with panic and pleaded earnestly; such were the initial expedients of the wondrous *śamatha* and so forth, leading up to this point.
Is this not like one who, lost to his own jewel within his garment, wanders in poverty seeking alms?

The World-Honored One’s successive elucidations—was this not the wise man pointing out the jewel? The previous passage stated that "resting is itself Bodhi"; this metaphor corresponds precisely to that.
"When one is deluded, the pearl has never diminished; it is only the deluded person who errs.
At that moment, Ānanda prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet amidst the great assembly, then rose and addressed the Buddha:
'World-Honored One, you have just spoken of the karmic retributions for killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct... [omitted] ...the principle of naturalness and causality is exhausted in this.'"
Previously, when Ānanda heard that there is neither cause nor condition, neither spontaneity nor combination, he seemed to have attained a point of entry;
thus, he spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha. Now, hearing that because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise, he again doubts whether cause and condition are correct.
If one relies on the present teaching, then the previous teaching is incorrect; if one relies on the previous teaching, then the present teaching is incorrect. Standing between these two...

This is difficult; therefore, this question is asked. The previous statement that it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor spontaneously formed was intended to clarify the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since the *tathāgatagarbha* is neither caused nor spontaneous, the present statement that "when causes are severed and conditions extinguished, this is Bodhi" follows from that.
This is precisely the meaning of "not being subject to causes and conditions," because Bodhi does not belong to causes and conditions.

Fearing that people might not understand this, he requests it again and further cites those such as Śāriputra who attained awakening upon hearing the meaning of causes and conditions. This is what is meant by saying that the cited analogies are not uniform.
Why is this? Regarding those such as Śāriputra who heard [the teaching on] causes and conditions, the verse says: "Phenomena arise from causes and conditions; phenomena..."
Arising and ceasing proceed from causes and conditions; arising and ceasing are themselves the causes and conditions. Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is neither arising nor ceasing.

Since it is said that "nature is neither arising nor ceasing," it is clear that it is not [produced by] causes and conditions. The Buddha said: "They speak of spontaneity (*svayambhū*); I speak of causes and conditions.

This refutation of spontaneity is not something known by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Thus, both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely established as provisional designations; they never possess any ultimate reality.
Since spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is not produced by causes and conditions, why did Ānanda, on the contrary, harbor doubts?

Because there are differences between spontaneity and causes and conditions, the World-Honored One further cited the causes and conditions of madness to provide clarification: madness is not spontaneous; it arises from a single moment of non-awakening.
One loses one's mind and wanders about in madness; therefore, causes and conditions are taught. When the madness ceases, there is naturally a nature of non-madness.

If this were so, then for one who is not mad, both causes and conditions and natural spontaneity would both become mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). It is like a person who falls ill and recovers by taking medicine: there is illness and there is recovery.
But for one who has no illness, there is neither illness nor recovery. Therefore it is said: "The principle of causes and conditions and natural spontaneity."
It ends here.
○ Regarding the passage from "Ānanda, the head of Yajñadatta was originally natural" to "the head was originally without delusion;
why did he run about in madness," the text is divided into three sections. The first section generally states that the head was originally natural, meaning it was neither "natural" nor "not natural."
To speak of "spontaneity" (zìrán) by means of a name is for the name itself not to be established spontaneously—just as the eye cannot see itself and the mind cannot know itself.
Since it is not spontaneous, what need is there to wait for causes and conditions? To run about in a frenzy out of fear for one's head is the next point:

if the head were spontaneous and yet one went mad because of causes and conditions, then the head should have already been lost. Since the head is not lost, why indulge in such frantic fear and calculations regarding causes and conditions?
...then he has fallen [into error]. Third, it is said: If madness were natural—if there were an inherently existing nature of madness—then everyone should be mad, for that could be called "natural.
If this nature of madness and fear were inherently possessed, then when one is mad and at other times not mad, where would that madness reside in the person who is not mad?
If only Yan-ruo were mad while the rest of the people were not, then madness would not [be inherent].

It is clear that the nature is spontaneously endowed with it. If this state of madness were necessarily produced by causes and conditions, then since the causal condition of each person looking into a mirror is the same, why is it that while all others remain sane, only Yan-ruo is mad?

Thus we know that neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity have anything to do with that original head. As the previous text says: "Deluded about oneself, one pursues external objects, taking objects to be..."
This concludes the single analogy of the frantic head, which serves to exhaust [all delusions].
Only when one awakens to the original head and recognizes that the consciousness was running wild—up to this point—is it called the Dharma free from frivolous proliferation (*aprapañca*).

Here, the initial passage is again cited as the conclusion. If one awakens to the fact that the head is fundamentally spontaneous (*svabhāva*), and that its fundamental spontaneity is such from the very beginning, then the conscious awareness of frantic wandering and the naturalness of causes and conditions are both considered frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). This refers to what was stated in the preceding text:

"Where there is only verbal expression, it is all frivolous conceptual proliferation. Just as when one cannot speak, one knows where to return, yet one gives rise again to false discrimination; because causes and conditions cease, there is bodhi.

As for "arising," this refers merely to arising and ceasing; it is not the attainment of Bodhi. When both arising and ceasing are exhausted and nothing can be grasped, it is called the Path of Effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*).
To fail to intuitively realize this and instead cling to the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is to fall back into arising and ceasing.

That which is without arising and ceasing is called spontaneous. As it was said at the beginning: "That which is fundamentally so of itself—there is no 'so-ness' that is not of itself. Therefore, [the text] cites the world...

"Harmony and combination. To explain this: "harmony and combination" refers to the meaning of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); "original suchness" (*bennian*) refers to the meaning of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

These are all what the world conceptualizes. If one awakens to the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*), which is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), then "original suchness" is not suchness, and "harmony and combination" is not combination.
Being free from both combination and suchness means that one distances oneself from both causes and conditions and spontaneity, yet it is also not a state of separation.

It is not a conjunction; when false conceptualization is thus dispelled, the true mind is present. Therefore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "One distances oneself from what is illusory, and one distances oneself from that distancing as well.
One distances oneself even from the distancing of illusory distancing. When there is nothing further to be distanced, all illusions are eliminated. This is precisely the meaning of this.
"Enlightenment and nirvana still lie far away... [only] increasing frivolous proliferation.
The Dharma-body possesses the virtue of realization; the Wisdom-body possesses the virtue of retribution; and Nirvana possesses the virtue of cessation. "Enlightenment" refers to the Wisdom-body.

It is the capacity to awaken to the state where both union and separation are transcended, and where both the transcendence of union and the transcendence of separation are non-existent. Thus one attains the path of effortlessness and realizes the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the Wisdom Body extensively cultivates the six perfections and enters all differentiated dharma-gates;

only then, with merit and wisdom perfected, does it become Vairocana. Nirvana involves severing afflictions until there are no further afflictions to be severed, at which point it is first termed the nature of great peace and bliss.
These two must be realized through cultivation over successive kalpas; therefore, they are said to be "remote. This is what is meant by: "Although the principle is..."
Sudden awakening receives the realization and simultaneously eliminates it; the phenomena must be gradually removed, for the causes are exhausted through a sequential process.
If one merely upholds the teachings of the Buddhas without practicing to achieve realization, it only increases frivolous discourse. Why is this?

For instance, Śāriputra, upon hearing a single verse, immediately achieved realization, severed his fetters, and forever transcended birth and death; whereas Ānanda, though fully possessing the Dharma-treasury, could only extend his words to pose questions.
As these views shift and turn into doubt, how vast is the difference between them—like heaven and abyss!
Although Ānanda was a manifestation of great spiritual power, he did so precisely for the sake of those like us who indulge in empty discourse yet gain nothing at all.
"Although you discourse on causes and conditions and spontaneity (up to the point of 'how can you still deceive yourself by remaining to watch and listen'), the text consists of three sections.
The first is that although one may realize the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*), Bodhi and Nirvana remain far distant."

One must practice and realize this; it cannot be anticipated through mere erudition. Next, I shall explain that one who is learned and possesses clear understanding will naturally be free from frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
If one does not practice and realize, then much learning is of no benefit; therefore, one cannot escape the calamity of the Mātanga woman.
If this extensive learning were sufficient for Bodhi, then why wait for the empowerment of my divine mantra before attaining liberation?
Thirdly, it encourages the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), which is superior to that mere learning; their distance is as vast as that between a day and an eon.

This secretly reveals the efficacy of the divine mantra as a causal condition for aiding the Path, with the primary intent being to initiate the practice of the Way. The Sūtra is divided into five sections. [End of] the Vision.

The demarcation of the Path concludes here; the rest need not be elaborated upon. Question: Since everything discussed in this single session is nothing other than the True Dharma, why stop at this point?
Answer: Regarding the divisions of the Path, one must simply select the "perfect penetration of the ear-organ" as the essential core of the teaching for this region.
However, the specific methods of praise employed within the gateway of the teaching are not fixed. Why is this? It is like the twenty-five types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

The realization of perfect penetration is, in truth, without superiority or inferiority. Yet, in order to enable Ānanda to achieve swift and easy accomplishment, how could it possibly encompass all types of capacities?
This is because capacities have their sharpness and dullness, and the underlying minds are not equal.

Thus, while this [method] is easy for Avalokiteśvara to enter, those twenty-four sages each chose what was most convenient for them among the eighteen realms; hence, Xiangyan attained enlightenment by striking a bamboo stalk, and Ling...
Yunmen saw the colors and enlightened his mind; Linji received the "painful staff"; Xuansha attained awakening upon injuring his toe; Guishan shifted the fire; and Dongshan beheld the water.
Even if a Tathāgata were to appear again in this world, he could not deny their enlightenment.

Thus, one knows that there is no single fixed path. In the section on "Aiding the Path," the divine mantras are extolled; if one can believe them immediately, one will certainly obtain secret empowerment. [The section on] "Realizing the Fruit" follows.
This is the realm of the sages and worthies; it cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings. As for the ascending progress of the various devas, it is likewise unknowable.

Even the retributions of the three miserable realms—how could I fully understand them? As for the fifty demonic hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), only a Buddha can investigate them exhaustively. From the lower stages up to the delusions of the ground, they remain obscure and unresolved;
thus, whether something is right or wrong, one must rely entirely upon the ancients. Only this single portion concerning the realization of the Way (*darśana-mārga*) may be studied.
One should exhaust one's own mind in this matter; therefore, I venture to present my humble views for the common benefit of all quarters.
Nevertheless, as the Sage’s intent is unfathomable, should there be any error in my interpretation, I humbly entreat my learned friends to grant me their repentance.
Question: If a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the worlds of the ten directions all vanish and perish.
Since our own teacher Śākyamuni, successive patriarchs have appeared one after another; are these not themselves those who have awakened to the truth and returned to the origin?
"Why does it emerge from the interval and return to its former state? Is there not a purpose for this?
He replied, "In the dreams you have previously experienced, were the mountains, rivers, and great earth the same as they are during the day?
He said, "Yes. [The Master continued,] "Suppose ten people were to share the same dream; would what each of the ten people saw be different? He said, "It would not be different. Suppose...
"When one person awakens, has the world seen by that one person already perished? "It has already perished.
"Since it has already perished, have the worlds seen by the other nine people who have not yet awakened also perished together with it? "No, they have not."
Those nine people have not yet awakened; how could they share in the same dissolution? If this is so, why do you doubt that the worlds of the sages do not dissolve?
When one person awakens, the world of that one person has already dissolved. When ten people awaken together, the worlds of those ten people perish.
What is there that is impossible? For when one person awakens, it is as if the other nine have also awakened.
This is like being in a dream; one cannot doubt that one person is awake simply because nine others are dreaming. Therefore it is said:

"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, together with the great Bodhisattvas and those who dwell in their own samādhis, see these mountains, rivers, and the great earth as being like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
Moreover, our current aggregation of the four great elements and six sense organs is like a dream."
To speak of waking discourse to one who is dreaming—is that possible?

He asked: "In what you have discussed for this session, you say that one falls into fear when encountering lustful things, and feels delight upon seeing the marks of form; yet, one seeks these in vain and cannot obtain them."
All are termed false conceptions; they are perfectly equal and without distinction. If this were so, one need not cultivate the Noble Path, nor need one sever lust and killing.
Yet now it is said that for sentient beings, craving is the root, and for the seeds of karma, lust and killing are the root.
Because these three causes are severed, the three conditions do not arise. The madness within the mind naturally subsides; this subsiding is itself Bodhi. If this were so—
Lust and killing must certainly be severed; only then can one achieve the Buddha-way. If the former explanation were correct, it would constitute a denial of reality (nāstika-vāda);
if the latter explanation were correct, it would constitute a false conceptualization (vikalpa). How, then, may these be distinguished?
The answer is: Revealing the principle supports the phenomenon, each having its own fundamental purpose.

Previously, because Ānanda did not understand the true mind and instead recognized those external objects, giving rise to false grasping and rejecting, he was led to select and grasp the true mind until it was found to be non-existent.
Since the mind does not exist, what is there to grasp or reject? Subsequently, because Ānanda gave rise to the fear of "no-mind," he was again led to select his vision. Its...

In the interim, one perceives that the nature of seeing does not return; this seeing is neither distant nor near, neither large nor small, neither expanding nor contracting, neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously, and even ultimately, seeing is not a combination of factors.
Only then does one know that the true nature is immovable, while the deluded mind merely comes and goes of its own accord, like a phantom or a dream.
Even if one clings to the notion that there is a fixed, unmoving nature of seeing, it is still called the deluded mind. Directly...
Even when one reaches the point of seeing, that very act of seeing is already transcended, for such seeing cannot be grasped; this alone is true seeing.

Extending this principle broadly, one finds that the five aggregates, six sense bases, twelve spheres, and eighteen elements—the seven great elements being all-pervasive and manifesting in accordance with their nature—are beyond the categories of "is" and "is not.
Within this state, how could there be the "rightness" of practicing the Way or the "wrongness" of lust and killing? Therefore, in principle, one must achieve sudden awakening.
Awakening and the elimination [of delusion] occur simultaneously. If one insists on making choices or exclusions within this state, it is not true suchness (tathatā);

it is like grasping at empty space, which only increases one's own toil. All verbal expressions are devoid of substantial meaning. If one understands how to manifest according to the nature (dharmatā), then the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (sāgaramudrā-samādhi) will radiate light;
yet if one applies even a slight degree of conscious mentation (manovijñāna), then afflictions (kleśa) will first arise. Such is the nature of reality; these are not mere forced words. Within this...
Supportive matters must be severed and eliminated. If they are not severed, one will merely produce deluded understandings and ultimately gain no benefit.

Therefore, the seeds of karma take lust and killing as their root; among the three gradual stages, the severing of lust is primary. To cultivate and realize the holy positions, one must first dry up the craving for desire.
Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm, advancement is distinguished solely by the degree of lightness or heaviness of desire. As for the Brahma heavens...
Through the clear awakening of the mind regarding desire, one does not transgress the dust of sensual passion; thus the body becomes a companion to the Brahmā realm.

Regarding the ten causes and six intersections, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* discusses lust extensively as the demonic karma of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra-karman*). It is invariably said that through the continuous transmission of lustful acts, one falls into the path of demons.

If lust is thus [a cause of bondage], so too are killing and stealing. Such is the difference between being attached to desire and severing desire. How could one attain liberation without severing them?

Therefore it is said: "Affairs are gradually eliminated through expedient means, and their causes are exhausted in successive order. The scriptural text addresses both phenomena and principle with repeated and earnest intent;
one must not fail to discern this. What you have asked is indeed a vital question.
